entries.text: Do you think there should be many natural places in cities?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think cities really need plenty of natural places, like parks or green spaces.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我觉得城市非常需要大量的自然场所，比如公园或绿地。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: City life is often filled with concrete, traffic, and noise, so having accessible green areas gives residents a place to escape that intensity without having to leave the city entirely.
ideaNotes.textZh: 城市生活常常充斥着水泥建筑、交通和噪音，所以有可以方便到达的绿色区域，能让居民有个地方摆脱这种压迫感，而不必完全离开城市。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a city park allows office workers to take a short break outdoors during lunch, or families to enjoy a weekend picnic without a long drive out of town.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，城市公园能让上班族在午休时到户外短暂休息一下，也能让家庭在周末野餐而不用开车跑很远。

ideaNotes.text: Beyond mental wellbeing, green spaces also help with practical things like air quality and reducing urban heat.

entries.text: Do Chinese people like to visit others’ homes?

ideaNotes.text: Visiting someone's home in Chinese culture is seen as a sign of closeness and respect — it's a way of saying you care about that person and want to spend real time with them rather than just meeting somewhere outside.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在中国文化中，拜访某人的家被视为亲密和尊重的象征，这是一种表达你关心那个人并想与他们真正共度时光而不仅仅是在外面见面的方式。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, during Chinese New Year it's almost like a tradition for families to go from house to house, bringing gifts, eating together, and catching up — some families visit five or six different homes over just a few days.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，在春节期间，家人们几乎有一种从一家到另一家拜访的传统，带着礼物、一起吃饭、叙旧，一些家庭在短短几天内就拜访了五六个不同的家庭。

entries.text: What do Chinese people do when they visit others?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most common things are sharing a meal, chatting, and bringing some kind of gift — these three things pretty much sum up a typical Chinese home visit.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为最常见的事情是共享一顿饭、聊天和带一些礼物，这三件事几乎概括了典型的中国家庭拜访。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Food is really central to Chinese culture, so whenever someone visits, the host almost always cooks a big spread and everyone sits around the table together. And showing up empty-handed is generally considered quite rude, so people usually bring things like fruit, snacks, or something local.
ideaNotes.textZh: 食物在中国文化中真的非常重要，所以每当有人拜访时，主人几乎总是做一大桌菜，大家围坐在一起。而且空手而来通常被认为相当失礼，所以人们通常带水果、零食或当地特产。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, whenever my relatives come over, my mum starts cooking for hours beforehand and the table ends up completely covered in dishes — it's always way more food than anyone could possibly eat, but that's just how Chinese hospitality works.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，每当我的亲戚来访时，我妈妈提前几个小时就开始做饭，桌子最终完全摆满了菜，总是比任何人可能吃得完的多得多，但这就是中国待客之道。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, a lot of the time people just sit around and talk for hours — catching up on family news, discussing life, maybe watching TV together — it's very relaxed and informal, nothing like a planned event. 另外，很多时候人们只是围坐在一起聊上几个小时，叙叙家常、聊聊生活，也许一起看电视，非常轻松随意，完全不像一个计划好的活动。

entries.text: What kind of place do people in your country like to live in?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think most people in China want to live somewhere that is convenient, safe, and close to good schools and transport.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为中国大多数人想住在方便、安全、靠近好学校和交通的地方。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Basically, being close to subway stations, supermarkets, hospitals, and schools is what most families prioritise when choosing where to live — people want everything within easy reach so daily life doesn't become a hassle.
ideaNotes.textZh: 基本上，靠近地铁站、超市、医院和学校是大多数家庭选择住所时优先考虑的，人们希望一切都触手可及，这样日常生活就不会变得麻烦。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, when my family was looking for a new apartment, the first thing my parents checked was whether it was in a good school district and how many minutes it was from the nearest subway — the actual size of the apartment came second.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，当我家在找新公寓时，我父母首先查看的是它是否在好的学区内，以及距离最近的地铁有多少分钟，公寓的实际大小反而是其次的。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 Still, a lot of people also dream of living somewhere with more greenery and open space — somewhere quieter where kids can play outside and you don't feel so boxed in all the time. 不过，很多人也梦想住在有更多绿化和开放空间的地方，一个更安静的地方，孩子可以在外面玩耍，你不会总是感到被困住。

entries.text: What's the difference between homes in cities and those in the countryside?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest difference is size and cost — city homes are usually much smaller and more expensive, while countryside homes tend to be larger and more affordable.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为最大的区别是大小和价格，城市住房通常更小更贵，而农村住房往往更大更实惠。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: In cities, most people live in apartments stacked on top of each other with very little outdoor space, and even a small flat can cost a fortune. But in the countryside, families often have their own standalone house with a yard or garden, and the whole feel is just much more open and relaxed.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在城市，大多数人住在层层叠叠的公寓里，几乎没有户外空间，即使是一个小公寓也可能价格不菲。但在农村，家庭通常有自己的独立房屋，带院子或花园，整体感觉就更加开阔和轻松。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, my grandparents' house in the countryside has a big courtyard, several bedrooms, and even a small vegetable patch, which would be completely impossible to have in the city for the same price — you'd probably just get a single tiny room.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我祖父母在农村的房子有一个大院子、几个卧室，甚至还有一小块菜地，这在城市里以同样的价格是完全不可能的，你可能只能得到一个小单间。• 转折【可选】 But then again, city homes make up for it with location and convenience — everything is nearby and you have access to so much more in terms of work, entertainment, and services, which countryside homes simply can't offer. 但反过来说，城市住房以位置和便利性弥补了这一点，一切都近在咫尺，在工作、娱乐和服务方面你能接触到的更多，而这些是农村住房根本无法提供的。

entries.text: Can't offerWhat kind of gifts do people usually bring when they visit others?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think in China, people tend to bring practical and thoughtful gifts rather than anything too extravagant — the most common ones are food, fruit, and drinks.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为在中国，人们倾向于带实用且有心意的礼物，而不是太奢华的东西，最常见的是食物、水果和饮料。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: The idea is that a gift should feel generous but not over the top — something the host can actually use or enjoy rather than just putting on a shelf. Things like fruit baskets, pastries, nice tea, or health supplements are really popular because they show you care without making things awkward. For closer relationships or more formal visits, people might bring something more personal or expensive, like a bottle of nice wine or a branded item.
ideaNotes.textZh: 送礼的理念是礼物应该感觉慷慨但不过分，是主人实际上可以使用或享用的东西，而不只是放在架子上的东西。像水果篮、糕点、好茶或保健品这样的东西非常受欢迎，因为它们表达了你的关心而不会让事情变得尴尬。对于更亲密的关系或更正式的拜访，人们可能会带更个人化或昂贵的东西，比如一瓶好酒或一件品牌商品。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, whenever my family visits relatives, my mum always picks up some fruit or traditional pastries on the way — she says showing up empty-handed just feels disrespectful, and the gift doesn't need to be expensive, it just needs to show that you put in some thought.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，每当我家拜访亲戚时，我妈妈总是在路上买一些水果或传统糕点，她说空手而来感觉就是不尊重，礼物不需要昂贵，只需要表明你用心思考过。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, during festivals like Chinese New Year or Mid-Autumn Festival, gift-giving becomes much more elaborate — people bring things like mooncakes, hampers, or specialty food that are specifically tied to the occasion, which adds an extra layer of meaning. 另外，在春节或中秋节等节日期间，送礼变得更加讲究，人们带来月饼、礼篮或特色食品，这些专门与场合相关联，增添了额外的意义。

entries.text: How often do you visit your relatives or friends?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Honestly, I visit friends quite regularly but relatives a lot less — most of my family gatherings happen around festivals and holidays rather than throughout the year.
ideaNotes.textZh: 说实话，我相当定期地拜访朋友，但拜访亲戚的频率少很多，大多数家庭聚会发生在节日和假期前后，而不是全年都有。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: With friends, it's much easier to just make casual plans — grab food, hang out, or do something spontaneous without needing a big occasion. But visiting relatives usually involves more planning and effort, especially if they live far away, so it tends to only happen a few times a year when there's a natural reason to get together.
ideaNotes.textZh: 和朋友在一起，随意制定计划容易得多，吃饭、闲逛，或者自发地做些什么，不需要什么大场合。但拜访亲戚通常需要更多计划和努力，尤其是如果他们住得很远，所以往往一年只发生几次，当有自然的理由聚在一起时。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I see my close friends at least once or twice a week, but I only really see my extended family during Chinese New Year or Golden Week — and even then it's more of a big family gathering than a proper one-on-one visit.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我至少每周一两次见亲密朋友，但我只在春节或黄金周期间才真正见到大家庭成员，即使那时也更多是大型家庭聚会，而不是真正的一对一拜访。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think video calls have replaced a lot of in-person visits these days — especially for relatives who live far away, a quick call feels like enough to stay connected without the effort of travelling, which is convenient but also a little sad in a way. 另外，我认为视频通话这些天已经取代了很多当面拜访，尤其是对于住得很远的亲戚，一个简短的通话感觉足以保持联系，而不需要旅行的努力，这很方便但在某种程度上也有点遗憾。

entries.text: Describe a pubilc building you enjoy visiting(e.g. a library, a shopping mall,etc)

paragraphs: The building I'd like to talk about is a shopping mall, not far from where I live. It's located in the city centre, in one of the most bustling commercial areas in the city — always packed with people no matter what time of day.
So I've known about it for a long time. From the outside, the whole building is covered in glass, looking really modern and sleek during the day.

And at night it gets even more impressive — the exterior has these LED light displays showing all kinds of dynamic patterns. Unlike a lot of other buildings that just plaster advertisements all over their walls, this one feels more like an art installation.
Every time I walk past at night, I always end up just standing there staring at it. Inside, it's basically a one-stop destination — shopping, dining, entertainment, all under one roof.
Every floor is packed with all kinds of stores — clothes, food, cinemas, bookshops — there's something for everyone. It's the kind of place you walk in and hours just disappear.
My favourite part is the top floor — there's an observation deck, a restaurant, and a huge Ferris wheel. You can sit there with a coffee, watch the sunset, and look out over the whole city.
It's really romantic and relaxing. I go there quite often with friends — sometimes to shop, sometimes just to grab food, walk around and chat.

And even on days when I'm not feeling great, just wandering around there for a bit always seems to lift my mood. Overall, this mall is so much more than just a place to shop — it's somewhere you go to unwind and just enjoy yourself.
paragraphsZh: 我想说的这栋建筑是一个购物中心，离我家不远。 它就位于市中心，是城里最繁华的商圈之一——不管什么时候去都人满为患。
所以我很早就知道这个地方了。 从外观来看，整栋建筑都覆盖着玻璃，白天看起来非常现代、非常简洁。
到了晚上就更加impressive了——外层有各种动态图案的LED灯光。 不像很多其他建筑把墙面全部用来打广告，这栋楼的灯光更像是一个艺术装置。
每次晚上路过，我总是忍不住就站在那里盯着看。 里面基本上是一个一站式目的地——购物、餐饮、娱乐，什么都有。
每一层都有各种各样的店铺——衣服、美食、电影院、书店——总有适合你的东西。 就是那种一走进去，时间就消失了的地方。
我最喜欢的是顶楼——那里有一个观景台、一家餐厅，还有一个很大的摩天轮。 你可以坐在那里喝着咖啡，看日落，俯瞰整个城市。
真的非常浪漫、非常放松。 我经常和朋友一起去——有时候去购物，有时候就是去吃东西、逛逛、聊天。
就算是心情不太好的时候，在里面随便逛一逛，心情也总是会好起来。 总体来说，这个购物中心不只是一个购物的地方——它是一个让你放松、好好享受自己的地方。

entries.text: Do you think all old buildings should be demolished ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: No, I don't think all old buildings should be demolished.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不，我不认为所有老建筑都应该被拆除。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Some old buildings hold significant historical or cultural value, so tearing them down means permanently losing a piece of a city's identity that can never be rebuilt the same way.
ideaNotes.textZh: 有些老建筑承载着重要的历史或文化价值，拆掉它们意味着永久失去一座城市身份的一部分，而这是永远无法以同样方式重建的。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a centuries-old temple or traditional courtyard house tells a story about the past that a modern building simply can't replicate.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一座有几百年历史的寺庙或传统四合院，讲述着关于过去的故事，这是现代建筑根本无法复制的。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, buildings that are structurally unsafe or have no real historical significance probably should be replaced for practical reasons.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，那些结构不安全、或者没有真正历史意义的建筑，出于实际考虑或许应该被拆除重建。

paragraphs: No, I don't think all old buildings should be demolished.
Some old buildings hold significant historical or cultural value, so tearing them down means permanently losing a piece of a city's identity that can never be rebuilt the same way.
For instance, a centuries-old temple or traditional courtyard house tells a story about the past that a modern building simply can't replicate.
That said, buildings that are structurally unsafe or have no real historical significance probably should be replaced for practical reasons.
paragraphsZh: 不，我不认为所有老建筑都应该被拆除。
有些老建筑承载着重要的历史或文化价值，拆掉它们意味着永久失去一座城市身份的一部分，而这是永远无法以同样方式重建的。
比如，一座有几百年历史的寺庙或传统四合院，讲述着关于过去的故事，这是现代建筑根本无法复制的。
不过，那些结构不安全、或者没有真正历史意义的建筑，出于实际考虑或许应该被拆除重建。

entries.text: Do you think old buildings are valuable ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think old buildings are genuinely valuable, beyond just their appearance.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为老建筑除了外观之外，确实具有真正的价值。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: These buildings serve as living evidence of how people lived and built things in the past, offering insight that books or photos alone can't fully capture.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这些建筑是过去人们生活方式和建造方式的活生生的见证，能提供书本或照片本身无法完全呈现的洞察。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, walking through an old city wall or ancient street lets people physically experience history in a way that reading about it in a textbook never could.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，走过一段古老的城墙或古代街道，能让人以一种读教科书永远无法实现的方式，亲身体验历史。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: Beyond cultural value, old buildings also attract tourism, which can bring real economic benefits to a city.
ideaNotes.textZh: 除了文化价值之外，老建筑也能吸引旅游业，为一座城市带来实际的经济利益。

entries.text: Are there many tall buildings in your country?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, absolutely — China has some of the tallest and most numerous skyscrapers in the world, and you see them everywhere especially in the bigger cities.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，绝对是，中国拥有世界上一些最高、数量最多的摩天大楼，尤其在大城市随处可见。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: China has been developing incredibly fast over the past few decades, and building upwards is just the most practical way to fit millions of people into a limited amount of land. Almost every major city now has a skyline full of skyscrapers — not just for offices but also for residential buildings, hotels, and shopping centres.
ideaNotes.textZh: 中国在过去几十年发展极为迅速，向上建造只是将数百万人容纳在有限土地上最实际的方式。几乎每个主要城市现在都有满是摩天大楼的天际线，不只是办公室，还有住宅楼、酒店和购物中心。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, cities like Shanghai and Shenzhen have skylines that honestly look like something out of a science fiction movie — buildings like the Shanghai Tower are genuinely among the tallest in the world, and new ones are still being built all the time.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，像上海和深圳这样的城市有的天际线说实话看起来像科幻电影里的场景，像上海中心大厦这样的建筑真的是世界上最高的建筑之一，而且新的建筑还在不断建造中。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, it's not just the major cities — even smaller second and third tier cities across China have seen huge amounts of construction over the past twenty years, so tall residential blocks have become a completely normal part of everyday life for most Chinese people. 另外，不只是主要城市，中国各地甚至较小的二三线城市在过去二十年里也经历了大量建设，所以高层住宅楼已经成为大多数中国人日常生活中完全正常的一部分。

entries.text: What are the differences between those tall buildings in your country?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest differences are in their purpose and appearance — some are sleek modern office towers, some are plain residential blocks, and some are iconic landmarks that are meant to represent the city.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为最大的区别在于它们的用途和外观，有些是光滑现代的办公楼，有些是普通住宅楼，有些是旨在代表城市的标志性地标。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: In city centres you tend to see glass and steel towers that house big companies and luxury hotels — they're designed to look impressive and modern. But in residential areas, most tall buildings are much more plain and practical — they're just there to house as many people as possible without much thought about how they look. The difference in quality and design between the two is really quite noticeable.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在市中心你往往能看到容纳大公司和豪华酒店的玻璃和钢铁塔楼，它们被设计成看起来令人印象深刻和现代。但在住宅区，大多数高楼更加普通和实用，它们只是为了尽可能多地容纳人，不太考虑外观。两者在质量和设计上的差异真的非常明显。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, in the financial district of Shanghai you have these stunning buildings with incredible lighting and unique shapes, but just a few stops away on the subway you'll find rows of identical grey residential towers that all look exactly the same — it's quite a contrast.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，在上海金融区你有这些有着令人难以置信灯光和独特形状的惊人建筑，但在地铁上几站之外你会发现一排排一模一样的灰色住宅楼，看起来完全相同，这形成了相当大的对比。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, there are big differences between cities too — buildings in older cities like Beijing tend to have more restrictions on height to preserve the historical feel, while cities like Shenzhen that were built more recently have gone all out with futuristic and bold designs. 另外，城市之间也有很大差异，像北京这样的老城市建筑往往在高度上有更多限制以保留历史感，而像深圳这样建造较晚的城市则全力以赴地采用未来主义和大胆的设计。

entries.text: Why are different places laid out and designed differently?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think places look and feel different mainly because of their history, culture, and practical needs — no two cities or neighbourhoods have developed in exactly the same way.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为地方看起来和感觉不同主要是因为它们的历史、文化和实际需求，没有两个城市或社区以完全相同的方式发展。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Older cities were often built around things like rivers, trade routes, or historical centres, so their layout follows those original patterns even today. Newer areas are usually designed more efficiently and on a grid because planners had a blank slate and could think about things like traffic flow, population density, and modern infrastructure from the start. Climate and geography also play a big role — a city in a hot country will be designed very differently from one in a cold one.
ideaNotes.textZh: 老城市通常是围绕河流、贸易路线或历史中心建造的，所以即使在今天，它们的布局仍然遵循那些原始模式。新区域通常设计得更加高效并采用网格式，因为规划者有一张白纸，可以从一开始就考虑交通流量、人口密度和现代基础设施。气候和地理也起着很大的作用，在炎热国家的城市与在寒冷国家的城市设计会非常不同。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, you can really feel the difference walking around old Shanghai versus Pudong — the old parts have narrow winding streets and traditional architecture, while Pudong was basically built from scratch in the last thirty years and has wide roads, huge towers, and everything neatly planned out in advance.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，你真的可以在行走于老上海和浦东时感受到差异，老区有狭窄蜿蜒的街道和传统建筑，而浦东基本上是在过去三十年从头开始建造的，有宽阔的道路、巨大的塔楼，一切都提前有序规划。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸

paragraphs: I think places look and feel different mainly because of their history, culture, and practical needs — no two cities or neighbourhoods have developed in exactly the same way.

Older cities were often built around things like rivers, trade routes, or historical centres, so their layout follows those original patterns even today. Newer areas are usually designed more efficiently and on a grid because planners had a blank slate and could think about things like traffic flow, population density, and modern infrastructure from the start. Climate and geography also play a big role — a city in a hot country will be designed very differently from one in a cold one.

For instance, you can really feel the difference walking around old Shanghai versus Pudong — the old parts have narrow winding streets and traditional architecture, while Pudong was basically built from scratch in the last thirty years and has wide roads, huge towers, and everything neatly planned out in advance.

entries.text: What are the advantages of living in tall buildings?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest advantages of living in a tall building are the views, the location, and the convenience — you get things that you simply can't get living in a low-rise house.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为住在高楼里最大的好处是视野、位置和便利性，你能得到住在低层房屋里根本无法得到的东西。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Living high up means you're away from street noise and pollution, you get much more natural light and fresh air, and the view is obviously incredible. On top of that, tall buildings in cities are usually in really central locations close to transport, shops, and work, so daily life is just much more convenient and time-saving.
ideaNotes.textZh: 住在高处意味着你远离街道噪音和污染，你得到更多自然光和新鲜空气，视野显然也很棒。此外，城市里的高楼通常位于非常中心的位置，靠近交通、商店和工作地点，所以日常生活更加便利和节省时间。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a friend of mine lives on the thirty-second floor of an apartment building and her view of the city at night is absolutely stunning — she always says it makes coming home feel like something special, even after a long and tiring day.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我的一个朋友住在公寓楼的三十二层，她的城市夜景绝对令人惊叹，她总是说这让回家感觉很特别，即使在漫长而疲惫的一天之后。• 转折【可选】 But then again, living very high up does have its downsides — if the lift breaks down you're in trouble, and some people find it feels quite isolated and disconnected from street life and the community around them. 但反过来说，住在很高的地方确实有其缺点，如果电梯坏了你就麻烦了，一些人发现感觉与街道生活和周围社区相当孤立和脱节。

entries.text: Why do some people like to remodel and decorate their homes themselves?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people like decorating their own homes because it gives them a chance to express who they are and create a space that feels truly theirs rather than just generic and standard.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们喜欢自己装饰家，因为它给了他们一个表达自己是谁的机会，创造一个感觉真正属于自己而不只是普通和标准的空间。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When someone else designs your space, it might look fine but it won't really reflect your personality or taste. Doing it yourself means every detail — the colours, the furniture, the decorations — is a personal choice that makes the home feel more comfortable and meaningful to live in. And honestly, there's also a real sense of pride and satisfaction when you look at something and think "I did that".
ideaNotes.textZh: 当别人设计你的空间时，它可能看起来不错，但不会真正反映你的个性或品味。自己做意味着每个细节，颜色、家具、装饰，都是个人选择，使家感觉更加舒适和有意义。说实话，当你看着某样东西想"我做了那个"时，也有真正的自豪感和满足感。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I know someone who spent months painting feature walls, putting up shelves, and choosing every piece of furniture herself, and her apartment looks completely unique — nothing like the standard show flat. She always says the process was just as enjoyable as the end result.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识一个人花了几个月自己粉刷特色墙、安装搁板、挑选每件家具，她的公寓看起来完全独特，与标准样板房完全不同。她总是说这个过程和最终结果一样令人愉快。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, doing it yourself is usually much cheaper than hiring someone — you save a lot of money and at the same time learn new practical skills along the way, which makes it even more rewarding. 另外，自己做通常便宜得多，你节省了很多钱，同时也在这个过程中学到了新的实用技能，这使它更加有成就感。

entries.text: What kind of interior design style do most people like?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most popular interior design style among people in China right now is minimalist and modern — clean lines, neutral colours, and a generally uncluttered and calm feel.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为目前中国人中最受欢迎的室内设计风格是简约和现代，干净的线条、中性色调，整体整洁平静的感觉。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: I think people are drawn to this style because life is already so busy and noisy that when they come home they want their space to feel calm and easy to live in — not overwhelming. A simple, tidy space with good lighting and clean furniture just feels really comfortable and restful after a long day. Japanese-influenced styles like Muji or wabi-sabi have also become really popular for the same reason.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们被这种风格吸引是因为生活已经如此忙碌和嘈杂，当他们回家时，他们希望空间感觉平静且容易生活，而不是压迫感。有良好照明和干净家具的简单整洁空间在漫长一天之后感觉非常舒适和休闲。受日本影响的风格如无印良品或侘寂也因同样的原因变得非常流行。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, if you look at what most young people post about their apartments on Xiaohongshu, almost everything is light wood, white walls, simple furniture, and lots of plants — it's a very specific aesthetic that has become almost the default style for anyone doing up a new flat.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，如果你看看大多数年轻人在小红书上发布的公寓，几乎一切都是浅木色、白墙、简单家具和很多植物，这是一种非常特定的美学，已经成为任何人装修新公寓的几乎默认风格。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 That said, some people do still prefer a warmer and more traditional Chinese style — dark wood, rich colours, and decorative elements that feel more rooted in culture and heritage — especially among older generations who find the minimalist look a bit too cold and empty. 话虽如此，有些人确实仍然更喜欢更温暖、更传统中式风格，深色木材、浓郁色彩和感觉更加植根于文化和传承的装饰元素，尤其是在觉得简约风格有点太冷和空的老一辈中。

entries.text: Describe an activity you do regularly that you think is a waste of time

paragraphs: An activity I do regularly that I think is a real waste of time is watching short dramas.
Short dramas are basically mini TV shows — each episode is just a few minutes, but the storylines are super addictive and full of plot twists.
So once I started watching one episode, I just couldn't stop — I'd watch during meals, on the subway, before bed, sometimes until two or three in the morning.
It wasn't until one day I tried to watch a long video that I realised how serious it was — I couldn't sit through it anymore, let alone read a book.
Short dramas weren't just wasting my time — they were slowly destroying my attention span.
I tried deleting the app, but within a few days I'd always download it again — this cycle went on and on, and it really bothered me.
Then one day I came across the Pomodoro Technique online — the idea is basically: focus for 20 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, and after every four rounds, take a longer break.
I also downloaded an app called Pomodoro To-Do that locks your phone during focus time and sends you a reminder when the time is up.
It was really hard at first — I kept getting distracted and wanting to check my phone.
But I stuck with it every day, and slowly it got easier — eventually I could get through four Pomodoros in a row.
Now I've gotten really good at using this method — compared to those days when I was hooked on short dramas, I've saved so much time and actually managed to get so much more done.
I finally feel like I'm back in control of my life.
paragraphsZh: 我经常做但觉得很浪费时间的一件事，就是刷短剧。
我还下载了一个叫番茄ToDo的app，专注期间会锁定手机，时间到了会提醒你。
一开始真的很难坚持——总是容易分心，总想拿起手机。
但我每天都坚持，慢慢地就越来越容易了——最终能一口气完成四个番茄钟。
现在我已经很熟练地使用这个方法了——和之前沉迷短剧的日子相比，我节省了大量时间，完成了更多事情。
我终于感觉自己重新掌控了自己的生活。

entries.text: Why do some people refuse to abide by rules?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think some people refuse to follow rules because they feel rules limit their freedom to do things their own way.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得有些人拒绝遵守规则，是因为他们觉得规则限制了他们的自由，让他们没法按自己的方式做事。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When rules feel too strict or don't seem to make sense to a person, they start seeing them as an obstacle rather than something helpful, and that mindset makes them want to push back instead of comply.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当规则让人觉得太死板，或者不太合理时，他们就会开始把规则看作阻碍，而不是有帮助的东西，这种心态会让他们想要反抗而不是遵守。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, an employee who thinks a strict dress code doesn't make sense for their remote job might simply choose to wear whatever they want, feeling the rule doesn't fit their situation.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一个觉得严格的着装规定对自己的远程工作没有意义的员工，可能会直接选择想穿什么就穿什么，觉得这条规则不适合自己的情况。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: On the other hand, some people break rules not because they disagree with them, but simply because they think no one is watching, so there's little chance of facing any real consequences.
ideaNotes.textZh: 另一方面，有些人违反规则并不是因为不认同规则本身，而只是觉得没人在看，觉得不太可能面临真正的后果。

entries.text: What kinds of things make people feel pressured?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people usually feel pressured by things like tight deadlines and high expectations from others.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得人们通常会因为紧迫的截止日期和别人的高期望而感到有压力。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Pressure tends to build when there's a big gap between what someone needs to accomplish and how much time or resources they actually have to do it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当一个人需要完成的事和他们实际拥有的时间或资源之间存在很大差距时，压力就容易积累起来。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a student with three exams in the same week might feel completely overwhelmed, knowing there's simply not enough time to prepare properly for all of them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一个同一周有三场考试的学生可能会感到完全不堪重负，因为他知道根本没有足够的时间为每一场都做好充分准备。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: Interestingly, pressure from oneself — like wanting to be perfect — can actually feel even heavier than pressure coming from other people.
ideaNotes.textZh: 有意思的是，来自自己内心的压力——比如想要做到完美——有时反而比来自别人的压力感觉更重。

entries.text: Will you continue doing something when you are aware that it’s a waste of time?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Honestly, yes, I think I'd probably keep doing it anyway, even knowing it's a waste of time.
ideaNotes.textZh: 说实话，会，我觉得即使知道在浪费时间，我可能还是会继续做下去。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Stopping something requires conscious effort, but continuing doesn't, so when I'm already in the middle of an activity, it's easier to just keep going than to actually break the pattern.
ideaNotes.textZh: 停下一件事需要主动的意志力，而继续做则不需要，所以当我已经处在一件事当中时，继续做往往比真正打破这个惯性更容易。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, if I'm halfway through scrolling on my phone and realize I've wasted 20 minutes, I often just keep scrolling instead of putting it down right away.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，如果我刷手机刷到一半，突然意识到已经浪费了20分钟，我常常还是会继续刷下去，而不是立刻放下手机。

ideaNotes.text: That said, if the activity is causing a real problem, like making me late for something important, that usually gives me enough of a push to actually stop.

entries.text: How do you balance life and work?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the key to balancing life and work is setting clear boundaries between the two.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得平衡生活和工作的关键在于给两者设定清晰的界限。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Without a clear line, work tends to spill over into personal time, since it's easy to keep checking messages or thinking about tasks even after the workday should be over.
ideaNotes.textZh: 如果没有明确的界限，工作往往会渗透到私人时间里，因为即使下班时间应该已经结束了，也很容易一直查看消息或惦记着工作任务。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, someone might turn off work notifications after a certain hour, so they can actually focus on things like exercising or cooking dinner without distraction.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，有人可能会在某个固定时间之后关闭工作通知，这样他们才能真正专心做一些事情，比如锻炼或做晚饭，不受打扰。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, balance doesn't always mean an equal split — sometimes it's okay to lean more toward work during busy periods, as long as it evens out over time.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，平衡并不总是意味着五五分——在忙碌时期更偏向工作也没关系，只要长期来看能保持平衡就行。

entries.text: Is it good to have a daily routine?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think having a daily routine is generally a good thing.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我觉得拥有每日固定作息通常是件好事。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When certain parts of the day are already planned out, people don't have to spend energy deciding what to do next, which frees up mental energy for more important decisions.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当一天中的某些部分已经提前规划好了，人们就不用花精力去决定接下来做什么，这能为更重要的决定腾出精力。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, someone who always exercises at the same time every morning doesn't need to convince themselves to do it — it just becomes automatic, like brushing their teeth.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一个每天早上都在固定时间锻炼的人，不需要每次都说服自己去做——这已经变成了一种自动的习惯，就像刷牙一样。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, a routine shouldn't be so rigid that it leaves no room for spontaneity, since occasionally breaking the pattern can also feel refreshing.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，作息也不应该太死板，以至于完全没有随性发挥的空间，因为偶尔打破常规也能让人感觉焕然一新。

entries.text: Do you think stress is important in people's lives?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I actually think a certain amount of stress plays an important role in people's lives.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我其实觉得一定程度的压力在人们的生活中扮演着重要角色。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Without any stress at all, people often lack the motivation to push themselves, but too much stress can lead to burnout, so there's a healthy middle ground where stress actually drives progress.
ideaNotes.textZh: 完全没有压力时，人们往往缺乏动力去逼自己进步，但压力太大又会导致身心俱疲，所以中间存在一个健康的平衡点，在那里压力反而能推动进步。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, the stress of an upcoming deadline often pushes someone to finally start a project they'd been putting off, getting more done in a few days than they had in weeks.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，即将到来的截止日期带来的压力，往往会推动一个人终于开始一个拖了很久的项目，几天内完成的工作量甚至超过之前好几周。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: The key is really about managing stress rather than eliminating it completely, since some pressure keeps life feeling meaningful rather than stagnant.
ideaNotes.textZh: 关键其实在于管理压力，而不是完全消除它，因为一定的压力能让生活感觉有意义，而不是停滞不前。

entries.text: Describe a person whose health and fitness you have helped to improve

paragraphs: I helped a friend improve her mental health through a book on positive psychology — one I'd read myself and found really helpful. There was a period when I was really burnt out — study / work [二选一]was non-stop, one thing after another from morning to night, with so much effort going in but nothing coming back.

Then one day I came across a post online recommending a book on positive psychology — the post said it was a self-help book about building a more positive mindset and managing negative emotions. So I decided to give it a try — and it turned out to be one of the best decisions I'd made.

I read it two or three times — going through it once to understand, and then again while actually putting the methods into practice — like meditating to focus on the present moment, keeping a gratitude journal, and maintaining a regular routine with some exercise. Whenever I felt anxious, I'd turn to these methods, and gradually things started to change.

The anxiety began to ease, I started noticing more of the good things around me, and I just felt so much happier overall. Around that same time, a close friend of mine was going through a really tough period — a family member of hers had fallen ill, and on top of that she'd just been laid off.
Seeing her go through all of that, I immediately thought of this book. I recommended it to her, hoping it might bring her the same comfort it had brought me.

We'd meet up whenever we could, and I'd also check in with her over WeChat — sharing things from the book and encouraging her to keep going. It wasn't easy at first — she told me she really struggled to sit still and focus during meditation, and sometimes felt like the gratitude journal was pointless.

But I believed that if it had worked for me, it could work for her too — so I just kept encouraging her and stayed by her side. After a few weeks, she told me she finally felt a sense of relief and had started feeling more motivated — and she found a new job not long after.
I'm really glad I came across this book — not only did it pull me out of my own burnout, but it also helped my friend get her life back on track.
paragraphsZh: 我通过一本关于积极心理学的书帮助了一个朋友改善她的心理健康——这本书我自己读过，觉得很有帮助。 有一段时间我真的精疲力竭——学习/工作没完没了，从早到晚一件事接着一件事，付出了那么多努力却没有任何回报。
然后有一天我在网上看到一篇帖子推荐一本关于积极心理学的书——帖子说这是一本关于如何建立更积极的心态、管理负面情绪的自我提升类书籍。 于是我决定试一试——事实证明这是我做过的最好的决定之一。
我前后读了两三遍——第一遍用来理解，之后再读的时候同步付诸实践——比如冥想来专注于当下，坚持写感恩日记，以及保持规律的作息和适当的运动。 每当感到焦虑的时候，我就会用这些方法，慢慢地事情开始改变了。
焦虑开始减轻，我开始注意到生活中更多美好的东西，整个人感觉快乐多了。 就在那段时间，我的一个朋友也正在经历一段非常艰难的时期——她的家人生病了，同时她自己也失业了。
看到她经历这一切，我立刻想到了这本书。 我把书推荐给了她，希望它能给她带来和我一样的慰藉。
我们只要有空就会约出来见面，我也会经常在微信上联系她——跟她分享书里的内容，鼓励她坚持下去。 一开始并不容易——她告诉我，冥想的时候很难静下心来集中注意力，有时候也觉得写感恩日记没什么意义。
但我相信，既然这个方法对我有用，对她也一定能有用——所以我一直在鼓励她，陪伴在她身边。 几周后，她告诉我她终于感到一种释然，开始变得更有动力了——不久之后，她还找到了新工作。
我真的很庆幸自己遇到了这本书——它不仅帮我走出了自己的精疲力竭，也帮助我的朋友重新让生活步入正轨。

entries.text: Which group pays more attention to health , young people or old people ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think older people generally pay more attention to their health than young people.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得老年人通常比年轻人更关注自己的健康。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: As people age, they often start experiencing physical decline or health issues firsthand, which makes health feel urgent and real, rather than just something to worry about later.
ideaNotes.textZh: 随着年龄增长，人们常常会亲身经历身体机能的衰退或健康问题，这会让健康感觉变得紧迫而真实，而不只是以后才需要担心的事。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, an older person might carefully track their blood pressure and adjust their diet accordingly, while a young person might ignore minor symptoms and just push through them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一位老年人可能会仔细监测自己的血压并相应调整饮食，而一个年轻人可能会忽视一些小症状，直接硬扛过去。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, more young people today are also becoming health-conscious, especially with the rise of fitness culture and social media promoting healthy lifestyles.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，现在也有越来越多年轻人开始注重健康，尤其是随着健身文化的兴起，以及社交媒体对健康生活方式的宣传。

entries.text: What kind of books useful to everyone?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think books about practical life skills, like personal finance or communication, tend to be useful to almost everyone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得关于实用生活技能的书，比如个人理财或沟通技巧，几乎对每个人都有用。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: These topics apply to daily life regardless of someone's job or interests, so the advice inside can be applied immediately, unlike more specialized books that only appeal to a narrow audience.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这些话题适用于日常生活，不管一个人的工作或兴趣是什么，所以书里的建议可以立刻运用起来，不像一些专业性很强的书只对特定人群有用。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a book that teaches basic budgeting skills can help a student, a parent, or a retiree alike, since everyone needs to manage money at some point.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一本教基本理财技巧的书，对学生、父母或退休人员都同样有帮助，因为每个人在某个阶段都需要管理金钱。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, "useful" can mean different things to different people, so a book on emotional wellbeing might be just as valuable to some as a practical skills guide.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，"有用"对不同的人来说可能意味着不同的东西，所以一本关于情绪健康的书，对某些人来说可能和一本实用技能指南一样有价值。

entries.text: Do you think people should read the original book before watching the movie?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think it's generally a good idea to read the book first, though it's not absolutely necessary.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得先读原著通常是个不错的主意，不过这也不是绝对必要的。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Reading first lets someone build their own imagination of the characters and setting, whereas watching the movie first can limit how they picture the story when they later read the book.
ideaNotes.textZh: 先读书能让人建立起自己对角色和场景的想象，而先看电影则可能会限制他们之后读书时对故事的想象方式。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, someone who reads a fantasy novel first might imagine the characters completely differently from the actors chosen for the movie, giving them a more personal connection to the story.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，先读一部奇幻小说的人，可能会把角色想象成和电影选角完全不同的样子，这会让他们和故事之间产生更个人化的连接。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, some people actually prefer watching the movie first, since it can make a long or complex book easier to follow afterward.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，也有些人反而更喜欢先看电影，因为这能让之后阅读一本又长又复杂的书变得更容易理解。

entries.text: Are success books useful to everyone ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: No, I don't think success books are actually useful to everyone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不，我不认为成功学书籍真的对每个人都有用。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: These books are usually written based on one person's specific experience, so the advice might not account for different circumstances, like someone's starting resources, industry, or personal situation.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这类书通常是基于某一个人的特定经历写出来的，所以书里的建议可能没有考虑到不同的处境，比如一个人的起点资源、所在行业或个人情况。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a success book written by a tech entrepreneur might offer advice that works well in Silicon Valley, but doesn't translate at all to someone running a small shop in a rural town.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一本科技创业者写的成功学书，里面的建议可能在硅谷很管用，但完全不适用于一个在乡镇经营小店的人。

ideaNotes.text: That said, these books can still offer some general inspiration or mindset shifts, even if the specific steps don't apply to everyone's situation.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，即使具体的方法不适用于所有人的情况，这些书仍然能提供一些普遍的启发或思维方式上的转变。

entries.text: Describe a time when you helped someone

paragraphs: There was a period when I was really burnt out — study / work [二选一]was non-stop, one thing after another from morning to night, with so much effort going in but nothing coming back. Then one day I came across a post online recommending a book on positive psychology — the post said it was a self-help book about building a more positive mindset and managing negative emotions.

So I decided to give it a try — and it turned out to be one of the best decisions I'd made. I read it two or three times — going through it once to understand, and then again while actually putting the methods into practice — like meditating to focus on the present moment, keeping a gratitude journal, and maintaining a regular routine with some exercise.

Whenever I felt anxious, I'd turn to these methods, and gradually things started to change. The anxiety began to ease, I started noticing more of the good things around me, and I just felt so much happier overall.

Around that same time, a close friend of mine was going through a really tough period — a family member of hers had fallen ill, and on top of that she'd just been laid off. Seeing her go through all of that, I immediately thought of this book.

I recommended it to her, hoping it might bring her the same comfort it had brought me. We'd meet up whenever we could, and I'd also check in with her over WeChat — sharing things from the book and encouraging her to keep going.

It wasn't easy at first — she told me she really struggled to sit still and focus during meditation, and sometimes felt like the gratitude journal was pointless. But I believed that if it had worked for me, it could work for her too — so I just kept encouraging her and stayed by her side.

After a few weeks, she told me she finally felt a sense of relief and had started feeling more motivated — and she found a new job not long after. I'm really glad I came across this book — not only did it pull me out of my own burnout, but it also helped my friend get her life back on track.
paragraphsZh: 有一段时间我真的精疲力竭——学习/工作没完没了，从早到晚一件事接着一件事，付出了那么多努力却没有任何回报。 然后有一天我在网上看到一篇帖子推荐一本关于积极心理学的书——帖子说这是一本关于如何建立更积极的心态、管理负面情绪的自我提升类书籍。
于是我决定试一试——事实证明这是我做过的最好的决定之一。 我前后读了两三遍——第一遍用来理解，之后再读的时候同步付诸实践——比如冥想来专注于当下，坚持写感恩日记，以及保持规律的作息和适当的运动。
每当感到焦虑的时候，我就会用这些方法，慢慢地事情开始改变了。 焦虑开始减轻，我开始注意到生活中更多美好的东西，整个人感觉快乐多了。
就在那段时间，我的一个朋友也正在经历一段非常艰难的时期——她的家人生病了，同时她自己也失业了。 看到她经历这一切，我立刻想到了这本书。
我把书推荐给了她，希望它能给她带来和我一样的慰藉。 我们只要有空就会约出来见面，我也会经常在微信上联系她——跟她分享书里的内容，鼓励她坚持下去。
一开始并不容易——她告诉我，冥想的时候很难静下心来集中注意力，有时候也觉得写感恩日记没什么意义。 但我相信，既然这个方法对我有用，对她也一定能有用——所以我一直在鼓励她，陪伴在她身边。
几周后，她告诉我她终于感到一种释然，开始变得更有动力了——不久之后，她还找到了新工作。 我真的很庆幸自己遇到了这本书——它不仅帮我走出了自己的精疲力竭，也帮助我的朋友重新让生活步入正轨。

entries.text: Should people be very kind when they help others ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people should be kind and patient when they help others, because the way we help can be just as important as the help itself.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得人们帮助别人时应该保持友善和耐心，因为帮助别人的方式和帮助本身一样重要。-

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: If we sound rude or act like helping is a burden, the other person may feel uncomfortable. But if we speak kindly, they will feel more comfortable asking for help.
ideaNotes.textZh: 如果我们说话不友善，或者表现得好像帮助别人是一种负担，对方可能会感到不自在。但如果我们说话友善，对方在寻求帮助时就会觉得更加自在。-

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, if someone doesn't know how to use a ticket machine, we can explain it patiently instead of making them feel silly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，如果有人不知道怎么使用售票机，我们可以耐心地向他们

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.textZh: 而不是让他们觉得自己很笨。-

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: We don't have to do everything for others, but we should always show respect and make them feel supported.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我们不必替别人做所有事情，但应该始终表现出尊重，让他们感受到支持。

paragraphs: I think people should be kind and patient when they help others, because the way we help can be just as important as the help itself.
If we sound rude or act like helping is a burden, the other person may feel uncomfortable. But if we speak kindly, they will feel more comfortable asking for help.
For example, if someone doesn't know how to use a ticket machine, we can explain it patiently instead of making them feel silly.
We don't have to do everything for others, but we should always show respect and make them feel supported.

entries.text: Should children be taught to be kind to others ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, definitely. I think children should be taught to be kind to others from a young age. Kindness is just as important as academic skills because it affects how they treat people and build relationships as they grow up.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，当然。我认为应该从小教育孩子友善待人。善良和学习能力一样重要，因为它会影响孩子在成长过程中如何对待他人，以及如何建立人际关系。-

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Children don't always know how their words and actions make others feel. Adults should teach them to share, listen, and say sorry when they make a mistake.
ideaNotes.textZh: 孩子并不总是知道自己的言语和行为会让别人有什么感受。成年人应该教他们学会分享、倾听，并在犯错时道歉。-

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, if a new student joins a class and looks lonely, a child could invite them to play or sit with them at lunch. This can make the student feel welcome and less nervous.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，如果一位新同学来到班里，看起来很孤单，其他孩子可以邀请他一起玩，或者午餐时和他坐在一起。这能让新同学感到自己受到欢迎，也不那么紧张。-

ideaNotes.text: Parents and teachers should set a good example because children often copy what adults do. At the same time, children should know that being kind doesn't mean they have to agree with everyone.

entries.text: Should parents help their kids with their homework ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: ： Yes, I think parents should help their kids with homework, especially when they find something difficult. But parents shouldn't do the work for them, because children also need to learn to do things on their own.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为父母应该帮助孩子完成家庭作业，尤其是在他们遇到难题时。但父母不应该替他们完成作业，因为孩子也需要学会独立做事。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: ： Parents can explain difficult parts and give children some hints instead of telling them the answers directly. This can help children understand the subject better and feel more confident. It also teaches them how to solve problems by themselves.

ideaNotes.label: 例子

第一步，然后让孩子自己尝试完成剩下的部分。如果孩子还是有困难，父母可以再给一些提示。

entries.text: What kind of advice should parents give to their children ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think parents should give their children practical advice about daily life, relationships, and making good decisions. These things can help children become more independent as they grow up.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为父母应该给孩子一些关于日常生活、人际关系和做出正确决定的实用建议。这些建议能帮助孩子在成长过程中变得更加独立。-

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Children don't have much life experience, so they may not know how to deal with certain problems. Parents can share what they have learned and teach children to think carefully before making a decision.
ideaNotes.textZh: 孩子没有太多的生活经验，所以他们可能不知道如何处理某些问题。父母可以分享自己的经验，并教孩子在做决定之前认真思考。-

entries.text: Can kids provide any help to parents ?

ideaNotes.text: Yes, definitely. I think kids can help their parents in many ways, even when they're still young. They can help with household chores and also provide emotional support.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当然可以。我认为孩子即使还很小，也能在很多方面帮助父母。他们可以帮忙做家务，也可以提供情感支持。-

ideaNotes.text: First, children can share some of the housework, so their parents don't have to do everything themselves. Also, small acts of kindness can make parents feel loved and appreciated. Kids don't need to do anything special to show that they care.

entries.text: Describe a movie/film you don't like

paragraphs: A movie I really didn't enjoy was an animated film called Niu Lai. A few weeks ago, my friend told me there was this movie that everyone was talking about online — she said it was really funny and kept pushing me to go see it.
So I went to the cinema. The movie was made by two people with absolutely no professional background — a mother and son — who spent five years making it entirely by hand.
It sounds kind of impressive, but it really wasn't. The animation was really stiff and slow, with movements that looked like a slideshow.

On top of that, the plot was really hard to follow — some scenes dragged on endlessly, and then out of nowhere jumped to something completely unrelated. And to make it worse, the dialogue felt so unnatural, like no real person would ever talk that way, and the voice acting was really amateur.

Despite all of that, I still sat there and kept listening to all the dialogue I had absolutely no interest in. After all, I'd already paid for the ticket and felt like I had to get something out of it.

And honestly, there was also a bit of curiosity — I just wanted to see how bad it could really get, and it turned out to be pretty painful to sit through. As soon as I left the cinema, the first thing I did was look up the reviews online — and most people were just as confused as I was.

But there were also some who actually appreciated it — saying that art has no fixed standard, and in an age where AI is taking over, that kind of genuine effort and passion deserves to be recognised. Either way, it's not a film I'd ever watch again.
paragraphsZh: 我真的很不喜欢的一部电影，是一部叫《牛来》的动画片。 几周前，我朋友跟我说网上有一部电影很火——她说特别好笑，一直推荐我去看。
于是我就去了电影院。 这部电影是两个完全没有专业背景的人——一对母子——花了五年时间完全手工制作的。
听起来挺了不起的，但实际上根本不是那么回事。 动画非常僵硬迟缓，动作看起来像在播幻灯片。
不仅如此，剧情也非常难以理解——有些场景拖沓得没完没了，然后突然毫无预兆地跳到完全不相关的情节。 更糟糕的是，对白非常不自然，完全不像正常人说话的方式，配音也非常业余。
尽管如此，我还是坐在那里听完了整部电影里我完全不感兴趣的对白。 毕竟，票已经买了，感觉总要得到点什么。
说实话，我也有点好奇心——就想看看这部电影到底能烂到什么程度，结果证明整个观影过程真的很煎熬。 一出电影院，我做的第一件事就是去查网上的评价——大部分人和我一样困惑。
但也有一些人真的欣赏这部电影——说艺术没有固定标准，而且在AI大行其道的今天，这种真诚的努力和热情值得被肯定。 不管怎样，这部电影我是再也不会看第二遍了。

entries.text: Do people’s movie preferences change as they get older ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think people's movie preferences definitely change as they get older.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我觉得人们的电影偏好确实会随着年龄增长而改变。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: As people gain more life experience, they often start looking for deeper meaning or emotional depth in a film, rather than just fast-paced action or simple entertainment.
ideaNotes.textZh: 随着人们积累更多人生阅历，他们往往开始在电影中寻找更深层的意义或情感深度，而不只是快节奏的动作或单纯的娱乐。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a teenager might love superhero movies for the action, while the same person in their 30s might prefer a slow, thoughtful drama that reflects real-life struggles.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一个青少年可能因为动作场面而喜欢超级英雄电影，而同一个人到了三十多岁，可能更喜欢一部反映现实生活困境的节奏缓慢、发人深省的剧情片。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, some people still enjoy the same genres throughout their lives, since personal taste isn't entirely defined by age.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，也有些人一辈子都喜欢同样类型的电影，因为个人品味并不完全由年龄决定。

entries.text: Should documentary films be completely truthful ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think documentary films should be as truthful as possible, since that's essentially the whole point of the genre.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我觉得纪录片应该尽可能真实，因为这本质上就是这个类型片存在的全部意义。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: People watch documentaries specifically to learn about real events or issues, so if the content is exaggerated or misleading, it defeats the purpose and could spread misinformation.
ideaNotes.textZh: 人们看纪录片正是为了了解真实的事件或议题，所以如果内容被夸大或误导，就违背了这个初衷，还可能传播错误信息。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, if a climate change documentary shows fake numbers to make the problem seem worse, and people later find out, they might stop trusting climate science altogether.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，如果一部气候变化纪录片为了让问题显得更严重而展示虚假数据，一旦人们发现，可能会从此不再信任气候科学。

entries.text: Can movies help people better understand the cultural background of a country ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think movies can definitely help people understand a country's cultural background better.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我觉得电影确实能帮助人们更好地理解一个国家的文化背景。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Movies show visual details like clothing, food, and daily behavior all at once, giving viewers a natural feel for a culture that reading a description simply can't convey as vividly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 电影能一次性展示视觉细节，比如服饰、食物和日常行为举止，让观众自然地感受到一种文化，而这是单纯阅读文字描述根本无法同样生动传达的。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, watching a movie set in India might show viewers how family gatherings, festivals, or everyday meals actually look, something hard to fully imagine from text alone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，看一部背景设定在印度的电影，可能会让观众看到家庭聚会、节日或日常饮食实际是什么样子，这是仅靠文字很难完全想象出来的。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, movies can also present a biased or exaggerated version of a culture, so they shouldn't be treated as a completely accurate source.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，电影也可能呈现出一种带有偏见或夸张的文化版本，所以不应该把它当作完全准确的信息来源。

entries.text: Are movies more likely to help people become more creative than books ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: No, I actually think books are more likely to boost creativity than movies.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不，我其实认为书籍比电影更能激发创造力。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: A movie shows everything visually, leaving little room for imagination, but a book only gives words, forcing the reader's brain to actively construct scenes, characters, and emotions on their own.
ideaNotes.textZh: 电影把一切都直观地展示出来，几乎没有留给想象的空间，而书籍只给出文字，迫使读者的大脑主动构建场景、人物和情感。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, reading a description of a fantasy world forces the reader to picture it uniquely in their own mind, while watching the movie version gives everyone the exact same image.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，阅读关于一个奇幻世界的描写，会让读者在自己脑海中独一无二地想象出画面，而看这部电影的改编版本，则给了每个人完全相同的画面。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, movies can still inspire creativity in a different way, like showing people new visual styles they might not have thought of before.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，电影仍然能以另一种方式激发创造力，比如展示人们之前可能没想过的新视觉风格。

entries.text: Describe a time when someone talked about something you were not interested in but you kept listening

paragraphs: One time I kept listening to something I had no interest in at all was during a film called Niu Lai. A few weeks ago, my friend told me there was this movie that everyone was talking about online — she said it was really funny and kept pushing me to go see it.
So I went to the cinema. The movie was made by two people with absolutely no professional background — a mother and son — who spent five years making it entirely by hand.
It sounds kind of impressive, but it really wasn't. The animation was really stiff and slow, with movements that looked like a slideshow.

On top of that, the plot was really hard to follow — some scenes dragged on endlessly, and then out of nowhere jumped to something completely unrelated. And to make it worse, the dialogue felt so unnatural, like no real person would ever talk that way, and the voice acting was really amateur.

Despite all of that, I still sat there and kept listening to all the dialogue I had absolutely no interest in. After all, I'd already paid for the ticket and felt like I had to get something out of it.

And honestly, there was also a bit of curiosity — I just wanted to see how bad it could really get, and it turned out to be pretty painful to sit through. As soon as I left the cinema, the first thing I did was look up the reviews online — and most people were just as confused as I was.

But there were also some who actually appreciated it — saying that art has no fixed standard, and in an age where AI is taking over, that kind of genuine effort and passion deserves to be recognised. Either way, it's not a film I'd ever watch again.
paragraphsZh: 有一次我坚持听着完全不感兴趣的内容，就是在看一部叫《牛来》的电影的时候。 几周前，我朋友跟我说网上有一部电影很火——她说特别好笑，一直推荐我去看。
于是我就去了电影院。 这部电影是两个完全没有专业背景的人——一对母子——花了五年时间完全手工制作的。
听起来挺了不起的，但实际上根本不是那么回事。 动画非常僵硬迟缓，动作看起来像在播幻灯片。
不仅如此，剧情也非常难以理解——有些场景拖沓得没完没了，然后突然毫无预兆地跳到完全不相关的情节。 更糟糕的是，对白非常不自然，完全不像正常人说话的方式，配音也非常业余。
尽管如此，我还是坐在那里听完了整部电影里我完全不感兴趣的对白。 毕竟，票已经买了，感觉总要得到点什么。
说实话，我也有点好奇心——就想看看这部电影到底能烂到什么程度，结果证明整个观影过程真的很煎熬。 一出电影院，我做的第一件事就是去查网上的评价——大部分人和我一样困惑。
但也有一些人真的欣赏这部电影——说艺术没有固定标准，而且在AI大行其道的今天，这种真诚的努力和热情值得被肯定。 不管怎样，这部电影我是再也不会看第二遍了。

entries.text: How can we tell if a listener is listening carefully?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the clearest sign is eye contact, along with small physical reactions like nodding.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得最明显的迹象就是眼神接触，再加上像点头这样的小小肢体反应。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Someone who's truly paying attention naturally responds to what's being said, whether through facial expressions or body language, while someone who's distracted tends to have a blank or wandering gaze.
ideaNotes.textZh: 一个真正在专注听的人，会自然地对所说的内容做出回应，无论是通过面部表情还是肢体语言，而一个走神的人往往眼神空洞或到处飘。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a listener who's engaged might lean forward slightly or ask a follow-up question, while someone not paying attention might keep glancing at their phone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一个专注的听众可能会稍微身体前倾，或者提出一个追问，而一个没在认真听的人可能会不停地看手机。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: That said, some people are just naturally quiet listeners, so a lack of obvious reactions doesn't always mean they aren't paying attention.
ideaNotes.textZh: 不过，有些人天生就是安静型的听众，所以没有明显的反应并不一定代表他们没在认真听。

entries.text: What would happen if the listener didn’t listen carefully?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think if a listener isn't paying attention, it can easily lead to misunderstandings or important information getting missed.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得如果听众没有认真听，很容易导致误解，或者重要信息被遗漏。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When someone isn't fully focused, they might catch only part of what's being said, and filling in the missing parts with guesses often leads to a completely different understanding than what was actually meant.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当一个人没有完全专注时，可能只听懂了部分内容，而用猜测去填补缺失的部分，往往会导致理解和实际意思完全不同。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, if an employee only half-listens to instructions during a meeting, they might end up doing the task wrong, requiring everything to be redone later.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，如果一个员工在会议中只听了一半的指示，他们最后可能会把任务做错，之后还得重新再做一遍。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: This kind of miscommunication can also damage trust over time, especially if it keeps happening in a professional setting.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这种沟通不畅长期下去也会损害信任，尤其是如果这种情况在职场环境中反复发生的话。

entries.text: Describe a time you made an important decision and were happy with the result

paragraphs: One important decision I made was signing up for a short-term study programme in Japan. I had been learning Japanese for about six months.
At first, I believed that watching online courses and reading textbooks would be enough. So I came up with a plan and followed it seriously.

But the results weren't great — I kept forgetting vocabulary and grammar, and without a real language environment, I felt like I was just going in circles. That's when my opinion changed — I realized I needed real practice, not just theory.

So I ended up changing my original plan as well, and decided to sign up for a one-week study programme in Japan last year. Honestly, it wasn't an easy decision — the programme wasn't cheap, and I had to take time off, so I hesitated for a bit.

But I figured it was worth the risk, so I went ahead and signed up. The programme was structured like this — every morning we had Japanese classes with local teachers, practising speaking face to face with classmates.

In the afternoons, we were out in the city, actually using Japanese in real situations — reading signs, ordering food, asking for directions. This time, there was no relying on textbooks — I just had to speak.

At first I was pretty nervous, and there were moments I got things completely wrong and felt a bit embarrassed. But by the end of the week, I could really feel my speaking improving — words that used to feel so unfamiliar just started coming out more naturally.
I was so happy with how much progress I'd made in just one week, way more than in the six months before it. Looking back, making that decision was just so crucial for me.

It totally changed my mindset — I realized language learning isn't about getting everything perfect, but actually using it to communicate. It also gave me so much more confidence — I realized I'm actually braver and more independent than I thought, which was huge personal growth for me.
paragraphsZh: 我做过的一个重要决定，就是报名参加了一个在日本的短期学习项目。 我已经学日语大概六个月了。
一开始我以为看网课、读课本就足够了。 所以我制定了一个计划并且认真地执行了。
但效果并不好——我总是忘记单词和语法，而且没有一个真实的语言环境，感觉自己一直在原地打转。 就是在那个时候，我的看法改变了——我意识到我需要真正的实践，而不只是理论。
所以我最终也改变了原来的计划，决定报名参加了一个去年在日本的为期一周的学习项目。 说实话，这不是一个容易做的决定——这个项目并不便宜，而且我得请假，所以我犹豫了一下。
但我觉得值得冒这个险，所以我还是报名了。 这个项目大概是这样安排的——每天早上我们有当地老师上的日语课，跟同学面对面练习口语。
下午我们就在城市里，真正地在实际场景中使用日语——看标识、点餐、问路。 这一次，没办法依赖课本了——我只能开口说。
一开始我特别紧张，也有一些时候完全说错了，感觉有点尴尬。 但到那周结束的时候，我真的能感觉到自己的口语在进步——那些曾经很陌生的词句，开始更自然地脱口而出了。
我对自己在短短一周内取得的进步感到特别开心，比之前六个月自学的进步还要多。 回过头来看，做出那个决定对我来说真的很关键。
它彻底改变了我的思维方式——我意识到学语言不是要追求完美，而是要真正用它来交流。 这也让我变得更加自信——我意识到自己其实比想象中更勇敢、更独立，这对我来说是一次很大的个人成长。

entries.text: Which is better, to make a decision quickly or slowly?

entries.text: Do you think most people's decisions are made in their 20s?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think a lot of life-changing decisions do tend to happen in someone's 20s.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我觉得很多改变人生的决定确实往往发生在一个人的20多岁。

entries.text: What little decisions do people make every day?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most common small decisions people make every day are things like what to eat and what to wear.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得人们每天最常做的小决定就是吃什么和穿什么。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: These choices come up repeatedly, every single day, so even though each one is minor on its own, people end up making dozens of these small decisions without even really thinking about them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这些选择每天都会反复出现，所以尽管每一个单独来看都很微小，人们最终每天会做出几十个这样的小决定，甚至都不怎么会去多想。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, deciding whether to take the bus or subway to work, or picking between coffee or tea in the morning, are the kinds of quick, low-stakes choices most people barely notice making.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，决定上班坐公交还是地铁，或者早上选咖啡还是茶，都是大多数人几乎不会注意到自己在做的、快速又无关紧要的选择。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: Interestingly, even though these decisions feel unimportant, making too many of them in a short time can actually lead to something called decision fatigue.

entries.text: Do you think it is a good idea to make a small decision every day?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think regularly making small decisions can actually be really beneficial.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我觉得经常做小决定其实很有好处。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Making decisions is a skill that improves with practice, so consistently making small choices helps build the confidence needed to handle bigger, more complicated decisions later.
ideaNotes.textZh: 做决定是一项通过练习能提升的技能，所以持续做一些小选择，能帮助建立处理以后更重大、更复杂决定所需要的信心。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, someone who gets used to quickly deciding what to cook for dinner each night may find it easier to make faster, more confident choices in other areas of life too.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，一个习惯每天快速决定晚饭做什么的人，可能会发现自己在生活其他方面也更容易做出更快、更自信的选择。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: On top of that, making small decisions gives people a low-risk way to practice trusting their own judgment, without worrying too much about serious consequences.
ideaNotes.textZh: 除此之外，做小决定也能让人以一种低风险的方式，练习相信自己的判断力，而不用太担心严重的后果。

entries.text: How can we tell the difference between an important and an easy decision?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the easiest way to tell is by looking at how big the consequences are and whether the decision can be easily undone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我觉得最简单的判断方式是看这个决定的后果有多大，以及这个决定是否容易被撤回。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: If a wrong choice would cause serious, long-lasting problems, it's an important decision, but if a mistake is easy to fix or barely affects anything, it's probably a minor one.
ideaNotes.textZh: 如果做错了会造成严重、长期的影响，那这就是一个重要的决定，但如果错误很容易纠正，或者几乎没什么影响，那大概就是一个次要的决定。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, choosing a college major is a big decision because it affects years of your life and is hard to reverse, while choosing what to have for breakfast barely matters at all.
ideaNotes.textZh: 比如，选择大学专业是一个重大决定，因为它会影响好几年的人生，而且很难改变，而选择早餐吃什么几乎无关紧要。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: Another sign is how many other people the decision affects — choices that impact family or a whole team usually deserve more careful thought.
ideaNotes.textZh: 另一个判断标准是这个决定会影响到多少其他人——影响到家人或整个团队的决定，通常更值得仔细考虑。

entries.text: Describe a time when you changed an important opinion of yours

paragraphs: Something I changed recently was actually the way I was learning Japanese. I had been learning Japanese for about six months.
At first, I believed that watching online courses and reading textbooks would be enough. So I came up with a plan and followed it seriously.

But the results weren't great — I kept forgetting vocabulary and grammar, and without a real language environment, I felt like I was just going in circles. That's when my opinion changed — I realized I needed real practice, not just theory.

So I ended up changing my original plan as well, and decided to sign up for a one-week study programme in Japan last year. Honestly, it wasn't an easy decision — the programme wasn't cheap, and I had to take time off, so I hesitated for a bit.

But I figured it was worth the risk, so I went ahead and signed up. The programme was structured like this — every morning we had Japanese classes with local teachers, practising speaking face to face with classmates.

In the afternoons, we were out in the city, actually using Japanese in real situations — reading signs, ordering food, asking for directions. This time, there was no relying on textbooks — I just had to speak.

At first I was pretty nervous, and there were moments I got things completely wrong and felt a bit embarrassed. But by the end of the week, I could really feel my speaking improving — words that used to feel so unfamiliar just started coming out more naturally.
I was so happy with how much progress I'd made in just one week, way more than in the six months before it. Looking back, making that decision was just so crucial for me.

It totally changed my mindset — I realized language learning isn't about getting everything perfect, but actually using it to communicate. It also gave me so much more confidence — I realized I'm actually braver and more independent than I thought, which was huge personal growth for me.
paragraphsZh: 我最近改变的一件事，其实就是我学日语的方式。 我已经学日语大概六个月了。
一开始我以为看网课、读课本就足够了。 所以我制定了一个计划并且认真地执行了。
但效果并不好——我总是忘记单词和语法，而且没有一个真实的语言环境，感觉自己一直在原地打转。 就是在那个时候，我的看法改变了——我意识到我需要真正的实践，而不只是理论。
所以我最终也改变了原来的计划，决定报名参加了一个去年在日本的为期一周的学习项目。 说实话，这不是一个容易做的决定——这个项目并不便宜，而且我得请假，所以我犹豫了一下。
但我觉得值得冒这个险，所以我还是报名了。 这个项目大概是这样安排的——每天早上我们有当地老师上的日语课，跟同学面对面练习口语。
下午我们就在城市里，真正地在实际场景中使用日语——看标识、点餐、问路。 这一次，没办法依赖课本了——我只能开口说。
一开始我特别紧张，也有一些时候完全说错了，感觉有点尴尬。 但到那周结束的时候，我真的能感觉到自己的口语在进步——那些曾经很陌生的词句，开始更自然地脱口而出了。
我对自己在短短一周内取得的进步感到特别开心，比之前六个月自学的进步还要多。 回过头来看，做出那个决定对我来说真的很关键。
它彻底改变了我的思维方式——我意识到学语言不是要追求完美，而是要真正用它来交流。 这也让我变得更加自信——我意识到自己其实比想象中更勇敢、更独立，这对我来说是一次很大的个人成长。

entries.text: Do children communicate more with teachers or with parents ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think children generally talk more to their parents overall, but the kind of things they talk about are quite different — parents get the personal and emotional stuff, while teachers get more of the academic side.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为孩子总体上更多地与父母交谈，但他们谈论的事情种类很不同，父母得到个人和情感方面的内容，而老师更多得到学业方面的内容。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: At home, children are relaxed and comfortable, so they naturally talk more freely about their feelings, worries, and daily life. With teachers, the relationship is more formal and structured — most conversations happen in the context of lessons or school tasks, so it stays more surface level. Unless a child has a particularly close relationship with a teacher, most of the communication is kept quite professional.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在家里，孩子放松和舒适，所以他们自然更自由地谈论他们的感受、担忧和日常生活。与老师的关系更加正式和有结构，大多数对话发生在课程或学校任务的背景下，所以保持更加表面。除非孩子与老师有特别亲近的关系，否则大多数沟通保持相当专业。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember always going to my parents first when something was bothering me — whether it was a friendship problem or feeling stressed about something. I would only go to a teacher if it was something directly related to school or studying, and even then it was usually quite a short and practical conversation.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得当有什么事情困扰我时，总是首先去找父母，无论是友谊问题还是对某事感到压力。只有当事情直接与学校或学习相关时，我才会去找老师，即使那样，通常也是相当简短和实际的对话。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 That said, some children who don't have a strong relationship with their parents actually end up being more open with a trusted teacher — for them, that teacher becomes someone they rely on for guidance and support beyond just academics. 话虽如此，一些与父母没有强烈关系的孩子实际上最终对信任的老师更开放，对他们来说，那位老师成为他们在学业之外依赖指导和支持的人。

entries.text: Who do young people like to share opinions with ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think young people share their opinions most openly with their close friends — it's the relationship where they feel the least judged and most understood.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为年轻人最公开地与亲密朋友分享意见，这是他们感到最少被评判和最被理解的关系。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: With friends, you can say what you actually think without worrying about consequences or disappointing someone. With parents, there's always this concern that they might react badly, worry, or try to change your mind, which makes young people hold back. And with teachers or other authority figures, most young people just don't feel comfortable sharing personal views at all.
ideaNotes.textZh: 与朋友在一起，你可以说出你真正的想法而不用担心后果或让某人失望。与父母在一起，总有这种担心他们可能会反应不好、担心或试图改变你的想法，这使年轻人有所保留。而与老师或其他权威人物在一起，大多数年轻人根本感到不舒服分享个人

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, there are things I would only ever tell my close friends — opinions about relationships, doubts about the future, or things I disagree with my parents about — because I know they'll listen without judging and give me an honest reaction rather than just telling me what they think I want to hear.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，有些事情我只会告诉我的亲密朋友，关于感情的看法、对未来的疑虑，或我与父母不同意的事情，因为我知道他们会不加评判地倾听，给我诚实的反应，而不只是告诉我他们认为我想听的话。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, a lot of young people now share opinions online too — through social media or anonymous platforms — because it feels even safer and freer than talking in person, especially about topics that might be sensitive or controversial. 另外，很多年轻人现在也在网上分享意见，通过社交媒体或匿名平台，因为感觉比当面交谈更加安全和自由，尤其是关于可能敏感或有争议的话题。

entries.text: Describe a plan that you had to change recently

paragraphs: Something I changed recently was actually the way I was learning Japanese. I had been learning Japanese for about six months.
At first, I believed that watching online courses and reading textbooks would be enough. So I came up with a plan and followed it seriously.

But the results weren't great — I kept forgetting vocabulary and grammar, and without a real language environment, I felt like I was just going in circles. That's when my opinion changed — I realized I needed real practice, not just theory.

So I ended up changing my original plan as well, and decided to sign up for a one-week study programme in Japan last year. Honestly, it wasn't an easy decision — the programme wasn't cheap, and I had to take time off, so I hesitated for a bit.

But I figured it was worth the risk, so I went ahead and signed up. The programme was structured like this — every morning we had Japanese classes with local teachers, practising speaking face to face with classmates.

In the afternoons, we were out in the city, actually using Japanese in real situations — reading signs, ordering food, asking for directions. This time, there was no relying on textbooks — I just had to speak.

At first I was pretty nervous, and there were moments I got things completely wrong and felt a bit embarrassed. But by the end of the week, I could really feel my speaking improving — words that used to feel so unfamiliar just started coming out more naturally.
I was so happy with how much progress I'd made in just one week, way more than in the six months before it. Looking back, making that decision was just so crucial for me.

It totally changed my mindset — I realized language learning isn't about getting everything perfect, but actually using it to communicate. It also gave me so much more confidence — I realized I'm actually braver and more independent than I thought, which was huge personal growth for me.
paragraphsZh: 我最近改变的一件事，其实就是我学日语的方式。 我已经学日语大概六个月了。
一开始我以为看网课、读课本就足够了。 所以我制定了一个计划并且认真地执行了。
但效果并不好——我总是忘记单词和语法，而且没有一个真实的语言环境，感觉自己一直在原地打转。 就是在那个时候，我的看法改变了——我意识到我需要真正的实践，而不只是理论。
所以我最终也改变了原来的计划，决定报名参加了一个去年在日本的为期一周的学习项目。 说实话，这不是一个容易做的决定——这个项目并不便宜，而且我得请假，所以我犹豫了一下。
但我觉得值得冒这个险，所以我还是报名了。 这个项目大概是这样安排的——每天早上我们有当地老师上的日语课，跟同学面对面练习口语。
下午我们就在城市里，真正地在实际场景中使用日语——看标识、点餐、问路。 这一次，没办法依赖课本了——我只能开口说。
一开始我特别紧张，也有一些时候完全说错了，感觉有点尴尬。 但到那周结束的时候，我真的能感觉到自己的口语在进步——那些曾经很陌生的词句，开始更自然地脱口而出了。
我对自己在短短一周内取得的进步感到特别开心，比之前六个月自学的进步还要多。 回过头来看，做出那个决定对我来说真的很关键。
它彻底改变了我的思维方式——我意识到学语言不是要追求完美，而是要真正用它来交流。 这也让我变得更加自信——我意识到自己其实比想象中更勇敢、更独立，这对我来说是一次很大的个人成长。

entries.text: Do people often change their plans?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think most people change their plans pretty regularly — life is unpredictable, and things come up that make it impossible or just not practical to stick to the original plan.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为大多数人相当频繁地改变计划，生活是不可预测的，发生的事情使得不可能或不实际坚持原来的计划。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Sometimes plans change because of things completely outside your control — bad weather, someone cancelling, work running over — and sometimes it's just because you change your mind or something better comes along. Either way, being able to adapt and adjust is just part of everyday life, and people who can't handle changes in their plans tend to find life a lot more stressful than it needs to be.
ideaNotes.textZh: 有时计划改变是因为完全超出你控制的事情，恶劣天气、有人取消、工作超时，有时只是因为你改变了主意或有更好的事情出现。无论如何，适应和调整只是日常生活的一部分，无法处理计划变化的人往往会发现生活比实际需要的更有压力。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I can't count how many times I've made plans with friends to go somewhere and then one person bails last minute or the weather turns bad and we end up doing something completely different — it happens so often that it doesn't even feel like a big deal anymore.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我数不清有多少次和朋友计划去某个地方，然后有人最后一刻放鸽子或天气变差，我们最终做了完全不同的事情，这发生得如此频繁，以至于不再感觉是什么大事。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think younger people are more comfortable with changing plans than older generations — they tend to be more flexible and spontaneous, whereas older people often prefer to stick to what was agreed and find last-minute changes quite disruptive and annoying. 另外，我认为年轻人比老一辈更适应改变计划，他们往往更加灵活和自发，而老年人通常更喜欢坚持已商定的事情，觉得最后一刻的变化相当破坏性和烦人。

entries.text: Would you tell others if you change your plan?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I always try to let people know as soon as possible if my plans change — I think it's just basic respect for other people's time.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，如果我的计划改变，我总是尽快通知别人，我认为这只是对他人时间的基本尊重。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: If someone has made arrangements based on what you agreed, and you just don't show up or change things without telling them, it wastes their time and can come across as really inconsiderate and rude. Even if the change is last minute, a quick message or call is always better than just going silent — most people are understanding as long as you communicate properly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 如果有人根据你们的约定做了安排，而你只是不出现或不告知就改变事情，这浪费了他们的时间，可能显得非常不体贴和无礼。即使变化是最后一刻，一条简短的消息或电话总是比只是沉默要好，只要你好好沟通，大多数人都会理解的。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I had a friend who used to just not show up without saying anything, and it was so frustrating — you'd be sitting there waiting and wondering what happened. After a while people just stopped making plans with her because nobody wanted to deal with that uncertainty.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我有一个朋友过去常常不打招呼就不出现，这真的很令人沮丧，你坐在那里等待，想知道发生了什么。过了一段时间，人们就不再和她制定计划了，因为没有人想处理那种不确定性。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, telling people early gives them a chance to adjust their own plans rather than just being left hanging — it's just a much more considerate and mature way to handle things. 另外，早点告诉别人给了他们一个调整自己计划的机会，而不是让他们悬在那里，这只是处理事情更加体贴和成熟的方式。

entries.text: Why do you think parents still make plans for their children nowadays?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think parents plan for their children mainly because they genuinely want the best for them, but also because there's a lot of social pressure to make sure their kids don't fall behind.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为父母为孩子计划主要是因为他们真心希望孩子得到最好的，但也因为有很多社会压力确保孩子不落后。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: In China especially, the competition for good schools and good jobs starts really early, so parents feel like if they don't plan ahead — signing their kids up for the right classes, getting them into the right schools — their children will miss out on opportunities that are hard to recover from later. It comes from a good place, but it can also put a lot of pressure on the child.
ideaNotes.textZh: 尤其在中国，对好学校和好工作的竞争开始得很早，所以父母感觉如果他们不提前计划，为孩子报名参加正确的课程、让他们进入正确的学校，孩子将错过以后难以弥补的机会。这出发点是好的，但也会给孩子带来很多压力。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I know lots of kids whose weekends are completely packed with extra classes — piano, maths, English, swimming — all arranged by their parents. The parents mean well, but some of those kids look genuinely exhausted and have no free time to just be kids.

entries.text: How does technology help people make plans?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think technology has made planning so much easier and more organised — things that used to take a lot of effort can now be done in just a few taps on your phone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为科技使计划更容易、更有条理，以前需要很多努力的事情现在只需在手机上点几下就能完成。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Whether it's scheduling meetings, booking travel, setting reminders, or coordinating with a group of people, there's basically an app for everything now. Technology also makes it easier to change and update plans in real time — you can let everyone know about a change instantly rather than having to call each person individually, which saves a huge amount of time.
ideaNotes.textZh: 无论是安排会议、预订旅行、设置提醒还是与一群人协调，现在基本上每件事都有一个应用程序。科技还使实时更改和更新计划更容易，你可以立即让所有人知道变化，而不必逐个打电话，这节省了大量时间。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, whenever my friends and I plan a trip, we just make a shared document or group chat and everyone can add their ideas, vote on options, and keep track of what's been booked — it's so much smoother and less chaotic than trying to organise everything through individual conversations.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，每当我和朋友们计划旅行时，我们只是制作一个共享文档或群聊，每个人都可以添加想法、投票选择并跟踪已预订的内容，这比试图通过个人对话组织一切顺畅得多、混乱更少。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, things like map apps and booking platforms have made it so much easier to plan the practical side of things — you can check travel times, compare prices, and book everything in one place without having to spend hours researching separately. 另外，像地图应用和预订平台这样的东西使计划实际事项变得容易得多，你可以查看旅行时间、比较价格，并在一个地方预订一切，而不必花几个小时分别研究。
