entries.text: What kind of plans do people often make?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people make all kinds of plans — from really small everyday ones to big life-changing decisions — and most of us are planning something all the time without even really thinking about it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们制定各种各样的计划，从非常小的日常计划到重大的改变人生的决定，我们大多数人一直在计划某件事，甚至没有真正想到这一点。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: On a day-to-day level, people plan things like what to eat, how to spend their weekend, or how to manage their schedule for the week. But people also make much bigger plans around things like career, travel, finances, and relationships — like saving up for something, deciding where to live, or figuring out the next step in their job. These bigger plans tend to take more thought and time but also matter a lot more in the long run.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在日常层面，人们计划吃什么、如何度过周末或如何安排一周的时间表。但人们也围绕职业、旅行、财务和人际关系制定更大的计划，比如为某事存钱、决定住在哪里，或者弄清楚工作的下一步。这些更大的计划往往需要更多思考和时间，但从长远来看也更加重要。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I think almost everyone plans their holidays and trips quite carefully — deciding where to go, when to book, and what to do once they're there. But at the same time, a lot of people also have longer term plans in the back of their mind, like saving up to buy a flat or planning when to start a family, even if they don't talk about them openly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认为几乎每个人都相当仔细地计划他们的假期和旅行，决定去哪里、何时预订以及到了那里做什么。但同时，很多人心里也有更长远的计划，比如存钱买房或计划何时组建家庭，即使他们不公开谈论这些。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think how much people plan varies a lot by personality — some people plan everything down to the last detail and feel anxious without a clear structure, while others just take things as they come and only make plans when they absolutely have to. 另外，我认为人们计划的多少因性格而异，有些人把每个细节都计划好，没有清晰的结构就感到焦虑，而其他人只是顺其自然，只在绝对必要时才制定计划。

entries.text: Do you think people like the process of making plans more, or the moment of carrying them out?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think most people actually enjoy both for different reasons, but if I had to pick, I'd say the moment of carrying it out tends to feel more rewarding in the end.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为大多数人实际上因为不同原因两者都喜欢，但如果我必须选择，我会说执行计划的时刻最终往往感觉更有成就感。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Planning has its own kind of enjoyment — there's something really satisfying about imagining how something will go, researching options, and getting everything organised. It feels exciting and full of possibility. But the moment you actually do the thing — go on the trip, start the project, achieve the goal — that feeling is on a completely different level because it's real rather than just in your head.
ideaNotes.textZh: 计划有其自身的乐趣，想象事情将如何进行、研究选项和把一切组织好有一种真正令人满足的感觉。它感觉令人兴奋且充满可能性。但当你真正做这件事，去旅行、开始项目、实现目标时，那种感觉完全不同，因为它是真实的而不只是在你脑海中。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, whenever I plan a trip I really enjoy looking up places, making lists, and getting excited about what's coming. But honestly, none of that compares to the feeling of actually being there — standing somewhere new, trying the food, and thinking "I made this happen". The planning was fun but the real thing is always better than you imagined.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，每当我计划旅行时，我真的很享受查找地方、列清单和对即将发生的事情感到兴奋。但说实话，这些都比不上真正到达那里的感觉，站在一个新地方，尝试食物，心想"我实现了这一切"。计划很有趣，但真实的事情总是比你想象的更好。• 转折【可选】 But then again, sometimes the reality doesn't quite match the plan — things go wrong, the weather is bad, or it's just not as good as you imagined — and in those cases people often look back and think the planning stage was actually the most enjoyable part. 但反过来说，有时现实与计划不太相符，事情出错、天气不好，或者就是没有你想象的那么好，在这些情况下，人们往往回头想，计划阶段实际上是最愉快的部分。

entries.text: Describe a change that you made recently

paragraphs: Something I changed recently was actually the way I was learning Japanese. I had been learning Japanese for about six months.
At first, I believed that watching online courses and reading textbooks would be enough. So I came up with a plan and followed it seriously.

But the results weren't great — I kept forgetting vocabulary and grammar, and without a real language environment, I felt like I was just going in circles. That's when my opinion changed — I realized I needed real practice, not just theory.

So I ended up changing my original plan as well, and decided to sign up for a one-week study programme in Japan last year. Honestly, it wasn't an easy decision — the programme wasn't cheap, and I had to take time off, so I hesitated for a bit.

But I figured it was worth the risk, so I went ahead and signed up. The programme was structured like this — every morning we had Japanese classes with local teachers, practising speaking face to face with classmates.

In the afternoons, we were out in the city, actually using Japanese in real situations — reading signs, ordering food, asking for directions. This time, there was no relying on textbooks — I just had to speak.

At first I was pretty nervous, and there were moments I got things completely wrong and felt a bit embarrassed. But by the end of the week, I could really feel my speaking improving — words that used to feel so unfamiliar just started coming out more naturally.
I was so happy with how much progress I'd made in just one week, way more than in the six months before it. Looking back, making that decision was just so crucial for me.

It totally changed my mindset — I realized language learning isn't about getting everything perfect, but actually using it to communicate. It also gave me so much more confidence — I realized I'm actually braver and more independent than I thought, which was huge personal growth for me.
paragraphsZh: 我最近改变的一件事，其实就是我学日语的方式。 我已经学日语大概六个月了。
一开始我以为看网课、读课本就足够了。 所以我制定了一个计划并且认真地执行了。
但效果并不好——我总是忘记单词和语法，而且没有一个真实的语言环境，感觉自己一直在原地打转。 就是在那个时候，我的看法改变了——我意识到我需要真正的实践，而不只是理论。
所以我最终也改变了原来的计划，决定报名参加了一个去年在日本的为期一周的学习项目。 说实话，这不是一个容易做的决定——这个项目并不便宜，而且我得请假，所以我犹豫了一下。
但我觉得值得冒这个险，所以我还是报名了。 这个项目大概是这样安排的——每天早上我们有当地老师上的日语课，跟同学面对面练习口语。
下午我们就在城市里，真正地在实际场景中使用日语——看标识、点餐、问路。 这一次，没办法依赖课本了——我只能开口说。
一开始我特别紧张，也有一些时候完全说错了，感觉有点尴尬。 但到那周结束的时候，我真的能感觉到自己的口语在进步——那些曾经很陌生的词句，开始更自然地脱口而出了。
我对自己在短短一周内取得的进步感到特别开心，比之前六个月自学的进步还要多。 回过头来看，做出那个决定对我来说真的很关键。
它彻底改变了我的思维方式——我意识到学语言不是要追求完美，而是要真正用它来交流。 这也让我变得更加自信——我意识到自己其实比想象中更勇敢、更独立，这对我来说是一次很大的个人成长。

entries.text: Do you think it is good to change one’s daily routine?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think changing your routine every now and then is actually really good for you — doing the exact same thing every day can make life feel repetitive and dull over time.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为偶尔改变你的习惯实际上对你很好，每天做完全相同的事情会随着时间推移让生活感觉重复和单调。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When you shake things up a bit — trying a new hobby, changing when you exercise, or even just taking a different route to work — it keeps your mind fresh and engaged. It also helps you discover things about yourself that you wouldn't find if you just stuck to the same pattern every day. But at the same time, having some stable structure is important too — without any routine at all, things can quickly feel chaotic and hard to manage.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当你稍微改变一下，尝试新爱好、改变锻炼时间，甚至只是走不同的路上班，它让你的思维保持新鲜和投入。它还帮助你发现自己。但同时，有一些稳定的结构也很重要，完全没有任何习惯，事情很快就会感觉混乱且难以管理。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a lot of people who work from home say that after months of the exact same schedule, they start feeling really drained and uninspired — but as soon as they change something small, like working from a café or adjusting their sleep time, they feel noticeably more motivated and refreshed.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，很多在家办公的人说，经过几个月完全相同的时间表后，他们开始感到非常疲惫和缺乏灵感，但一旦他们改变一些小事，比如在咖啡馆工作或调整睡眠时间，他们明显感到更有动力和精神焕发。转折【可选】 Even so, big sudden changes can be quite overwhelming — most people do better when changes happen gradually rather than all at once. 即便如此，突然的巨大变化可能相当令人不知所措，大多数人在变化逐渐发生而不是一次全部发生时表现更好。

Work from home exact same schedule drained uninspired
Overwhelming gradually not all at once

paragraphs: I think changing your routine every now and then is actually really good for you — doing the exact same thing every day can make life feel repetitive and dull over time.

When you shake things up a bit — trying a new hobby, changing when you exercise, or even just taking a different route to work — it keeps your mind fresh and engaged. It also helps you discover things about yourself that you wouldn't find if you just stuck to the same pattern every day. But at the same time, having some stable structure is important too — without any routine at all, things can quickly feel chaotic and hard to manage.

For instance, a lot of people who work from home say that after months of the exact same schedule, they start feeling really drained and uninspired — but as soon as they change something small, like working from a café or adjusting their sleep time, they feel noticeably more motivated and refreshed.

当你稍微改变一下，尝试新爱好、改变锻炼时间，甚至只是走不同的路上班，它让你的思维保持新鲜和投入。它还帮助你发现自己。但同时，有一些稳定的结构也很重要，完全没有任何习惯，事情很快就会感觉混乱且难以管理。

例如，很多在家办公的人说，经过几个月完全相同的时间表后，他们开始感到非常疲惫和缺乏灵感，但一旦他们改变一些小事，比如在咖啡馆工作或调整睡眠时间，他们明显感到更有动力和精神焕发。转折【可选】 Even so, big sudden changes can be quite overwhelming — most people do better when changes happen gradually rather than all at once. 即便如此，突然的巨大变化可能相当令人不知所措，大多数人在变化逐渐发生而不是一次全部发生时表现更好。

entries.text: Do you think it is good to change jobs?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think changing jobs can be really good — staying in the same job for too long without any growth can make people feel stuck and unmotivated.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为换工作真的很好，在同一份工作中待太久而没有任何成长会让人感到受困和缺乏动力。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Moving to a new job often means better pay, new skills, and fresh challenges — all of which help a person grow both professionally and personally. A lot of people also find that changing jobs gives them a chance to figure out what they actually want from their career, rather than just staying somewhere out of habit or fear of change. But switching jobs too frequently can also raise concerns — employers might wonder whether the person is reliable or committed.
ideaNotes.textZh: 换工作通常意味着更好的薪酬、新技能和新挑战，所有这些都帮助一个人在职业和个人方面成长。很多人也发现换工作给了他们一个机会弄清楚他们真正想要什么，而不只是出于习惯或害怕改变而留在某个地方。但换工作太频繁也会引发担忧，雇主可能会怀疑这个人是否可靠或有责任感。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, it's quite common to see people in their late twenties or thirties switching industries entirely — moving from finance to creative fields, or from corporate jobs to starting their own business — and a lot of them say it was one of the best decisions they ever made because they finally found work that felt meaningful.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，很常见看到二三十岁的人完全转行，从金融转到创意领域，或从企业工作转到创业，很多人说这是他们做过的最好决定之一，因为他们终于找到了感觉有意义的工作。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸

entries.text: Is it good for people to get a job promotion?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Getting a promotion is generally seen as a good thing — it means your work is being recognised and rewarded, which feels great for most people.
ideaNotes.textZh: 晋升通常被视为好事，它意味着你的工作被认可和奖励，这对大多数人来说感觉很好。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: A promotion usually comes with higher pay, more responsibility, and a greater sense of purpose, which can make someone feel much more invested and motivated at work. But it also brings more pressure and expectations — you're suddenly responsible for more people and bigger decisions, and not everyone handles that shift well. Some people actually find that after a promotion, the job they once loved starts to feel much more stressful and less enjoyable.
ideaNotes.textZh: 晋升通常伴随着更高的薪酬、更多责任和更强的目的感，这可以让某人在工作中感到更加投入和有动力。但它也带来更多压力和期望，你突然负责更多人和更大的决策，不是每个人都能很好地处理这种转变。一些人实际上发现晋升后，他们曾经热爱的工作开始感觉更加有压力且不那么令人愉快。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, it's quite common to hear people say they were much happier as a regular employee than after becoming a manager — the extra money is nice, but dealing with team conflicts, performance reviews, and constant pressure from above takes a real toll on people.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，经常听到人们说他们作为普通员工时比成为经理后快乐得多，额外的钱很好，但处理团队冲突、绩效评估和来自上面的持续压力对人们造成了真正的影响。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think whether a promotion is truly good depends on whether it aligns with what the person actually wants — for someone who values career growth and challenge, it's brilliant, but for someone who just wants a stable and manageable life, it might bring more stress than it's worth. 另外，我认为晋升是否真正好取决于它是否符合这个人真正想要的，对于重视职业成长和挑战的人来说，这很棒，但对于只想要稳定且可管理的生活的人来说，它可能带来的压力多于价值。

entries.text: Do people often make plans around their regular routines?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think most people do plan around their existing routines — it's just the most natural and practical way to fit new things into an already busy life.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为大多数人确实围绕现有习惯制定计划，这只是将新事物融入已经繁忙生活的最自然和实际的方式。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Most people have fixed commitments like work hours, family responsibilities, and regular obligations that they can't really move around, so any new plans naturally have to fit around those. It also gives people a sense of predictability and control — knowing roughly how your week will look makes it much easier to decide when you have space for something new.
ideaNotes.textZh: 大多数人有固定的承诺，如工作时间、家庭责任和定期义务，这些他们无法真正移动，所以任何新计划自然必须围绕这些安排。它还给人们一种可预测性和控制感，大致知道你的一周会是什么样子，使决定何时有空间做新事情变得容易得多。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, most working parents will only plan social activities or personal time around work schedules and school pick-ups — they're not going to book something on a Tuesday morning when they know they have a meeting. Everything else gets slotted in around the fixed points of their day.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，大多数在职父母只会围绕工作时间表和接送孩子计划社交活动或个人时间，他们不会在知道自己有会议的星期二早上预订什么。其他一切都被插入他们一天固定节点周围。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, people who don't have a regular routine often find it harder to make and stick to plans — without a clear framework, it's easy to keep putting things off because there's no obvious time to slot them in. 另外，没有固定习惯的人往往发现更难制定和坚持计划，没有清晰的框架，很容易不断推迟事情，因为没有明显的时间来安排它们。

entries.text: Who tend to change their daily routine more, young people or old people?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think young people tend to change their routines much more than older people — they're generally more open to new experiences and less attached to doing things a certain way.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为年轻人比老年人更倾向于改变习惯，他们通常对新体验更开放，对以特定方式做事的执着更少。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Young people are still at a stage where they're figuring out their lives — trying different jobs, moving to new cities, picking up and dropping hobbies — so their routines naturally shift a lot. Older people, on the other hand, have usually settled into a lifestyle that works for them and tend to find comfort and stability in doing the same things regularly. Change can feel more disruptive and unnecessary when you've already found a rhythm that suits you.
ideaNotes.textZh: 年轻人仍处于弄清楚自己生活的阶段，尝试不同工作、搬到新城市、开始和放弃爱好，所以他们的习惯自然会变化很多。另一方面，老年人通常已经定居于适合他们的生活方式，倾向于在定期做同样的事情中找到舒适和稳定。当你已经找到适合你的节奏时，改变可能感觉更加破坏性且不必要。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, it's really common to see young people completely overhauling their schedule after starting a new job or moving somewhere new, while older people — especially retirees — often have a very fixed and predictable daily structure that they stick to almost without thinking, like morning walks, regular mealtimes, and set TV programmes in the evening.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，经常看到年轻人在开始新工作或搬到新地方后完全改变他们的时间表，而老年人，尤其是退休人员，通常有一个非常固定且可预测的日常结构，他们几乎不假思索地坚持，比如早晨散步、固定用餐时间和晚上固定的电视节目。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, as people get older, their bodies and energy levels also play a role — keeping a consistent routine often just feels better physically, whereas young people have the energy to adapt and experiment without it taking as much of a toll. 另外，随着人们年龄增长，他们的身体和精力水平也起着作用，保持一致的习惯通常在身体上感觉更好，而年轻人有精力适应和尝试而不需要付出太多代价。

entries.text: Describe a time you made an important decision and were happy with the result

paragraphs: One important decision I made was signing up for a short-term study programme in Japan. I had been learning Japanese for about six months.
At first, I believed that watching online courses and reading textbooks would be enough. So I came up with a plan and followed it seriously.

But the results weren't great — I kept forgetting vocabulary and grammar, and without a real language environment, I felt like I was just going in circles. That's when my opinion changed — I realized I needed real practice, not just theory.

So I ended up changing my original plan as well, and decided to sign up for a one-week study programme in Japan last year. Honestly, it wasn't an easy decision — the programme wasn't cheap, and I had to take time off, so I hesitated for a bit.

But I figured it was worth the risk, so I went ahead and signed up. The programme was structured like this — every morning we had Japanese classes with local teachers, practising speaking face to face with classmates.

In the afternoons, we were out in the city, actually using Japanese in real situations — reading signs, ordering food, asking for directions. This time, there was no relying on textbooks — I just had to speak.

At first I was pretty nervous, and there were moments I got things completely wrong and felt a bit embarrassed. But by the end of the week, I could really feel my speaking improving — words that used to feel so unfamiliar just started coming out more naturally.
I was so happy with how much progress I'd made in just one week, way more than in the six months before it. Looking back, making that decision was just so crucial for me.

It totally changed my mindset — I realized language learning isn't about getting everything perfect, but actually using it to communicate. It also gave me so much more confidence — I realized I'm actually braver and more independent than I thought, which was huge personal growth for me.
paragraphsZh: 我做过的一个重要决定，就是报名参加了一个在日本的短期学习项目。 我已经学日语大概六个月了。
一开始我以为看网课、读课本就足够了。 所以我制定了一个计划并且认真地执行了。
但效果并不好——我总是忘记单词和语法，而且没有一个真实的语言环境，感觉自己一直在原地打转。 就是在那个时候，我的看法改变了——我意识到我需要真正的实践，而不只是理论。
所以我最终也改变了原来的计划，决定报名参加了一个去年在日本的为期一周的学习项目。 说实话，这不是一个容易做的决定——这个项目并不便宜，而且我得请假，所以我犹豫了一下。
但我觉得值得冒这个险，所以我还是报名了。 这个项目大概是这样安排的——每天早上我们有当地老师上的日语课，跟同学面对面练习口语。
下午我们就在城市里，真正地在实际场景中使用日语——看标识、点餐、问路。 这一次，没办法依赖课本了——我只能开口说。
一开始我特别紧张，也有一些时候完全说错了，感觉有点尴尬。 但到那周结束的时候，我真的能感觉到自己的口语在进步——那些曾经很陌生的词句，开始更自然地脱口而出了。
我对自己在短短一周内取得的进步感到特别开心，比之前六个月自学的进步还要多。 回过头来看，做出那个决定对我来说真的很关键。
它彻底改变了我的思维方式——我意识到学语言不是要追求完美，而是要真正用它来交流。 这也让我变得更加自信——我意识到自己其实比想象中更勇敢、更独立，这对我来说是一次很大的个人成长。

entries.text: Do you think children sometimes have to make important decisions?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think children do face decisions that matter — even if adults don't see them as a big deal, to the child they can feel really significant and stressful.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为孩子确实面临重要的决定，即使成年人不觉得是大事，对孩子来说可能感觉非常重要和有压力。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: I mean, kids have to make choices all the time — who to be friends with, whether to speak up when something feels wrong, what to spend their time on — and even though these things might seem small, they actually require real thought and judgement. Going through those small decisions is how children slowly get better at making bigger ones later on.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我的意思是，孩子一直都在做选择，和谁做朋友、当感觉不对时是否发声、把时间花在什么上，即使这些事情看起来很小，它们实际上需要真正的思考和判断。经历这些小决定是孩子慢慢在以后做更大决定时变得更好的方式。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember once having to decide whether to tell a teacher about something wrong happening at school — it sounds simple but at the time it felt really difficult and important because I knew whatever I chose would have consequences.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得有一次不得不决定是否告诉老师学校发生的不对的事情，听起来简单但当时感觉真的很困难和重要，因为我知道无论我选择什么都会有后果。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, letting children make small decisions and deal with whatever happens is actually one of the best things adults can do — kids learn so much more from going through it themselves than from being told what to do. 另外，让孩子做小决定并处理发生的事情实际上是成年人可以做的最好的事情之一，孩子从自己经历中学到的比被告知该做什么多得多。

entries.text: What important decisions do teenagers need to make after graduation?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest decisions teenagers face after graduation are around further education, career direction, and how independent they want to become.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为青少年毕业后面临的最大决定围绕继续深造、职业方向，以及他们想要变得多独立。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: The choice between going to university, getting a job straight away, or doing something else entirely is genuinely huge because it sets the direction for so much of what comes after. And within those choices there are more decisions — which subject to study, which city to live in, whether to follow what parents want or go your own way — and most teenagers have to figure all of this out at a time when they're still working out who they are.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在上大学、直接工作或完全做其他事情之间的选择真的很重大，因为它为之后很多事情设定了方向。在这些选择中还有更多决定，学什么专业、住在哪个城市、是否遵循父母的意愿或走自己的路，大多数青少年不得不在他们仍在弄清楚自己是谁的时候搞清楚这一切。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, when I finished high school the decision of which university and which major to choose felt absolutely overwhelming — everyone around me had opinions, my parents had expectations, and I had my own ideas, and trying to balance all of that while also thinking about my actual future was really stressful and confusing.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，当我高中毕业时，选择哪所大学和哪个专业的决定感觉绝对让人不知所措，我周围的每个人都有意见，我父母有期望，我有自己的想法，同时考虑这一切以及我真实的未来真的有压力且令人困惑。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, even small practical decisions like whether to stay close to home or move somewhere new can be really defining — they affect your social life, independence, and sense of identity in ways that are hard to predict at the time. 另外，甚至像是留在家附近还是搬到新地方这样的小实际决定也可以真的很有决定性，它们以当时难以预测的方式影响你的社交生活、独立性和身份认同感。

entries.text: Who can children turn to for help when making a decision?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the people children naturally turn to most are their parents and teachers — they're the adults closest to the child's life and usually have the most genuine interest in helping.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为孩子自然最多求助的人是他们的父母和老师，他们是最接近孩子生活的成年人，通常最真诚地有兴趣提供帮助。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Parents know their child better than almost anyone, so they can give advice that's personalised and comes from a place of real care. Teachers, on the other hand, have a different perspective — they've seen lots of students go through similar situations and can offer more objective and experience-based guidance. And of course, friends matter too — children often feel more comfortable talking to peers because they're going through the same things and there's less judgment.
ideaNotes.textZh: 父母比几乎任何人都更了解他们的孩子，所以他们可以给出个性化且出自真正关心的建议。另一方面，老师有不同的视角，他们见过很多学生经历类似情况，可以提供更加客观和基于经验的指导。当然，朋友也很重要，孩子通常感觉更舒适地和同龄人交谈，因为他们正在经历同样的事情，评判更少。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, when I had to make a decision about which direction to take after school, I talked to my parents first, but I also found it really helpful to speak to a teacher I trusted who had seen many students in the same position — they gave me a much more realistic and balanced view than I could have got just from family.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，当我不得不做出关于毕业后走哪个方向的决定时，我首先和父母谈，但我也发现和一位我信任的老师交谈真的很有帮助，他见过很多处于同样位置的学生，他们给了我比只从家人那里能得到的更加现实和平衡的

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, as children get older they might also look online for guidance — reading about other people's experiences or watching videos about the decision they're facing can actually be surprisingly useful and reassuring, as long as they're careful about where the information comes from. 另外，随着孩子年龄增长，他们也可能在网上寻求指导，阅读其他人的经历或观看关于他们面临决定的视频，实际上可以出乎意料地有用和令人放心，只要他们对信息来源谨慎。

entries.text: Do you think advertisements can influence our decisions when shopping?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, absolutely — I think advertising influences our shopping decisions way more than most people realise, and a lot of the time we don't even notice it happening.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，绝对是，我认为广告对我们购物决定的影响远超大多数人意识到的，很多时候我们甚至没有注意到它在发生。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Advertising works by repeatedly putting a brand or product in front of you until it starts to feel familiar and trustworthy — so when you're standing in a shop trying to decide between two similar products, you almost automatically reach for the one you've seen advertised, even if you don't consciously remember seeing the ad. It creates a feeling of familiarity that feels like trust.
ideaNotes.textZh: 广告通过反复将品牌或产品呈现在你面前直到它开始感觉熟悉和值得信赖，所以当你站在商店里试图在两个类似产品之间做决定时，你几乎自动拿起你见过广告的那个，即使你不记得有意识地看过广告。它创造了一种感觉像信任的熟悉感。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I've noticed that when I'm buying something like skincare or food, I almost always end up choosing the brand I've seen advertised on Douyin or Xiaohongshu, even when I had no particular reason to prefer it — the advertising had already done its job without me knowing.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我注意到当我购买护肤品或食品时，我几乎总是最终选择我在抖音或小红书上见过广告的品牌，即使我没有特别的理由更喜欢它，广告已经在我不知情的情况下完成了它的工作。• 转折【可选】 That said, people who are more aware of how advertising works are generally better at making more conscious and independent choices — knowing that you're being targeted makes you stop and actually think before you buy. 话虽如此，更了解广告如何运作的人通常更擅长做出更加有意识和独立的选择，知道你是目标对象会让你停下来在购买前真正思考。

entries.text: Do you think the influence of advertising is good?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think advertising has both good and bad sides — it can be genuinely useful, but it can also push people into buying things they don't need and create a culture of overconsumption.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为广告有好有坏，它可以真正有用，但也可以推动人们购买他们不需要的东西，创造一种过度消费的文化。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: On the positive side, advertising helps people discover new products and services that might genuinely improve their lives, and it supports businesses — especially smaller ones — to reach customers they wouldn't otherwise find. But on the negative side, a lot of advertising is designed to make people feel insecure or like they're missing out, which leads to unnecessary spending and even debt for some people.
ideaNotes.textZh: 积极方面，广告帮助人们发现可能真正改善生活的新产品和服务，并支持企业，尤其是较小的企业，触达他们否则无法找到的客户。但消极方面，很多广告被设计成让人感到不安全或错过什么，这导致一些人不必要的消费甚至负债。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I've seen so many people — including myself — buy things purely because of how they were advertised rather than because they actually needed them, and then the item just sits there unused. The advertising created a desire that wasn't really there before.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我见过很多人，包括我自己，纯粹因为广告的方式而购买东西，而不是因为真正需要它们，然后物品只是放在那里没有使用。广告创造了一种之前并不真正存在的欲望。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, advertising aimed at children is something I find particularly concerning — kids don't have the ability to critically think about what they're being sold, so they're very easily influenced in ways that put a lot of pressure on parents too. 另外，针对孩子的广告是我觉得特别令人担忧的，孩子没有能力批判性地思考他们被销售的东西，所以他们很容易被影响，这也给父母带来很大压力。

source.label: 腾讯文档《雅思口语9-12月题库【Part123】》

entries.text: How do people usually make important decisions?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think most people make important decisions by thinking through the pros and cons and talking to people they trust — very few people just go with their gut on something really significant.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为大多数人通过权衡利弊和与他们信任的人交谈来做出重要决定，很少有人在真正重要的事情上只是凭直觉行事。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: I mean, when a decision really matters, most people don't just go with their gut — they'll talk to people they trust, do some research, and think carefully about how it might affect their life. But emotions play a big role too — sometimes you've thought everything through and it all makes sense on paper, but something just doesn't feel right, and that feeling is often hard to ignore.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我的意思是，当一个决定真的很重要时，大多数人不会只是凭直觉，他们会和信任的人交谈、做一些研究，并仔细思考它可能如何影响他们的生活。但情感也起着很大作用，有时你已经想清楚了一切，纸面上都说得通，但就是感觉不对，那种感觉往往很难忽视。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, when I had to decide on my university major, I spent weeks talking to people, reading about different career paths, and making lists of what mattered to me — but in the end, the thing that actually tipped the decision was just a feeling that one option felt more right and exciting than the others.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，当我不得不决定大学专业时，我花了几周时间和人们交谈、阅读不同的职业道路，并列出对我重要的事情，但最终，真正促成决定的是一种感觉，一个选项感觉比其他选项更正确和令人兴奋。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, a lot of people find it helpful to sleep on it before deciding — giving yourself time to let things settle in your head often makes the right choice much clearer than trying to force a decision in the moment. 另外，很多人发现在决定之前睡一觉很有帮助，给自己时间让事情在脑海中沉淀往往比试图当场强迫做决定更能让正确的选择变得清晰。

keyPhrases.phrase: Pros and cons talk to people trust
Doesn't feel right hard to ignore
University major weeks talking reading lists
One option felt more right and exciting
Sleep on it things settle in your head clearer choice

paragraphs: I think most people make important decisions by thinking through the pros and cons and talking to people they trust — very few people just go with their gut on something really significant.

I mean, when a decision really matters, most people don't just go with their gut — they'll talk to people they trust, do some research, and think carefully about how it might affect their life. But emotions play a big role too — sometimes you've thought everything through and it all makes sense on paper, but something just doesn't feel right, and that feeling is often hard to ignore.

For instance, when I had to decide on my university major, I spent weeks talking to people, reading about different career paths, and making lists of what mattered to me — but in the end, the thing that actually tipped the decision was just a feeling that one option felt more right and exciting than the others.
paragraphsZh: 我认为大多数人通过权衡利弊和与他们信任的人交谈来做出重要决定，很少有人在真正重要的事情上只是凭直觉行事。
我的意思是，当一个决定真的很重要时，大多数人不会只是凭直觉，他们会和信任的人交谈、做一些研究，并仔细思考它可能如何影响他们的生活。但情感也起着很大作用，有时你已经想清楚了一切，纸面上都说得通，但就是感觉不对，那种感觉往往很难忽视。
例如，当我不得不决定大学专业时，我花了几周时间和人们交谈、阅读不同的职业道路，并列出对我重要的事情，但最终，真正促成决定的是一种感觉，一个选项感觉比其他选项更正确和令人兴奋。

可选】 And also, a lot of people find it helpful to sleep on it before deciding — giving yourself time to let things settle in your head often makes the right choice much clearer than trying to force a decision in the moment. 另外，很多人发现在决定之前睡一觉很有帮助，给自己时间让事情在脑海中沉淀往往比试图当场强迫做决定更能让正确的选择变得清晰。

entries.text: Describe a long-term goal/ambition you would like to achieve

paragraphs: Learning Japanese fluently has been one of my main goals recently. I had been learning Japanese for about six months.
At first, I believed that watching online courses and reading textbooks would be enough. So I came up with a plan and followed it seriously.

But the results weren't great — I kept forgetting vocabulary and grammar, and without a real language environment, I felt like I was just going in circles. That's when my opinion changed — I realized I needed real practice, not just theory.

So I ended up changing my original plan as well, and decided to sign up for a one-week study programme in Japan last year. Honestly, it wasn't an easy decision — the programme wasn't cheap, and I had to take time off, so I hesitated for a bit.

But I figured it was worth the risk, so I went ahead and signed up. The programme was structured like this — every morning we had Japanese classes with local teachers, practising speaking face to face with classmates.

In the afternoons, we were out in the city, actually using Japanese in real situations — reading signs, ordering food, asking for directions. This time, there was no relying on textbooks — I just had to speak.

At first I was pretty nervous, and there were moments I got things completely wrong and felt a bit embarrassed. But by the end of the week, I could really feel my speaking improving — words that used to feel so unfamiliar just started coming out more naturally.
I was so happy with how much progress I'd made in just one week, way more than in the six months before it. Looking back, making that decision was just so crucial for me.

It totally changed my mindset — I realized language learning isn't about getting everything perfect, but actually using it to communicate. It also gave me so much more confidence — I realized I'm actually braver and more independent than I thought, which was huge personal growth for me.
paragraphsZh: 流利地说日语其实一直是我最近最重要的目标之一。 我已经学日语大概六个月了。
一开始我以为看网课、读课本就足够了。 所以我制定了一个计划并且认真地执行了。
但效果并不好——我总是忘记单词和语法，而且没有一个真实的语言环境，感觉自己一直在原地打转。 就是在那个时候，我的看法改变了——我意识到我需要真正的实践，而不只是理论。
所以我最终也改变了原来的计划，决定报名参加了一个去年在日本的为期一周的学习项目。 说实话，这不是一个容易做的决定——这个项目并不便宜，而且我得请假，所以我犹豫了一下。
但我觉得值得冒这个险，所以我还是报名了。 这个项目大概是这样安排的——每天早上我们有当地老师上的日语课，跟同学面对面练习口语。
下午我们就在城市里，真正地在实际场景中使用日语——看标识、点餐、问路。 这一次，没办法依赖课本了——我只能开口说。
一开始我特别紧张，也有一些时候完全说错了，感觉有点尴尬。 但到那周结束的时候，我真的能感觉到自己的口语在进步——那些曾经很陌生的词句，开始更自然地脱口而出了。
我对自己在短短一周内取得的进步感到特别开心，比之前六个月自学的进步还要多。 回过头来看，做出那个决定对我来说真的很关键。
它彻底改变了我的思维方式——我意识到学语言不是要追求完美，而是要真正用它来交流。 这也让我变得更加自信——我意识到自己其实比想象中更勇敢、更独立，这对我来说是一次很大的个人成长。

entries.text: Why should children have ambitions?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think having ambitions is really important for children because it gives them something to work towards and get excited about — without any sense of direction, it's easy to just drift along without much purpose.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为有抱负对孩子来说非常重要，因为它给他们一些努力的方向和感到兴奋的事情，没有任何方向感，很容易就随波逐流而没有太多目的。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When a child has something they genuinely want to achieve, they're naturally more motivated to study, practise, and push through difficult moments. Ambition also helps children discover who they are — by setting goals and working towards them, they learn what they're good at, what they enjoy, and what kind of person they want to become.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当一个孩子有真正想要实现的事情时，他们自然更有动力学习、练习和度过困难时刻。抱负也帮助孩子发现自己是谁，通过设定目标和为之努力，他们了解自己擅长什么、喜欢什么以及想成为什么样的人。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a child who dreams of becoming a doctor or an athlete will put in more effort at school or training because they can see a reason for it — compared to a child with no particular goal who might struggle to find the motivation to try hard at anything.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，梦想成为医生或运动员的孩子会在学校或训练中付出更多努力，因为他们能看到原因，与没有特定目标、可能难以找到努力做任何事情的动力的孩子相比。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, even if a child's ambitions change as they grow up — which they almost always do — the habit of having goals and working towards them stays with them, and that's one of the most useful things a person can carry into adult life. 另外，即使孩子的抱负随着成长而改变，这几乎总是会发生，有目标并为之努力的习惯会伴随着他们，这是一个人能带入成年生活的最有用的东西之一。

entries.text: What do you think of people going after high positions?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think it's completely natural and understandable for people to want to move up and take on bigger roles — ambition is a normal part of being human.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们想要晋升并承担更大角色是完全自然且可以理解的，抱负是人类的正常组成部分。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Wanting a high position isn't a bad thing in itself — it often means someone is motivated, hardworking, and wants to make a bigger impact. The issue is more about how they go about it — people who work hard, develop their skills, and earn their way up are admirable, but those who step on others, take credit, or compromise their values just to climb the ladder are a different story.
ideaNotes.textZh: 想要高职位本身不是坏事，它往往意味着某人有动力、勤奋且想要产生更大的影响。问题更多在于他们如何实现它，努力工作、发展技能、凭实力晋升的人令人钦佩，但那些踩着别人、揽功或为了爬上阶梯而妥协自己的价值观的人则是另一回事。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I really admire people who work their way up from the bottom and eventually reach a senior position through years of dedication — that kind of success feels genuinely earned and inspiring. But I've also seen people who are so focused on getting promoted that they stop caring about doing good work or treating colleagues well, which I think is quite sad.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我非常钦佩那些从底层做起，通过多年的奉献最终达到高级职位的人，那种成功感觉真正值得且鼓舞人心。但我也见过一些人如此专注于晋升，以至于不再关心做好工作或善待同事，我认为这相当令人遗憾。转折【可选】 Even so, I think it's worth remembering that high positions come with a lot of pressure and responsibility — some people chase them without realising how much stress and sacrifice is actually involved, and end up regretting it. 即便如此，我认为值得记住的是高职位伴随着很多压力和责任，一些人追求它们而没有意识到实际上涉及多少压力和牺牲，最终后悔了。

entries.text: Why are some young people keen on being fans of superstars?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think young people become fans of superstars mainly because it gives them a sense of excitement, identity, and belonging that can be hard to find elsewhere at that stage of life.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为年轻人成为超级明星的粉丝主要是因为它给了他们一种兴奋感、身份认同和归属感，在那个人生阶段很难在其他地方找到。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Being a fan gives you something to be passionate about and look forward to — new music, new content, upcoming events — which makes everyday life feel more exciting. It also connects you to a community of people who share the same interest, which for young people who are still figuring out who they are, can feel really meaningful and comforting. And a lot of fans also genuinely admire and look up to the person they follow, seeing them as a kind of role model.
ideaNotes.textZh: 成为粉丝给你一些充满热情并期待的事情，新音乐、新内容、即将到来的活动，这让日常生活感觉更加令人兴奋。它还将你与分享相同兴趣的人社区联系起来，对于仍在弄清楚自己是谁的年轻人来说，这可以感觉非常有意义和令人安慰。很多粉丝也真正钦佩和仰望他们追随的人，把他们视为某种榜样。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I know people who started following a K-pop group in their early teens and said it genuinely helped them get through some tough and lonely periods — the music, the community, and having something to be excited about made a real difference to how they felt day to day.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识一些人在十几岁时开始追随一个韩流组合，他们说这真的帮助他们度过了一些艰难和孤独的时期，音乐、社区，以及有些令人兴奋的事情，对他们日常感受产生了真正的影响。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, in the age of social media, being a fan has become much more interactive and personal — fans can follow their favourite stars closely online, feel like they know them, and even interact with them directly, which makes the whole experience feel a lot more real and intense. 另外，在社交媒体时代，成为粉丝变得更加互动和个人化，粉丝可以在网上密切关注他们喜爱的明星，感觉他们了解他们，甚至直接与他们互动，这使整个体验感觉更加真实和强烈。

entries.text: Is it good for a person to be ambitious?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think being ambitious is generally a good thing — it pushes people to grow and achieve things they wouldn't otherwise.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为有抱负总体上是好事，它推动人们成长并实现他们否则不会实现的事情。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Without any ambition, people tend to just stay comfortable and never really challenge themselves, which means they often end up feeling unfulfilled. Ambition gives you energy and direction — it's what makes you study harder, work more creatively, and keep going when things get difficult. But it becomes a problem when someone is so focused on their goals that they start neglecting the people around them or sacrificing their health and wellbeing just to get ahead.
ideaNotes.textZh: 没有任何抱负，人们往往只是保持舒适，从不真正挑战自己，这意味着他们往往最终感到不满足。抱负给你能量和方向，它让你更努力学习、更有创意地工作，并在事情变困难时继续前进。但当某人如此专注于目标以至于开始忽视周围的人，或为了出人头地而牺牲健康和幸福时，它就成了问题。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I think the most successful and genuinely happy people I know are those who have clear goals but also know when to slow down — they work hard but also make time for family, friendships, and looking after themselves. That balance is what makes ambition healthy rather than destructive.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认为我认识的最成功且真正快乐的人是那些有明确目标但也知道何时放慢脚步的人，他们努力工作，但也为家庭、友谊和照顾自己腾出时间。这种平衡使抱负健康而不是破坏性的。转折【可选】 Even so, I think a little ambition is better than none — even if someone doesn't achieve everything they set out to do, the act of trying and pushing yourself tends to lead to a more interesting and fulfilling life than just sitting back and letting things happen. 即便如此，我认为有一点抱负总比没有好，即使某人没有实现他们设定的一切，尝试和推动自己的行为往往比只是坐下来让事情发生带来更有趣和充实的生活。

But it becomes a problem when someone is so focused on their goals that they start neglecting the people around them or sacrificing their health and wellbeing just to get ahead.

For instance, I think the most successful and genuinely happy people I know are those who have clear goals but also know when to slow down — they work hard but also make time for family, friendships, and looking after themselves. That balance is what makes ambition healthy rather than destructive.

entries.text: Do you think it is necessary to be ambitious when working in a team in a company?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think some level of ambition is helpful in a team, but it needs to be the right kind — ambition that drives you to do your best work rather than ambition that makes you compete against your own teammates.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为团队中一定程度的抱负是有帮助的，但需要是正确的那种，驱使你尽最大努力工作的抱负，而不是让你与队友竞争的抱负。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When team members are personally motivated and care about doing well, it naturally raises the standard for everyone — people push each other to be better and the whole team benefits. But when someone is only focused on standing out and getting credit for themselves, it creates tension and breaks the trust that makes a team work well together. The best teams have members who are ambitious about the team's success, not just their own.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当团队成员个人有动力且关心做好时，它自然提高了每个人的标准，人们互相推动变得更好，整个团队受益。但当某人只专注于脱颖而出并为自己揽功时，它会制造紧张并破坏信任，而信任使团队能够良好合作。最好的团队有对团队成功有抱负的成员，而不只是对自己的成功。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I've seen group projects where one person was clearly just trying to take over and get all the recognition, and it made everyone else feel undervalued and unmotivated — the whole dynamic fell apart. But when everyone in a group genuinely cares about making the project as good as possible, the energy is completely different and the results show it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我见过一些小组项目，其中一个人显然只是想接管并获得所有认可，这让其他人感到不被重视和缺乏动力，整个合作氛围崩溃了。但当小组中的每个人都真正关心使项目尽可能好时，氛围完全不同，结果也体现出来。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, in a company setting, showing ambition through taking initiative and suggesting new ideas is actually really valued — it shows you care about the work and want to contribute, which is very different from just being self-serving. 另外，在公司环境中，通过主动采取行动和提出新想法展示抱负实际上非常受重视，它表明你关心工作并想要贡献，这与只是自私自利非常不同。

entries.text: Should parents support their children in pursuing their ambitions?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think parents should absolutely support their children's ambitions — feeling backed by your parents makes a huge difference to whether a child is willing to try and keep going when things get hard.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为父母绝对应该支持孩子的抱负，感受到父母的支持对孩子是否愿意尝试并在事情变难时继续前进有巨大影响。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When children know their parents believe in them, they feel more confident taking risks and pursuing things that might seem difficult or uncertain. But support doesn't mean doing everything for them or pushing them too hard — the best kind of support is encouraging them, being there when they fail, and helping them figure out their own path rather than deciding it for them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当孩子知道父母相信他们时，他们对冒险和追求可能看起来困难或不确定的事情感到更自信。但支持不意味着为他们做所有事情或过于逼迫他们，最好的支持是鼓励他们、在他们失败时陪伴他们，帮助他们找出自己的道路，而不是替他们决定。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I know someone whose parents always pushed her towards a career in medicine even though she wanted to study art — she eventually gave up her dream and has always regretted it. Compare that to a friend whose parents supported his passion for music even when it seemed risky, and he's now doing really well doing something he genuinely loves.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识一个人，她的父母总是推动她从事医学职业，尽管她想学艺术，她最终放弃了梦想，一直后悔。相比之下，我的一个朋友，他的父母支持他对音乐的热情，即使看起来有风险，他现在做着真正热爱的事情，表现非常好。转折【可选】 Even so, there are times when parents need to gently guide their children — if an ambition seems completely unrealistic or harmful, a good parent will find a way to have an honest conversation about it rather than just blindly cheering them on. 即便如此，有时父母需要温和地引导孩子，如果一个抱负看起来完全不现实或有害，好的父母会找到方式进行诚实的对话，而不只是盲目地为他们加油。

entries.text: Describe a person who is good at learning and speaking new languages

paragraphs: The person I'd like to talk about is my childhood best friend. We've known each other for a long time — actually, more than 20 years.
We first met in kindergarten as classmates, and just got closer and closer from then on. Actually, she wasn't naturally gifted at learning and speaking languages.

She told me that when she first started learning Japanese, she tried all kinds of things — like watching online courses, reading textbooks, using language apps. But no matter how hard she tried, she was just going in circles and making no real progress.

Then one day, she made up her mind to find a completely different way to learn — that is, she signed up for a short-term study programme in Japan. The programme was basically structured like this: every morning she had Japanese classes taught by local teachers, and in class they constantly practised speaking face to face with classmates.

Then in the afternoons, she was out in the city using the language in real life situations — like reading signs, ordering food, and asking for directions. She told me it was challenging at first, but by the end of the programme, her speaking had improved so much.

What really impresses me is that she took this same method and applied it to other languages too — and that's how she learned French and Spanish. So now she can speak Japanese, French, and Spanish on top of her native language.
I really admire her — she's hardworking, never gives up, and was smart enough to figure out what actually works for her. She really inspired me too.
I think everyone needs to find their own way of learning a language, just like she did, and that's something I'm still working on myself.
paragraphsZh: 我想聊的是我的童年好友。 我们认识很久了——其实已经超过20年了。
我们在幼儿园作为同班同学第一次相识，从那以后就越来越亲近。 其实，她并不是天生就擅长学习和说语言的。
她告诉我，当她刚开始学日语的时候，她尝试了各种各样的方法——比如看网课、读教材、用语言学习app。 但不管她多努力，就是原地打转，没有任何实质性的进步。
后来有一天，她下定决心要找一种完全不同的学习方式——也就是说，她报名参加了日本的一个短期游学项目。 这个项目大概是这样安排的：每天早上她上由当地老师教的日语课，课堂上他们经常面对面练习口语。
然后下午，她出去在城市里，在真实场景中使用这门语言——比如看路牌、点餐、问路。 她告诉我一开始很有挑战性，但到项目结束时，她的口语进步了很多。
真正让我佩服的是，她把同样的方法迁移到了其他语言上——这就是她学会法语和西班牙语的方式。 所以现在她除了母语，还能说日语、法语和西班牙语。
我真的很佩服她——她勤奋努力，从不放弃，而且足够聪明找到了真正适合自己的方法。 她也真的激励了我。
我觉得每个人都需要找到自己的语言学习方式，就像她一样，而这也是我目前还在努力探索的事情。

entries.text: Are there many people who can speak foreign languages in your country?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Well, I think a lot of people in China have studied English, but only a small percentage can actually speak it fluently.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为中国有很多人学过英语，但真正能流利使用的人只占少数。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: This is because the education system tends to focus more on grammar and exams rather than actual communication, so students spend years learning English but rarely get the chance to practice speaking.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这是因为教育体系更侧重于语法和考试，而非实际交流，所以学生学了多年英语，却很少有机会练习口语。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I myself studied English for over ten years in school, but I still felt nervous and lo st the first time I tried to have a real conversation with a foreign teacher.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我自己在学校学了超过十年英语，但第一次尝试与外教进行真正对话时，仍然感到紧张和不知所措。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸[可选]
ideaNotes.text: However, if the teaching method shifted more towards speaking and listening practice, I believe far more Chinese people would be able to communicate confidently in English.
ideaNotes.textZh: 然而，如果教学方式更多地转向口语和听力练习，我相信会有更多中国人能够自信地用英语交流。

entries.text: Does speaking other languages help at work?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think speaking a foreign language definitely gives you an edge in the workplace, especially in international companies.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为会说外语在职场中绝对让你更有竞争力，尤其是在国际公司。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: This is because companies are increasingly working with overseas clients and partners, so employees who can communicate across languages are far more valuable to the team.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这是因为公司越来越多地与海外客户和合作伙伴合作，能够跨语言沟通的员工对团队来说价值更高。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, a colleague of mine got promoted much faster than others simply because she could handle English meetings and negotiate with foreign clients directly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我的一位同事晋升速度比其他人快得多，就因为她能主持英语会议并直接与外国客户谈判。• 转折【可选】However, if your job is purely domestic-focused, speaking another language may not make as big a difference in your daily work. 然而，如果你的工作完全以国内业务为主，外语能力在日常工作中可能不会带来那么大的差异。

entries.text: Do people learn any languages other than English?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think more and more people are starting to learn languages beyond English, especially Japanese, Korean, and French.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为越来越多的人开始学习英语以外的语言，尤其是日语、韩语和法语。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: This is largely driven by pop culture, such as K-pop, anime, and French films, which make people curious about the language behind the content they enjoy.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这很大程度上是由流行文化推动的，比如韩流、动漫和法国电影，让人们对自己喜欢的内容背后的语言产生了好奇。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, many of my friends started learning Korean simply because they were obsessed with K-dramas, and they just wanted to understand the dialogue without subtitles.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我很多朋友开始学韩语，纯粹是因为痴迷于韩剧，想不看字幕就能听懂对话。• 转折【可选】 However, if it weren't for this cultural influence, most people would probably still stick to English only, as it remains the most practical choice for career and travel. 然而，如果不是这种文化影响，大多数人可能仍然只学英语，因为它在职业和旅行方面依然是最实用的选择。

entries.text: Why is it easier for children to learn new things than for adults?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the main reason is that children's brains are like a sponge, they just soak everything up naturally without even trying.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为主要原因是孩子的大脑就像一块海绵，他们不需要刻意努力就能吸收一切。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: This is because children have no fear of making mistakes, and they don't overthink things. They just jump in and try, which means they pick things up much faster than adults who tend to worry too much about getting it wrong.
ideaNotes.textZh: 这是因为孩子不怕犯错，也不会想太多，他们只是直接上手去试，这意味着他们比总是过于担心出错的成人学得快得多。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I have a little cousin who started picking up English words just from watching cartoons every day, without any formal lessons at all. Adults would never learn that effortlessly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我有个小表弟，仅仅通过每天看动画片就开始学会了英语单词，完全没有上过正式的课。成人绝对不可能学得这么轻松。转折【可选】 However, if adults really put their mind to it and create the right habits and routine, they can still make great progress, just maybe not as naturally and quickly as kids do. 然而，如果成人真的下定决心并养成良好的习惯和规律，他们仍然可以取得很大进步，只是可能不像孩子那样自然和迅速。

entries.text: How do people learn new things?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Well, I think people learn new things in all sorts of ways, but the most common ones are through formal education, personal experience, and learning from other people.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们通过各种方式学习新事物，但最常见的是通过正规教育、个人经历以及向他人学习。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Some people prefer to learn in a structured environment like school or classes, while others just pick things up naturally through daily life and experience. And a lot of people now also learn through online platforms like YouTube or social media.
ideaNotes.textZh: 有些人喜欢在有组织的环境中学习，比如学校或课堂；而另一些人则通过日常生活和经历自然地习得新事物。如今很多人也通过网络平台如YouTube或社交媒体来学习。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I personally learned how to edit videos not from any class, but just by watching tutorials online and copying what others did until I figured it out myself.

entries.text: What is the most important thing for learning a language well?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most important thing is actually using the language in real situations — not just studying it from books or memorising grammar rules.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为最重要的是真正在实际情况中使用语言，而不只是从书本上学习或背语法规则。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: I mean, you can spend years learning vocabulary and grammar, but if you never actually speak or use it, you won't really make progress. The brain picks up language best when you're actively communicating and making real mistakes — that's when things actually stick. People who improve fastest are usually the ones who just throw themselves in and aren't afraid to sound imperfect.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我的意思是，你可以花多年学习词汇和语法，但如果你从不真正说或使用它，你不会真正取得进步。当你积极沟通和犯真实错误时，大脑对语言的吸收最好，那才是真正记住的时候。进步最快的人通常是那些直接投入、不怕听起来不完美的人。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I improved so much more from chatting with people online and watching shows without subtitles than from all the grammar exercises I did in school — real exposure just works in a completely different way.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我从在网上和人聊天、不看字幕看节目中取得的进步，远比在学校做的所有语法练习多，真实接触的效果就是完全不同。• 转折【可选】 Even so, having some basic foundation first does help — if you jump in with absolutely no knowledge, it can feel really overwhelming and confusing rather than useful. 即便如此，先有一些基础确实有帮助，如果你完全没有任何知识就投入，可能感觉非常不知所措和困惑，而不是有用。

entries.text: Describe a new law you would like to introduce in your country

paragraphs: If I could introduce a new law, it would be an environmental law about light pollution. The topic caught my attention straight away, so I decided to read it out of curiosity.

Specifically, it covered a wide range of animals — migratory birds losing their way because city lights confuse their navigation, and insects and bats facing the exact same problem, with artificial lights completely disrupting their natural instincts and rhythms. It made me realise something I'd never really thought about before — we talk a lot about air pollution and water pollution, but light pollution is just as serious, yet rarely gets mentioned.

What really struck me is that the damage doesn't stop with animals — when their ecosystems are disrupted, it eventually comes back to affect humans too. That's when I started looking into it more, and found that the main sources of light pollution are street lights, advertising boards, and the exterior lighting of buildings.
Right now in China, there are some guidelines about this, but they're not mandatory, so the problem just keeps getting worse. The law I'd like to introduce would focus on two key areas.

First, strictly limiting the brightness of outdoor lights, especially commercial advertising boards — this would improve the sleep quality of nearby residents and let animals follow their natural rhythms again. Second, setting a clear time limit — all unnecessary lights off after 10 PM, which would also reduce carbon emissions and help fight climate change.
This law would definitely be controversial. Businesses wouldn't want to turn off their lights because it may reduce their advertising impact.

But most ordinary people would strongly support it, especially those who live near commercial areas. Honestly, I can't make this happen on my own — but I really hope more people start paying attention to this issue, and that one day it gets taken seriously at a policy level.
paragraphsZh: 如果我能颁布一项新法律，那将是一项关于光污染治理的环保法律。
第二，设定明确的时间限制——晚上十点后关闭所有不必要的灯光，这也能减少碳排放，有助于对抗气候变化。
这项法律肯定会引发一些争议。
商家不会愿意关掉灯，因为这可能会影响他们的广告效果。
但大多数普通市民会强烈支持这项法律，尤其是那些住在商业区附近的人。
说实话，靠我一个人的力量是无法推动这件事的——但我真的希望越来越多的人开始关注这个问题，有一天能够在政策层面得到认真对待。

entries.text: What rules should students follow at school?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most important rules at school are ones that help students respect each other and create a safe and focused environment where everyone can actually learn.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为学校最重要的规则是帮助学生互相尊重并创造一个安全专注的环境，让每个人都能真正学习。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Rules like being on time, not disrupting the class, treating teachers and classmates with respect, and keeping phones away during lessons are all really important because without them, the whole learning environment just breaks down. School isn't just about studying — it's also about learning how to behave in a community and be considerate of the people around you.
ideaNotes.textZh: 像准时、不打扰课堂、尊重老师和同学、上课期间放下手机这样的规则都非常重要，因为没有它们，整个学习环境就会崩溃。学校不只是关于学习，也是关于学习如何在社区中行为举止，体贴周围的人。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember in my school there was a strict rule about no phones during class, and honestly even though we all found it annoying at the time, it really did make lessons more focused and productive — nobody was distracted and the teacher could actually get through the material properly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得在我的学校有一条关于上课期间不能用手机的严格规定，说实话即使我们当时都觉得很烦，它确实使课堂更加专注和高效，没有人分心，老师也能真正完成课程内容。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, rules around treating others kindly and not bullying are just as important as academic ones — a school where students feel safe and respected is one where people actually want to come and learn every day. 另外，关于善待他人和不欺凌的规则与学业规则同样重要，一所学生感到安全和受尊重的学校，人们才真正愿意每天来学习。

entries.text: Do people in your country usually obey the law?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think most people in China do follow the law in general, but like anywhere, how strictly people follow rules often depends on whether they think they'll get caught.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为中国大多数人总体上遵守法律，但像任何地方一样，人们遵守规则的严格程度往往取决于他们是否认为会被抓到。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: For major laws, most people do comply — things like serious crimes or major traffic violations are generally avoided. But for smaller everyday rules — like jaywalking, littering, or not queuing properly — a lot of people will bend the rules if they feel like nobody is watching or there are no real consequences. It's human nature really, not just a Chinese thing.
ideaNotes.textZh: 对于主要法律，大多数人确实遵守，像严重犯罪或重大交通违规通常会避免。但对于较小的日常规则，比如乱穿马路、乱扔垃圾或不好好排队，如果人们感觉没有人在看或没有真实后果，很多人会违反规则。这真的是人性，不只是中国特有的事情。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, in China you can really see the difference between places with heavy camera surveillance and those without — in areas where people know they're being watched, behaviour is noticeably more orderly and rule-following, whereas in quieter spots people are much more relaxed about bending the rules.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，在中国你真的可以看到有大量摄像头监控的地方和没有的地方之间的差异，在人们知道自己被监视的区域，行为明显更有秩序和遵守规则，而在较安静的地方，人们对违反规则则宽松得多。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think younger generations are generally more rule-conscious than before — there's more awareness of civic responsibility and people are more likely to speak up or report things they see as wrong, which is a positive change. 另外，我认为年轻一代总体上比以前更有规则意识，对公民责任的意识更强，人们更有可能发声或举报他们认为不对的事情，这是一个积极的变化。

entries.text: What kinds of behavior are considered as good behavior?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think good behaviour basically comes down to treating others the way you'd want to be treated — being respectful, considerate, and taking responsibility for your own actions.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为良好行为基本上归结为以你希望被对待的方式对待他人，尊重、体贴，并为自己的行为承担责任。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Things like being polite, keeping your word, helping others when they need it, and not making life harder for the people around you are all seen as good behaviour in most cultures. It's also about how you handle things when they go wrong — owning up to mistakes rather than blaming others says a lot about someone's character.
ideaNotes.textZh: 像有礼貌、信守承诺、在别人需要时帮助他们、不给周围人增加麻烦这样的事情在大多数文化中都被视为良好行为。这也关于当事情出错时你如何处理，承认错误而不是责怪他人，这很能说明一个人的品格。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, something as simple as giving up your seat on the subway for an elderly person, holding the door open for someone, or not being loud in a public space — these small things add up and make a real difference to how comfortable and pleasant life is for everyone around you.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，像在地铁上为老年人让座、为别人扶着门、在公共场所不大声喧哗这样简单的事情，这些小事积累起来，对周围每个人的舒适和愉快生活产生真正的影响。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think good behaviour includes being honest and reliable — if people can trust that you mean what you say and do what you promise, that's probably the most important kind of good behaviour there is. 另外，我认为良好行为包括诚实和可靠，如果人们可以相信你说到做到，这可能是最重要的良好行为。

像有礼貌、信守承诺、在别人需要时帮助他们、不给周围人增加麻烦这样的事情在大多数文化中都被视为良好行为。这也关于当事情出错时你如何处理，承认错误而不是责怪他人，这很能说明一个人的品格。

可选】 And also, I think good behaviour includes being honest and reliable — if people can trust that you mean what you say and do what you promise, that's probably the most important kind of good behaviour there is. 另外，我认为良好行为包括诚实和可靠，如果人们可以相信你说到做到，这可能是最重要的良好行为。

entries.text: Do you think children can learn about the law outside of school?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think children actually learn a lot about rules and the law from everyday life — not just from textbooks or classroom lessons.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为孩子实际上从日常生活中学到了很多关于规则和法律的知识，而不只是从教科书或课堂课程中。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: A lot of what children learn about right and wrong comes from watching their parents and the people around them — how adults behave in public, how they talk about fairness, and how they react when rules are broken. Media like news, social media, and even TV dramas also expose kids to real-world legal situations in a way that feels much more relatable than reading a law textbook.
ideaNotes.textZh: 孩子对对错的很多了解来自观察父母和周围的人，成年人在公共场合如何行为、如何谈论公平，以及当规则被打破时如何反应。新闻、社交媒体甚至电视剧等媒体也以比阅读法律教科书更有共鸣的方式让孩子接触到现实世界的法律情况。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember learning a lot about basic rules and fairness just from watching how my parents handled situations — like when they talked about why someone got in trouble for doing something wrong, or why certain things are not allowed. That kind of casual conversation probably taught me more than any formal lesson did.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得仅仅通过观察父母处理情况就学到了很多关于基本规则和公平的知识，比如当他们谈论为什么有人因做错事而惹麻烦，或者为什么某些事情不被允许。那种随意的对话可能比任何正式课程教给我的都多。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, community activities, sports teams, and even games teach children about rules and consequences in a really hands-on way — when you play a game and someone cheats, you understand very quickly why rules exist and why breaking them matters. 另外，社区活动、运动队，甚至游戏以非常实践的方式教会孩子规则和后果，当你玩游戏有人作弊时，你很快就明白了为什么规则存在以及为什么违反规则很重要。

entries.text: Why rules exist matterWhat are the benefits for people to obey rules?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest benefit of following rules is that it makes life safer and more predictable for everyone — when people know what to expect from each other, things just run more smoothly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为遵守规则最大的好处是它使每个人的生活更安全、更可预测，当人们知道彼此的预期时，事情就运转得更顺畅。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Rules exist to protect people and keep things fair — without them, everything would just be chaotic and every person for themselves. When most people follow the rules, it creates an environment where people feel safe, trusted, and treated equally, which makes daily life so much more pleasant and stable for everyone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 规则的存在是为了保护人们并保持公平，没有它们，一切都会混乱，每个人各自为政。当大多数人遵守规则时，它创造了一个人们感到安全、被信任和被平等对待的环境，这使每个人的日常生活更加愉快和稳定。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, think about traffic rules — if everyone just drove however they wanted, roads would be completely dangerous and nobody could get anywhere safely. The fact that people generally stop at red lights and follow road signs is what makes it possible for millions of people to travel every day without constant accidents.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，想想交通规则，如果每个人都随心所欲地驾驶，道路将完全危险，没有人能安全到达任何地方。人们普遍在红灯前停车并遵循路标，这使数百万人每天出行而不会不断发生事故成为可能。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, on a personal level, people who follow rules and behave well tend to be more trusted and respected by others — which opens up more opportunities in work, relationships, and daily life compared to people who constantly cut corners or break rules. 另外，在个人层面，遵守规则和行为良好的人往往更受他人信任和尊重，与经常走捷径或违反规则的人相比，这在工作、人际关系和日常生活中开拓了更多机会。

entries.text: How can parents teach children to obey rules?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most effective way for parents to teach children about rules is to simply lead by example — children copy what they see, so if parents follow rules themselves, kids will naturally do the same.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为父母教孩子规则最有效的方式就是以身作则，孩子模仿他们所见，所以如果父母自己遵守规则，孩子自然会做同样的事。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Children are always watching and picking up on what adults do — if a parent tells a child to be honest but then lies in front of them, or tells them to follow traffic rules but jaywalks themselves, the child will see through it immediately. The message only really lands when the behaviour matches the words. Parents should also explain why rules exist rather than just saying "because I said so" — kids are much more likely to follow rules they actually understand the reason for.
ideaNotes.textZh: 孩子总是观察和学习成年人的行为，如果父母告诉孩子要诚实但当着他们面撒谎，或者告诉他们遵守交通规则但自己乱穿马路，孩子会立刻看穿。只有当行为与言语相符时，信息才真正传达。父母还应该

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: 解释
ideaNotes.textZh: 规则存在的原因，而不只是说"因为我说了算"，孩子对他们真正理解原因的规则更有可能遵守。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember my parents always made a point of queuing properly, saying please and thank you, and not littering even in situations where nobody was watching — and I just grew up thinking that was normal behaviour, which I still do today without even thinking about it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得我父母总是特意在没有人看的情况下也好好排队、说请和谢谢、不乱扔垃圾，我就是在认为这是正常行为的环境中长大的，我今天仍然不假思索地这样做。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, praising children when they do follow rules rather than only reacting when they break them is really important — positive reinforcement makes kids feel good about doing the right thing and makes them want to keep doing it. 另外，当孩子遵守规则时表扬他们，而不只是在他们违反规则时做出反应，这真的很重要，积极强化让孩子对做正确的事感觉良好，使他们想要继续这样做。

entries.text: Describe an environmental law you would like your country to introduce

paragraphs: If I could introduce a new law, it would be an environmental law about light pollution. The topic caught my attention straight away, so I decided to read it out of curiosity.

Specifically, it covered a wide range of animals — migratory birds losing their way because city lights confuse their navigation, and insects and bats facing the exact same problem, with artificial lights completely disrupting their natural instincts and rhythms. It made me realise something I'd never really thought about before — we talk a lot about air pollution and water pollution, but light pollution is just as serious, yet rarely gets mentioned.

What really struck me is that the damage doesn't stop with animals — when their ecosystems are disrupted, it eventually comes back to affect humans too. That's when I started looking into it more, and found that the main sources of light pollution are street lights, advertising boards, and the exterior lighting of buildings.
Right now in China, there are some guidelines about this, but they're not mandatory, so the problem just keeps getting worse. The law I'd like to introduce would focus on two key areas.

First, strictly limiting the brightness of outdoor lights, especially commercial advertising boards — this would improve the sleep quality of nearby residents and let animals follow their natural rhythms again. Second, setting a clear time limit — all unnecessary lights off after 10 PM, which would also reduce carbon emissions and help fight climate change.
This law would definitely be controversial. Businesses wouldn't want to turn off their lights because it may reduce their advertising impact.

But most ordinary people would strongly support it, especially those who live near commercial areas. Honestly, I can't make this happen on my own — but I really hope more people start paying attention to this issue, and that one day it gets taken seriously at a policy level.
paragraphsZh: 如果我能颁布一项新法律，那将是一项关于光污染治理的环保法律。
第二，设定明确的时间限制——晚上十点后关闭所有不必要的灯光，这也能减少碳排放，有助于对抗气候变化。
这项法律肯定会引发一些争议。
商家不会愿意关掉灯，因为这可能会影响他们的广告效果。
但大多数普通市民会强烈支持这项法律，尤其是那些住在商业区附近的人。
说实话，靠我一个人的力量是无法推动这件事的——但我真的希望越来越多的人开始关注这个问题，有一天能够在政策层面得到认真对待。

entries.text: How does technology affect the law ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think technology has changed the law in two main ways — it has created new problems that the law needs to deal with, and at the same time given law enforcement better tools to do their job.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为科技从两个主要方面改变了法律，它创造了法律需要处理的新问题，同时给执法部门提供了更好的工具来完成工作。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: On one hand, things like online scams, privacy issues, and fake content made by AI are all pretty new, and the law simply wasn't ready for them — so governments are always trying to write new rules to keep up. On the other hand, technology like cameras, digital records, and tracking tools has made it a lot easier for police to catch criminals and prove what happened.
ideaNotes.textZh: 一方面，像网络诈骗、隐私问题和AI制造的虚假内容这样的事情都相当新，法律根本没有准备好应对它们，所以政府总是在努力制定新规则来跟上。另一方面，像摄像头、数字记录和追踪工具这样的技术使警察抓住罪犯和证明发生了什么变得容易得多。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, AI-generated fake videos of real people are becoming a serious problem — people are using them to spread false information or harm someone's reputation, and the law is only just starting to figure out how to deal with that.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，真实人物的AI生成虚假视频正在成为一个严重问题，人们用它们来传播虚假信息或损害某人的声誉，法律才刚刚开始弄清楚如何处理这个问题。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, because so much happens online and across different countries, it's become really hard to know which country's laws apply when something goes wrong — that's a problem that governments are still trying to work out together. 另外，因为很多事情在网上和跨国发生，当出问题时很难知道适用哪个国家的法律，这是各国政府仍在努力共同解决的问题。

entries.text: What kinds of rules do schools in China have ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think schools in China tend to have quite strict and detailed rules compared to many other countries — covering everything from how you dress to how you behave in and out of class.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为与很多其他国家相比，中国学校往往有相当严格和详细的规则，涵盖从着装方式到课内外行为的一切。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Most schools have rules around wearing a uniform, keeping hair a certain way, arriving on time, and not using phones during school hours. There are also rules about behaviour in class — like not talking when the teacher is speaking and standing up to greet the teacher when they enter. The overall idea is to create a disciplined and focused environment where everyone is treated the same.
ideaNotes.textZh: 大多数学校有关于穿校服、保持特定发型、准时到达和上学期间不使用手机的规则。还有关于课堂行为的规则，比如老师说话时不说话，老师进入时站起来问好。总体思路是创造一个纪律严明、专注的环境，每个人都被平等对待。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, in my school we had really strict rules about phones — they had to be handed in at the start of the day and you wouldn't get them back until school ended. At the time it felt quite frustrating, but looking back it did mean we were much more focused during the day.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，在我的学校，我们有非常严格的手机规定，手机必须在一天开始时上交，直到学校结束才能拿回来。当时感觉相当令人沮丧，但回头看，这确实意味着我们白天专注得多。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, many schools in China have rules around academic performance too — like minimum grade requirements or mandatory study periods — which shows that the rules aren't just about behaviour but also about pushing students to take their studies seriously. 另外，中国很多学校也有关于学业成绩的规则，比如最低成绩要求或强制自习时间，这表明规则不只是关于行为，也是关于推动学生认真对待学习。

Academic performance minimum grades mandatory study

paragraphs: I think schools in China tend to have quite strict and detailed rules compared to many other countries — covering everything from how you dress to how you behave in and out of class.

Most schools have rules around wearing a uniform, keeping hair a certain way, arriving on time, and not using phones during school hours. There are also rules about behaviour in class — like not talking when the teacher is speaking and standing up to greet the teacher when they enter. The overall idea is to create a disciplined and focused environment where everyone is treated the same.

For instance, in my school we had really strict rules about phones — they had to be handed in at the start of the day and you wouldn't get them back until school ended. At the time it felt quite frustrating, but looking back it did mean we were much more focused during the day.
paragraphsZh: 我认为与很多其他国家相比，中国学校往往有相当严格和详细的规则，涵盖从着装方式到课内外行为的一切。
大多数学校有关于穿校服、保持特定发型、准时到达和上学期间不使用手机的规则。还有关于课堂行为的规则，比如老师说话时不说话，老师进入时站起来问好。总体思路是创造一个纪律严明、专注的环境，每个人都被平等对待。
例如，在我的学校，我们有非常严格的手机规定，手机必须在一天开始时上交，直到学校结束才能拿回来。当时感觉相当令人沮丧，但回头看，这确实意味着我们白天专注得多。

可选】 And also, many schools in China have rules around academic performance too — like minimum grade requirements or mandatory study periods — which shows that the rules aren't just about behaviour but also about pushing students to take their studies seriously. 另外，中国很多学校也有关于学业成绩的规则，比如最低成绩要求或强制自习时间，这表明规则不只是关于行为，也是关于推动学生认真对待学习。

entries.text: Will there be a law that is universally accepted ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Honestly, I think it's very unlikely that there will ever be a single law that every country in the world fully agrees on and accepts — the differences between countries are just too deep and fundamental.
ideaNotes.textZh: 说实话，我认为世界上每个国家完全同意并接受同一部法律的可能性非常小，国家之间的差异太深刻和根本了。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Every country has its own history, culture, religion, and political system, and these shape what people consider right and wrong in very different ways. What's completely normal and legal in one country can be totally unacceptable in another. For a universal law to exist, every government would need to give up some of their own authority, which most countries are not willing to do.
ideaNotes.textZh: 每个国家都有自己的历史、文化、宗教和政治制度，这些以非常不同的方式塑造人们对对错的看法。在一个国家完全正常合法的事情在另一个国家可能完全不可接受。要使普遍法律存在，每个政府都需要放弃一些自己的权威，大多数国家不愿意这样做。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, even something that seems obvious like human rights — most people would agree everyone deserves basic rights — but different countries still disagree massively on what those rights actually include, and some governments actively resist any international pressure to change their laws.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，即使是看起来显而易见的人权，大多数人会同意每个人都应该有基本权利，但不同国家对这些权利实际上包括什么仍然存在巨大分歧，一些政府积极抵制任何改变其法律的国际压力。• 转折【可选】 Even so, there are some areas where countries have managed to agree on basic rules — things like international trade laws or agreements about nuclear weapons — so it's not impossible, it just works better when there's a very clear shared interest involved. 即便如此，有些领域国家已经设法就基本规则达成一致，比如国际贸易法或关于核武器的协议，所以这并非不可能，只是当涉及非常明确的共同利益时效果更好。

entries.text: What environmental laws does your country already have ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think China actually has quite a comprehensive set of environmental laws already — the issue is less about having the laws and more about how consistently they are enforced.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为中国实际上已经有相当全面的环境法律体系，问题与其说是有没有法律，不如说是关于执行的一致性。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: China has laws covering things like air pollution, water quality, waste management, and protecting endangered species. There are also regulations on how much factories can pollute and penalties for companies that break the rules. In recent years the government has also been pushing hard on carbon emissions and renewable energy as part of its bigger environmental goals.
ideaNotes.textZh: 中国有涵盖空气污染、水质、废物管理和保护濒危物种的法律。还有关于工厂排放多少污染物的规定以及违规公司的处罚。近年来，政府还在作为其更大环境目标一部分的碳排放和可再生能源方面大力推进。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, China introduced a plastic bag ban in many cities a few years ago, and you can now see in most supermarkets that people either bring their own bags or pay extra for plastic ones — it's a small change but it's become completely normal now.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，中国几年前在很多城市引入了塑料袋禁令，你现在可以在大多数超市看到人们要么自带袋子或为塑料袋额外付费，这是一个小变化，但现在已经完全正常了。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think the challenge going forward is making sure these laws are actually followed everywhere — especially in smaller cities and rural areas where enforcement can be much weaker and less consistent than in the big cities. 另外，我认为未来的挑战是确保这些法律在各地真正被遵守，尤其是在较小的城市和农村地区，那里的执法可能比大城市更弱、更不一致。

entries.text: Describe a law on environmental protection

paragraphs: The environmental law I'd like to talk about is China's new law on light pollution control. For the first time, light pollution is officially included in our national law.

I got interested in this topic after visiting my grandma in the countryside — the night sky there looked so different from the city. So I went online to search for more information, and found out that this difference is actually caused by light pollution.
That's also when I came across this new law — it was passed in March 2026 and will take effect later this year. The law includes a few key points.

First, things like advertising boards, light boxes, and large display screens must be properly designed and installed according to national standards, and regularly maintained to reduce light pollution. Second, local governments are required to manage light pollution in different areas, with stricter controls in places that need special protection.

Finally, if businesses fail to take action and their lighting ends up disturbing people's daily lives or traffic, they can be ordered to make changes — and if they refuse, they can be fined anywhere from 5,000 to 50,000 yuan. This law benefits a lot of people — ordinary residents who live near busy commercial areas can finally expect some protection for their sleep and daily lives.

Animals like birds and insects also benefit, as their normal lives are often disrupted by artificial light. And this would also save a significant amount of energy — less electricity used means lower carbon emissions, which helps tackle climate change, and cities would also spend a lot less on electricity bills.

Honestly, this is a law that has been needed for too long. Light pollution might not be as visible as air or water pollution, but the impact on our health, our sleep, and the natural world around us is significant.

I really hope this kind of law receives more attention and gets properly enforced. 📄 https://docimg9.docs.qq.com/image/AgAABfznf8_hGr4hs8lNKomVuqtls9Up.jpeg? w=1080&h=1676 https://docimg9.docs.qq.com/image/AgAABfznf89j_4JzgVxNEbJEOR64QlZM.jpeg? w=1080&h=548 https://docimg9.docs.qq.com/image/AgAABfznf8-OjjgVzjRPJZm5bwfiKv37.jpeg? w=1080&h=1182
paragraphsZh: 我想聊的环保法律是中国关于光污染防治的新法律。 这是光污染首次被正式纳入国家法律。
我对这个话题产生兴趣是因为去农村探望了奶奶——那里的夜空看起来和城市截然不同。 于是我上网搜索相关信息，发现这种差异其实是由光污染造成的。
就在这时我发现了这部新法律——它于2026年3月通过，并将在今年晚些时候生效。 这部法律包含了几个关键点。
首先，广告屏、灯箱和大型显示屏等必须按照国家标准进行合理设计和安装，并定期维护以减少光污染。 其次，地方政府需要对不同区域进行光污染分区管理，对需要特殊保护的地方实施更严格的管控。
最后，如果企业未采取有效措施，其照明干扰了他人的日常生活或交通出行，将被责令整改——拒不整改的，将被处以5000元至5万元的罚款。 这部法律让很多人受益——住在繁华商业区附近的普通居民终于能够得到一些关于睡眠和日常生活的保障。
鸟类和昆虫等动物也将受益，因为人工光常常干扰它们的正常生活。 这也将节省大量能源——减少用电量意味着降低碳排放，有助于应对气候变化，城市也将在电费上节省很多开支。
说真的，这是一部早就应该出台的法律。 光污染可能不像空气或水污染那样明显，但它对我们的健康、睡眠和周围自然世界的影响是不可忽视的。
我真的希望这类法律能获得更多关注，并得到认真落实。
