entries.text: Do you think school rules are important ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I do think school rules are important — without them it would be really hard to maintain any kind of order, and everyone would just do whatever they wanted.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我确实认为校规很重要，没有它们真的很难维持任何秩序，每个人只会做任何他们想做的事。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: School is a place where lots of different people have to share the same space and learn together, so rules are what make that possible. They make sure everyone gets a fair chance to learn without being disturbed, and they also teach students that there are boundaries and expectations in life — which is something they'll need long after they leave school.
ideaNotes.textZh: 学校是很多不同的人必须共享同一空间和一起学习的地方，所以规则使这成为可能。它们确保每个人都有公平的学习机会而不被打扰，也教给学生生活中有界限和期望，这是他们离开学校很久之后仍然需要的东西。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, something as simple as not talking during class makes a huge difference — without it, teachers can't teach properly and students who actually want to learn get constantly distracted. It's a small rule but it affects everyone in the room.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，像上课期间不说话这样简单的事情产生了巨大的差异，没有它，老师无法好好教学，真正想学习的学生不断分心。这是一个小规则，但它影响房间里的每个人。• 转折【可选】 Even so, rules work best when students understand the reason behind them — when the reasoning makes sense, people are much more likely to actually follow the rules rather than just looking for ways around them. 即便如此，当学生理解规则背后的原因时，规则效果最好，当推理有意义时，人们更有可能真正遵守规则而不只是寻找绕过它们的方法。

entries.text: Are children unhappy with the school rules?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think most children have some rules they're not happy with — especially the ones that feel overly strict or pointless — but they generally accept that rules need to exist.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为大多数孩子都有一些他们不满意的规则，尤其是那些感觉过于严格或毫无意义的规则，但他们通常接受规则需要存在。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: The rules children tend to complain about most are the ones that feel too personal or controlling — like strict uniform policies or rules about hairstyles — because they don't seem to have anything to do with learning. But rules around respect and safety are generally accepted more easily because kids can see why they matter.
ideaNotes.textZh: 孩子倾向于最多抱怨的规则是那些感觉太个人化或控制性的规则，比如严格的校服政策或关于发型的规则，因为它们似乎与学习无关。但关于尊重和安全的规则通常更容易被接受，因为孩子可以看到它们为什么重要。

entries.text: What are the rules people should obey at work ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most important rules at work are around being professional, responsible, and respectful towards the people you work with.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为工作中最重要的规则是关于对与你共事的人专业、负责和尊重。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Things like showing up on time, meeting deadlines, communicating clearly, and treating colleagues with respect are all really fundamental — they're what make a workplace function properly and feel like a good environment to be in. There are also things like not sharing confidential information and being honest — these are about trust, and without trust, working relationships fall apart quickly.
ideaNotes.textZh: 像准时出现、按时完成任务、清晰沟通和尊重同事这样的事情都非常基本，它们使工作场所正常运转，感觉像一个良好的环境。还有像不分享机密信息和诚实这样的事情，这些是关于信任的，没有信任，工作关系很快就会崩溃。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, always meeting your deadlines sounds simple but it affects the whole team — if one person keeps missing them without communicating, it creates stress and problems for everyone around them, not just themselves.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，总是按时完成任务听起来简单，但它影响整个团队，如果一个人不断错过而不沟通，它为周围每个人创造压力和问题，不只是他们自己。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸

entries.text: What is the purpose of punishment ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the main purpose of punishment is to stop the behaviour from happening again — both for the person being punished and to send a message to others.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为惩罚的主要目的是阻止行为再次发生，既针对被惩罚的人，也向他人传达信息。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: If there are no consequences for doing something wrong, people have no real reason to change their behaviour or think twice before doing it again. Punishment creates that reason. But I also think the best kind of punishment isn't just about making someone suffer or feel bad — it should help them understand what they did wrong and why it matters, so they actually want to do better rather than just avoiding getting caught.
ideaNotes.textZh: 如果做错事没有后果，人们没有真正的理由改变行为或在再次做之前三思。惩罚创造了那个理由。但我也认为最好的惩罚不只是让某人受苦或感觉不好，它应该帮助他们理解他们做错了什么以及为什么重要，所以他们真正想做得更好，而不只是避免被抓到。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, in school if a student cheats on an exam and nothing happens, others will think it's fine to do too. But if there's a clear punishment, it makes students think twice and also shows everyone that rules are taken seriously. The punishment doesn't need to be harsh — it just needs to be consistent and meaningful.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，在学校如果一个学生考试作弊而什么都没发生，其他人会认为这样做也没问题。但如果有明确的惩罚，它使学生三思，也向所有人表明规则被认真对待。惩罚不需要严厉，只需要一致和有意义。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, for more serious situations, punishment also plays a role in protecting other people — keeping someone away from a situation where they might cause more harm is just as important as teaching them a lesson. 另外，对于更严重的情况，惩罚也在保护他人方面发挥作用，让某人远离可能造成更多伤害的情况与教训他们同样重要。

entries.text: Describe a story/book with animals in it

paragraphs: The book I'd like to talk about is called "The Vanishing Night" Not long ago, I was scrolling through social media and came across a post recommending a book about light pollution and its impact on wildlife. The topic caught my attention straight away, so I decided to read it out of curiosity.

Specifically, it covered a wide range of animals — migratory birds losing their way because city lights confuse their navigation, and insects and bats facing the exact same problem, with artificial lights completely disrupting their natural instincts and rhythms. It made me realise something I'd never really thought about before — we talk a lot about air pollution and water pollution, but light pollution is just as serious, yet rarely gets mentioned.

What really struck me is that the damage doesn't stop with animals — when their ecosystems are disrupted, it eventually comes back to affect humans too. That's when I started looking into it more, and found that the main sources of light pollution are street lights, advertising boards, and the exterior lighting of buildings.
Right now in China, there are some guidelines about this, but they're not mandatory, so the problem just keeps getting worse. The law I'd like to introduce would focus on two key areas.

First, strictly limiting the brightness of outdoor lights, especially commercial advertising boards — this would improve the sleep quality of nearby residents and let animals follow their natural rhythms again. Second, setting a clear time limit — all unnecessary lights off after 10 PM, which would also reduce carbon emissions and help fight climate change.
This law would definitely be controversial. Businesses wouldn't want to turn off their lights because it may reduce their advertising impact.

But most ordinary people would strongly support it, especially those who live near commercial areas. Honestly, I can't make this happen on my own — but I really hope more people start paying attention to this issue, and that one day it gets taken seriously at a policy level.
paragraphsZh: 我想说的这本书叫做《消失的夜晚》。
第二，设定明确的时间限制——晚上十点后关闭所有不必要的灯光，这也能减少碳排放，有助于对抗气候变化。
这项法律肯定会引发一些争议。
商家不会愿意关掉灯，因为这可能会影响他们的广告效果。
但大多数普通市民会强烈支持这项法律，尤其是那些住在商业区附近的人。
说实话，靠我一个人的力量是无法推动这件事的——但我真的希望越来越多的人开始关注这个问题，有一天能够在政策层面得到认真对待。

entries.text: Should schools teach children about animals?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think schools should definitely teach children about animals because it helps them understand the natural world and learn to care about living things beyond just themselves.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为学校绝对应该教孩子关于动物的知识，因为它帮助他们了解自然界并学会关心自身以外的生命。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: I mean, a lot of children these days grow up in cities and barely have any real contact with animals or nature — if schools don't teach them, many kids will just never learn basic things like how different animals live, what they eat, or why they matter to the environment. Learning about animals also helps children develop empathy and a sense of responsibility towards other living creatures.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我的意思是，如今很多孩子在城市长大，几乎没有任何与动物或自然的真实接触，如果学校不教他们，很多孩子将永远不会学到基本的东西，比如不同动物如何生活、吃什么，或者它们对环境为何重要。了解动物也帮助孩子培养对其他生命的同理心和责任感。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember in primary school we had lessons about different types of animals and their habitats, and it genuinely made me feel curious and excited about nature — it's one of the few things from school that I still remember clearly because it felt so real and interesting.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得在小学时我们有关于不同类型动物及其栖息地的课程，这真的让我对自然感到好奇和兴奋，这是学校少数我至今仍清晰记得的事情之一，因为感觉如此真实和有趣。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, teaching children about animals naturally leads to conversations about protecting the environment and endangered species, which are things every young person really needs to understand and care about as they grow up. 另外，教孩子关于动物的知识自然会引发关于保护环境和濒危物种的对话，这些是每个年轻人在成长过程中真正需要了解和关心的事情。

entries.text: Some people think pets should not be kept in cities. What do you think?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people should be allowed to keep pets in cities, but only if they are responsible owners who can properly look after the animal's needs.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为应该允许人们在城市里养宠物，但前提是他们是能够妥善照顾动物需求的负责任的主人。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: I mean, the worry makes sense — cities are busy and crowded, and not every owner is careful or responsible. entries.text: Many people regard pets as members of their family. What do you think?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I completely understand why people feel that way — when you spend every day with an animal, care for it, and build a bond with it, it really does start to feel like part of the family.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我完全理解为什么人们有这种感觉，当你每天与动物在一起，照顾它、与它建立感情，它真的开始感觉像是家庭的一部分。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Pets are there for you when you come home, they notice when you're sad, and they give you unconditional company and affection without judging you — that kind of relationship is really meaningful, and for a lot of people, especially those who live alone or don't have much family nearby, their pet genuinely is their closest companion.
ideaNotes.textZh: 宠物在你回家时等着你，它们注意到你悲伤，给你无条件的陪伴和感情而不评判你，这种关系真的很有意义，对很多人来说，尤其是那些独居或附近没有太多家人的人，他们的宠物真的是他们最亲密的伴侣。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I know someone who lives alone and her cat is genuinely the first thing she thinks about when she gets home — she buys it birthday presents, takes it to the vet regularly, and talks about it the way most people talk about their kids. It's clearly more than just an animal to her.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识一个独居的人，她的猫真的是她回家后第一个想到的事情，她给它买生日礼物、定期带它去看兽医，谈论它的方式就像大多数人谈论他们的孩子一样。对她来说，它显然不只是一只动物。

ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think as long as the pet is well looked after and happy, it doesn't really matter whether you call it a family member or not — what matters is that the relationship is built on genuine care and affection. 另外，我认为只要宠物被好好照顾和快乐，你是否称它为家庭成员并不重要，重要的是这种关系建立在真诚的关爱和感情上。

entries.text: Do many people keep pets in your country?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, keeping pets has become really popular in China over the past few years — you see people walking dogs and carrying cats everywhere these days.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，近年来养宠物在中国变得非常流行，如今你到处都能看到人们遛狗和抱猫。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: I think the big change is that younger generations are much more into pets than their parents were — a lot of young people who live alone or don't have children see their pets as companions and treat them almost like family. The whole pet industry has also grown massively, with pet cafes, pet hotels, and pet clothing becoming completely normal things.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为巨大的变化是年轻一代比他们的父母更喜欢宠物，很多独居或没有孩子的年轻人把宠物视为伴侣，几乎把它们当作家人对待。整个宠物行业也大幅增长，宠物咖啡馆、宠物酒店和宠物服装成为完全正常的事情。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, almost everyone I know my age either has a cat or a dog — and some people spend more money on their pets than on themselves, buying them special food, toys, and even clothes. It's become a really big part of people's lives.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识的几乎每个同龄人都养了猫或狗，有些人在宠物身上花的钱比在自己身上花的多，给它们买特殊食物、玩具甚至衣服。这已经成为人们生活中真正重要的一部分。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 That said, older generations are still a bit less into the idea — many of them grew up in a time when pets were more of a practical thing like a guard dog, rather than a companion, so they sometimes find it hard to understand why people spend so much on animals. 话虽如此，老一辈人仍然对这个想法不那么感兴趣，他们中的很多人在宠物更多是实用性的东西如看门狗而不是伴侣的时代长大，所以他们有时难以理解为什么人们在动物身上花那么多钱。

entries.text: What are the advantages of keeping a pet?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest advantages of keeping a pet are the companionship and emotional support they give you — having a pet genuinely makes daily life feel warmer and less lonely.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为养宠物最大的好处是它们给你的陪伴和情感支持，养宠物真的让日常生活感觉更温暖、更不孤独。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Pets give you something to look forward to coming home to — they're always happy to see you and never in a bad mood with you, which is really comforting after a long day. On top of that, caring for a pet gives you a sense of routine and responsibility which can actually be really good for your mental health, especially if you live alone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 宠物给你一个期待回家的理由，它们总是很高兴见到你，从不对你情绪不好，在漫长的一天之后这真的很安慰。此外，照顾宠物给你一种日常规律和责任感，这实际上对你的心理健康非常有益，尤其是如果你独居的话。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I've heard many people say that getting a dog completely changed their lifestyle for the better — they started going for walks every day, meeting other dog owners, and just generally feeling more active and connected to the world around them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我听说很多人说养了一只狗后生活方式完全变好了，他们开始每天散步、认识其他狗主人，总体上感觉对周围的世界更加活跃和有联系。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, for children especially, growing up with a pet teaches them responsibility, kindness, and how to care for something other than themselves — those are really valuable lessons that are hard to teach any other way. 另外，尤其对孩子来说，与宠物一起成长教会他们责任心、善良以及如何照顾自身以外的东西，这些都是很难通过其他方式教导的非常宝贵的课程。

entries.text: Why do people always tell children stories with animals?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the main reason is that animals make stories feel fun, safe, and easy for children to connect with — a talking fox or a brave little rabbit is just so much more appealing to a child than a regular human character.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为主要原因是动物使故事感觉有趣、安全且容易与孩子产生共鸣，一只会说话的狐狸或一只勇敢的小兔子对孩子来说比普通的人类角色更有吸引力。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Animals are really easy for kids to understand — a wolf is scary, a rabbit is sweet, a lion is brave — children just get it straight away without needing any explanation. And because the characters are animals and not real people, the stories feel safe and light, so kids can learn about things like being brave, being kind, or dealing with fear without it feeling too serious or scary.
ideaNotes.textZh: 动物对孩子来说真的很容易理解，狼是可怕的，兔子是可爱的，狮子是勇敢的，孩子立刻就明白，不需要任何

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.textZh: 而且因为角色是动物而不是真实的人，故事感觉安全轻松，所以孩子可以学习勇敢、善良或面对恐惧等事情，而不会感觉太严肃或可怕。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, a story about a tortoise and a hare racing each other is a really easy way to teach children about not giving up and staying focused — the lesson is clear, the characters are memorable, and kids remember it for years without even realising they were being taught something.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，一个关于乌龟和兔子赛跑的故事是一个非常简单的方式来教孩子不要放弃和保持专注，教训很清晰，角色令人难忘，孩子们记住它很多年，甚至没有意识到他们在被教导什么。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, children are naturally drawn to animals anyway — they find them cute, funny, and interesting — so using animals in stories is just a really smart way to grab their attention and keep them engaged from start to finish. 另外，孩子本来就被动物吸引，他们觉得动物可爱、有趣且有意思，所以在故事中使用动物只是一个非常聪明的方式来抓住他们的注意力并让他们从头到尾都投入。

entries.text: Describe a piece of technology that you didn't know how to use(e.g. a computer,a smartphone,etc.)

paragraphs: Some time ago, I bought a wireless printer from a well-known brand. It turned out to be a complete nightmare.
I thought setting it up would be easy, but it turned out to be much harder than I expected. The instructions were confusing, with lots of technical terms I didn't understand.

I tried several times but still couldn't get it to work, and I really started to doubt myself. I mean, it was just a printer, not some highly specialized piece of equipment, yet I still couldn't figure out how to use it.
In the end, I had to ask a friend who was good with technology to help me. My friend managed to set up the printer pretty quickly.
Just when we thought everything was finally ready, we ran into another problem. For some reason, my computer still couldn't detect the printer, even though we'd finished all the settings.
I restarted both devices and checked the network connection again, but nothing worked. Eventually, I contacted the manufacturer's customer service and explained the whole situation.
They told me that the issue needed to be reported to a higher-level department and promised to get back to me. However, after a whole week, I still hadn't received a reply.
I contacted them again, but they gave me pretty much the same answer. Two weeks later, I finally received an email from them.
They just suggested that I send the printer back for repair and pay for a technical inspection. I was really disappointed because it was a big brand, and I'd only bought the printer recently.
I had expected much better after-sales service. At the moment, the printer is still being repaired, so I haven't really learned how to use it properly yet.
In the future, I'll make sure to check the instruction manual and after-sales policy before buying a new electronic device.
paragraphsZh: 前段时间，我买了一台无线打印机，是一个知名品牌的产品。 结果，这次购买简直成了一场噩梦。
我原以为安装设置会很简单，但实际上却比我预想的要难得多。 说明书让人很困惑，里面有很多我看不懂的专业术语。

以后，在购买新的电子设备之前，我一定会先查看使用说明书和售后政策。

entries.text: Describe a challenging technological problem you faced

paragraphs: Some time ago, I bought a wireless printer from a well-known brand. It turned out to be a complete nightmare.
I thought setting it up would be easy, but it turned out to be much harder than I expected. The instructions were confusing, with lots of technical terms I didn't understand.

I tried several times but still couldn't get it to work, and I really started to doubt myself. I mean, it was just a printer, not some highly specialized piece of equipment, yet I still couldn't figure out how to use it.
In the end, I had to ask a friend who was good with technology to help me. My friend managed to set up the printer pretty quickly.
Just when we thought everything was finally ready, we ran into another problem. For some reason, my computer still couldn't detect the printer, even though we'd finished all the settings.
I restarted both devices and checked the network connection again, but nothing worked. Eventually, I contacted the manufacturer's customer service and explained the whole situation.
They told me that the issue needed to be reported to a higher-level department and promised to get back to me. However, after a whole week, I still hadn't received a reply.
I contacted them again, but they gave me pretty much the same answer. Two weeks later, I finally received an email from them.
They just suggested that I send the printer back for repair and pay for a technical inspection. I was really disappointed because it was a big brand, and I'd only bought the printer recently.
I had expected much better after-sales service. At the moment, the printer is still being repaired, so I haven't really learned how to use it properly yet.
In the future, I'll make sure to check the instruction manual and after-sales policy before buying a new electronic device.

entries.text: What are the advantages and disadvantages of AI ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think AI has made a lot of things in our lives much easier and faster, but at the same time it has brought some real concerns that we can't ignore.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为AI让我们生活中很多事情变得更加容易和快速，但同时它也带来了一些我们无法忽视的真实担忧。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: On the good side, AI can handle boring and repetitive tasks for us, help us find information quickly, and even spot health problems that doctors might miss. But on the bad side, a lot of people worry about losing their jobs to AI, and there are also concerns about things like fake content and privacy.
ideaNotes.textZh: 好的方面是，AI可以为我们处理无聊和重复的任务，帮助我们快速找到信息，甚至发现医生可能遗漏的健康问题。但不好的方面是，很多人担心因AI而失业，也有关于虚假内容和隐私的担忧。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I use AI tools almost every day to help me check my writing or look things up, and it saves me so much time. But I've also seen cases where people used AI to create fake photos and videos of real people, which feels really wrong and dangerous.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我几乎每天都使用AI工具帮我检查写作或查找信息，节省了我很多时间。但我也见过有人使用AI创建真实人物的虚假照片和视频，这感觉真的很错误和危险。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, one thing a lot of people don't think about is that the more we rely on AI, the less we might actually think for ourselves — and that's something worth paying attention to. 另外，很多人没有想到的一点是，我们越依赖AI，我们自己独立思考的能力可能就越少，这是值得关注的事情。

entries.text: Do you think people today should learn about AI technology ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I genuinely think everyone should have at least a basic understanding of AI these days because it's becoming part of almost every area of life.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我真心认为现在每个人都应该至少对AI有基本了解，因为它正在成为生活几乎每个领域的一部分。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: You don't need to know how to build AI or understand all the technical details, but knowing what it can do, how it works roughly, and where it might go wrong is really important — otherwise people will just use it without thinking and be easily misled or taken advantage of.
ideaNotes.textZh: 你不需要知道如何构建AI或了解所有技术细节，但了解它能做什么、大致如何运作以及可能在哪里出错非常重要，否则人们只会不加思考地使用它，容易被误导或利用。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a lot of older people have been tricked by AI-generated voices or images pretending to be someone they know — if they had a better understanding of what AI can do, they would have been much less likely to fall for it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，很多老年人被AI生成的声音或图像欺骗，假装成他们认识的人，如果他们对AI能做什么有更好了解，他们就不太可能上当。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, for younger people especially, understanding AI is becoming almost like a basic skill for getting a job — more and more companies expect their staff to be comfortable working alongside AI tools in their daily work. 另外，尤其对年轻人来说，了解AI正变得几乎像是找工作的基本技能，越来越多的公司希望员工能够自如地在日常工作中与AI工具协作。

entries.text: Should children learn to use AI ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think children should learn about AI, but with proper guidance and boundaries — it's less about teaching them to use every tool and more about helping them understand what AI is and isn't.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为孩子应该了解AI，但需要适当的引导和界限，与其教他们使用每一个工具，不如帮助他们理解AI是什么以及不是什么。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: AI is going to be a huge part of their future, so completely keeping it away from them doesn't really make sense. But at the same time, children need to first develop their own ability to think, create, and solve problems, and if they start relying on AI too early they might never build those skills properly. AI
ideaNotes.textZh: 将成为他们未来的重要组成部分，所以完全不让他们接触并没有太大意义。但同时，孩子需要先培养自己思考、创造和解决问题的能力，如果他们过早开始依赖AI，可能永远无法正确建立这些技能。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, if a child uses AI to write their essays or solve their homework, they might get good grades but they're not actually learning anything — and when they face a situation where AI isn't there to help, they'll be completely lost.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，如果孩子使用AI写作文或解决作业，他们可能会得到好成绩，但实际上什么都没学到，当他们面临没有AI帮助的情况时，他们将完全不知所措。• 转折【可选】 Still, used in the right way — like for exploring ideas or learning about the world — AI can actually be a really great tool for curious kids who want to dig deeper into topics they're interested in. 不过，以正确的方式使用，比如探索想法或了解世界，AI实际上对于想要深入探索感兴趣话题的好奇孩子来说是一个很好的工具。

entries.text: Do you think students are overly reliant on AI ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Honestly, I do think a lot of students rely on AI way too much, especially when it comes to schoolwork and writing.
ideaNotes.textZh: 说实话，我确实认为很多学生过度依赖AI，尤其是在学业和写作方面。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: The problem is that AI makes it so easy to get an answer that students often just go straight to it without even trying to think first. And when you do that over and over again, you slowly stop developing the ability to work things out on your own, which is actually the whole point of education.
ideaNotes.textZh: 问题是AI让得到答案变得如此容易，以至于学生经常直接找AI，甚至不先尝试自己思考。当你一遍又一遍地这样做，你慢慢停止培养自己解决问题的能力，而这实际上才是教育的全部意义所在。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I know plenty of people who use AI to write their essays from start to finish and just hand them in — they get the grade but they haven't actually practised writing or thinking at all, which will catch up with them eventually.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识很多人使用AI从头到尾写作文然后直接提交，他们得到了分数，但实际上完全没有练习写作或思考，这最终会让他们付出代价。• 转折【可选】 But then again, it's not entirely the students' fault — if schools don't teach them how to use AI responsibly or set clear rules about when it's okay to use it, students will just do whatever is easiest. 但反过来说，这不完全是学生的错，如果学校不教他们如何负责任地使用AI或制定明确规则说明何时可以使用，学生只会做最简单的事。

entries.text: What can teachers do to stop students relying too much on AI ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most effective thing teachers can do is change the way they assess students so that AI simply can't do the work for them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为老师能做的最有效的事情是改变评估学生的方式，使AI根本无法替他们完成工作。

ideaNotes.label: 解释

entries.text: Describe a time when you sent a message or an email to someone but received no reply for a long time

paragraphs: Some time ago, I bought a wireless printer from a well-known brand. It turned out to be a complete nightmare.
I thought setting it up would be easy, but it turned out to be much harder than I expected. The instructions were confusing, with lots of technical terms I didn't understand.

I tried several times but still couldn't get it to work, and I really started to doubt myself. I mean, it was just a printer, not some highly specialized piece of equipment, yet I still couldn't figure out how to use it.
In the end, I had to ask a friend who was good with technology to help me. My friend managed to set up the printer pretty quickly.
Just when we thought everything was finally ready, we ran into another problem. For some reason, my computer still couldn't detect the printer, even though we'd finished all the settings.
I restarted both devices and checked the network connection again, but nothing worked. Eventually, I contacted the manufacturer's customer service and explained the whole situation.
They told me that the issue needed to be reported to a higher-level department and promised to get back to me. However, after a whole week, I still hadn't received a reply.
I contacted them again, but they gave me pretty much the same answer. Two weeks later, I finally received an email from them.
They just suggested that I send the printer back for repair and pay for a technical inspection. I was really disappointed because it was a big brand, and I'd only bought the printer recently.
I had expected much better after-sales service. At the moment, the printer is still being repaired, so I haven't really learned how to use it properly yet.
In the future, I'll make sure to check the instruction manual and after-sales policy before buying a new electronic device.
paragraphsZh: 前段时间，我买了一台无线打印机，是一个知名品牌的产品。 结果，这次购买简直成了一场噩梦。
我原以为安装设置会很简单，但实际上却比我预想的要难得多。 说明书让人很困惑，里面有很多我看不懂的专业术语。
我试了好几次，还是没能让它正常工作，这让我开始怀疑自己。 我的意思是，它只不过是一台打印机，又不是什么需要高度专业技能才能操作的设备，可我居然还是搞不懂该怎么用。
最后，我只好向一位擅长使用电子设备的朋友求助。 我的朋友很快就成功地设置好了打印机。
就在我们以为一切终于准备就绪的时候，另一个问题又出现了。 不知道为什么，我的电脑还是无法识别这台打印机，尽管我们已经完成了所有设置。
我重启了电脑和打印机，又检查了一遍网络连接，但还是没有任何效果。 最后，我联系了品牌方的客服，向他们解释了整个情况。
他们告诉我，这个问题需要上报给更高一级的部门，并承诺会再联系我。 然而，整整一周过去了，我仍然没有收到任何回复。
我再次联系了他们，但他们给出的答复基本上还是一样的。 两周后，我终于收到了他们的邮件。
他们只是建议我把打印机寄回去维修，并支付一笔技术检测费。 我真的很失望，因为这是一个大品牌，而且我买这台打印机也没多久。
我原本期待他们能提供更好的售后服务。 目前，这台打印机仍在维修中，所以我还没有真正学会如何正确使用它。
以后，在购买新的电子设备之前，我一定会先查看使用说明书和售后政策。

entries.text: In what situations do people spend a long time responding to others messages?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people take a long time to reply mainly when the message requires a careful or thoughtful response — not everything can just be answered with a quick yes or no.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们花很长时间回复主要是当消息需要谨慎或深思熟虑的回应时，不是所有事情都可以用简单的是或不是来回答。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Things like difficult questions, sensitive topics, or messages that could easily be misunderstood need more time because you want to make sure you say the right thing. People also take longer when they're responding to something emotionally heavy — like a friend going through a hard time — because a quick careless reply can feel really dismissive and hurtful.
ideaNotes.textZh: 像困难的问题、敏感话题或容易被误解的消息这样的事情需要更多时间，因为你想确保说正确的话。当回应情感上沉重的事情时，人们也会花更长时间，比如正在经历困难时期的朋友，因为快速粗心的回复可能感觉真的敷衍和伤人。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, if a close friend messages me saying they're going through something really tough, I won't just type something quickly and send it — I'll actually sit and think about what I want to say because I want them to feel genuinely heard and supported, not like I just replied to get it done.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，如果一个亲密朋友给我发消息说他们正在经历非常艰难的事情，我不会只是随便打几个字发出去，我会真正坐下来思考我想说什么，因为我希望他们感到真正被倾听和支持，而不是像我只是为了完成任务而回复。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, work or formal messages can take a long time too — people want to make sure the tone is right, nothing comes across as rude, and everything is clear and professional before hitting send. 另外，工作或正式消息也可能花很长时间，人们想确保语气正确，没有任何内容显得无礼，并且在发送之前一切都清晰和专业。

entries.text: In what situations do people not respond to messages right away ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people delay replying mainly when they're either genuinely busy or when the message is something they don't quite know how to deal with yet.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们推迟回复主要是当他们真的很忙或消息是他们还不知道如何处理的事情时。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Sometimes it's completely innocent — you're in a meeting, driving, eating, or just focused on something and you see the message but don't have the right moment to reply properly. But other times people delay because the message is awkward or uncomfortable — maybe it's asking for something they don't want to do, or it's a conversation they're just not ready to have, so they leave it on read and hope they'll feel more ready later.
ideaNotes.textZh: 有时完全是无辜的，你在开会、开车、吃饭或只是专注于某事，你看到了消息但没有合适的时机好好回复。但其他时候人们推迟是因为消息尴尬或不舒服，也许是在要求他们不想做的事情，或者是他们还没准备好进行的对话，所以他们已读不回，希望以后会更准备好。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I know that when someone sends me a message asking for a favour I'm not sure about, I often read it and then just put my phone down without replying, because I need time to figure out what I actually want to say — and sometimes I end up avoiding it for way longer than I should.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我知道当有人给我发消息要求一个我不确定的帮忙时，我经常阅读它然后只是放下手机不回复，因为我需要时间弄清楚我真正想说什么，有时我最终回避它的时间比应该的长得多。转折【可选】 That said, with messaging apps showing read receipts, not replying quickly can sometimes come across as rude or cold even when it isn't meant that way — which adds a whole new kind of social pressure that didn't exist before. 话虽如此，随着消息应用显示已读回执，不快速回复有时可能显得无礼或冷漠，即使不是这个意思，这增加了一种以前不存在的全新社交压力。

entries.text: What would you do if you haven’t received a reply after sending out a message ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Honestly, my first reaction is usually to just wait and give the person some time — I try not to assume the worst straight away.
ideaNotes.textZh: 说实话，我的第一反应通常是只是等待并给那个人一些时间，我尽量不立刻往最坏处想。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Most of the time when someone doesn't reply it's just because they're busy, missed the message, or forgot — it's rarely personal. So I'd usually wait a reasonable amount of time before doing anything. But if it's something urgent or important, I'd probably send a follow-up message or just give them a call to make sure they got it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 大多数时候，当有人不回复时，只是因为他们忙、错过了消息或忘记了，很少是针对个人的。所以我通常会等待合理的时间再做任何事情。但如果是紧急或重要的事情，我可能会发一条跟进消息或直接给他们打电话确保他们收到了。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, if I message a close friend and they don't reply for a day or two, I'd probably just send a casual follow-up like "hey did you see this?" without making it a big deal. But if it's a work message that needs a response, I'd follow up much sooner and more directly because there's an actual deadline involved.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，如果我给一个亲密朋友发消息，他们一两天没有回复，我可能只是发一条随意的跟进消息，比如"嘿你看到这个了吗？"而不把它当成大事。但如果是需要回复的工作消息，我会更快更直接地跟进，因为涉及到实际的截止日期。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think it's important not to overthink it or take it personally — jumping to conclusions about why someone hasn't replied can cause unnecessary anxiety and tension in a relationship when the real reason is probably just that they're caught up in their own life. 另外，我认为重要的是不要想太多或往个人方向想，对某人为何没有回复妄下结论可能在关系中造成不必要的焦虑和紧张，而真正的原因可能只是他们忙于自己的生活。

entries.text: Why do some people prefer sending a message instead of making a call ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the main reason is that messaging gives you more control and flexibility — you can reply when you're ready, and there's no pressure to respond instantly the way a phone call demands.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为主要原因是发消息给你更多控制和灵活性，你可以在准备好时回复，没有像电话那样要求立即回应的压力。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Phone calls require both people to be available and focused at exactly the same time, which isn't always possible. With messages, you can think about what you want to say before sending, edit it if needed, and the other person can reply whenever it suits them. It's also just much less socially pressured — a lot of people find phone calls quite draining and stressful, especially with people they don't know well.
ideaNotes.textZh: 电话需要双方在完全相同的时间都可以接听并专注，这并不总是可能的。发消息时，你可以思考你想说什么再发送，如果需要可以编辑，另一方可以在方便时回复。这也社交压力小得多，很多人觉得打电话相当费力和有压力，尤其是与不太熟的人。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I almost always prefer to message rather than call when I need to arrange something or ask a question — it just feels so much less intrusive and gives the other person the chance to reply when they have a moment, rather than putting them on the spot.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，当我需要安排什么事情或问一个问题时，我几乎总是更喜欢发消息而不是打电话，感觉侵入性小得多，给另一方在有空时回复的机会，而不是让他们当场回答。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, messages create a record of the conversation — you can go back and check what was said, which is really useful for things like plans, addresses, or important information that you don't want to forget or get wrong. 另外，消息创建了对话记录，你可以回去查看说了什么，对于计划、地址或重要信息这样不想忘记或弄错的事情真的很有用。

keyPhrases.phrase: Message rather than call less intrusive reply when ready
Record of conversation plans addresses important info

paragraphs: I think the main reason is that messaging gives you more control and flexibility — you can reply when you're ready, and there's no pressure to respond instantly the way a phone call demands.

Phone calls require both people to be available and focused at exactly the same time, which isn't always possible. With messages, you can think about what you want to say before sending, edit it if needed, and the other person can reply whenever it suits them. It's also just much less socially pressured — a lot of people find phone calls quite draining and stressful, especially with people they don't know well.

For instance, I almost always prefer to message rather than call when I need to arrange something or ask a question — it just feels so much less intrusive and gives the other person the chance to reply when they have a moment, rather than putting them on the spot.
paragraphsZh: 我认为主要原因是发消息给你更多控制和灵活性，你可以在准备好时回复，没有像电话那样要求立即回应的压力。
电话需要双方在完全相同的时间都可以接听并专注，这并不总是可能的。发消息时，你可以思考你想说什么再发送，如果需要可以编辑，另一方可以在方便时回复。这也社交压力小得多，很多人觉得打电话相当费力和有压力，尤其是与不太熟的人。
例如，当我需要安排什么事情或问一个问题时，我几乎总是更喜欢发消息而不是打电话，感觉侵入性小得多，给另一方在有空时回复的机会，而不是让他们当场回答。

可选】 And also, messages create a record of the conversation — you can go back and check what was said, which is really useful for things like plans, addresses, or important information that you don't want to forget or get wrong. 另外，消息创建了对话记录，你可以回去查看说了什么，对于计划、地址或重要信息这样不想忘记或弄错的事情真的很有用。

entries.text: How do you show your respect in your messages ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think showing respect in messages mainly comes down to how you write and how quickly you respond — both say a lot about how much you value the other person.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为在消息中表达尊重主要取决于你如何写作和多快回复，两者都很能说明你有多重视对方。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: With people like teachers, bosses, or older relatives, I always make sure to use proper language, avoid slang, and start with a greeting rather than just diving straight into what I want. I also try to reply in a reasonable time rather than leaving messages unanswered for days, because that can feel quite disrespectful and dismissive. The overall tone just needs to feel considerate and thoughtful rather than rushed or careless.
ideaNotes.textZh: 对于老师、上司或年长亲戚这样的人，我总是确保使用正式语言、避免俚语，并以问候语开头，而不是直接说我想要什么。我也尽量在合理的时间内回复，而不是让消息几天没有回应，因为那可能感觉相当不尊重和敷衍。整体语气只需要感觉体贴和深思熟虑，而不是仓促或粗心。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, if I'm messaging a professor or a manager, I'd always start with something like "Professor Zhang" or "Manager Li" and use more formal and polite language throughout — compared to messaging a friend where I'd just send a few casual words or a voice message. The way you address someone at the start really shows straight away how much respect you have for them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，如果我给教授或经理发消息，我总是以"张教授"或"李经理"这样的方式开头，并全程使用更加正式和礼貌的语言，与给朋友发消息相比，我只会发几句随意的话或语音消息。你开头如何称呼某人真的立刻显示出你对他们有多少尊重。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, avoiding one-word replies when someone has clearly put effort into their message is important — even if you're busy, a slightly more thoughtful response shows that you actually read what they said and took it seriously. 另外，当某人明显在他们的消息中花了心思时，避免单词回复很重要，即使你很忙，稍微更深思熟虑的回应也表明你实际上读了他们说的并认真对待。

entries.text: Why do some people feel angry when others don't reply to their messages ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people get angry mainly because being ignored feels like the other person is saying "you're not worth my time" — even if that's not what they mean at all.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们生气主要是因为被忽视感觉像是对方在说"你不值得我花时间"，即使这根本不是他们的意思。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: We're all used to seeing that messages have been read — so when someone reads your message and still doesn't reply, it's hard not to take it personally. It creates this feeling that you're just being ignored, which is really uncomfortable, especially if you were waiting for an answer or needed a reply for something important. The longer it goes without a response, the more rejected and overlooked that person tends to feel.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我们都习惯于看到消息已被阅读，所以当有人阅读了你的消息但仍不回复时，很难不往个人方向想。它创造了一种只是被忽视的感觉，真的很不舒服，尤其是如果你在等待回答或需要回复某件重要的事情。没有回应的时间越长，那个人往往感到越被拒绝和被忽视。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I think most people have experienced sending a message to someone and seeing it was read but not replied to, and that small thing can actually make you feel quite hurt and frustrated — especially if it's from someone you care about or were counting on.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认为大多数人都经历过给某人发消息，看到它被阅读但没有回复，那件小事实际上可以让你感到相当受伤和沮丧，尤其是如果是来自你关心或依赖的人。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, I think people are just more emotionally invested in messaging than they used to be — because we're on our phones all the time, the expectation that someone will reply quickly and easily has gone up, so when they don't it feels more like a deliberate choice to ignore you. 另外，我认为人们对消息的情感投入比以前更多，因为我们一直在使用手机，对某人会快速轻松地回复的期望已经提高，所以当他们不回复时，感觉更像是故意忽视你的选择。

entries.text: Describe a time when you got up early

paragraphs: I'd like to talk about my experience volunteering at a Su Super football match. Not long ago, I came across a report on a local WeChat public account about the Su Super football league.
It's a football competition between 13 cities in Jiangsu Province, where amateur and professional players compete together. It attracted huge crowds and a lot of media coverage.
After reading about it, I was really intrigued and decided to sign up as a volunteer. On the day of the match, I got up really early — probably the earliest I had in a long time.

Volunteers had to show up really early, and I had to commute there on top of that, so I ended up waking up at around five or six in the morning. I was pretty sleepy, but once I got there and things got busy, the tiredness just disappeared.
Volunteering at a big event like this isn't something one person can do alone — you really need a team to make it work. In our volunteer team, my main job was to guide the crowd.

But at one point way more people showed up than expected and things got really crowded at the entrance. We quickly figured out a plan, split into smaller groups, and each took charge of a different area — everyone just stepped up, and it worked out pretty well.

That's when I truly understood what teamwork really means. Apart from the match itself, what really stayed with me was an ad that played on the big screen during half-time — Mbappé promoting an electrolyte drink, saying "我是姆巴佩，补水啦" in this really funny Chinese accent.

You know, Mbappé is known for being so intense and focused on the field, so seeing him say something that playful and goofy in Chinese was just so unexpected. Everyone around me just burst out laughing.
I was so curious that I actually went and bought a bottle afterwards. Pretty refreshing — maybe that's the power of a good advertisement.

After the match, the organisers arranged for all the volunteers to make Suzhou-style mooncakes together — it was coming up to Mid-Autumn Festival, a time when families come together and share mooncakes as a symbol of reunion. Suzhou mooncakes are quite different from the regular kind — the outside is made of this really crispy, layered pastry skin, with fillings like rose paste and red bean.
It was already a pretty special experience just being there as a volunteer, but making mooncakes together at the end made it feel even more memorable.
paragraphsZh: 我想说的是我在苏超足球比赛中做志愿者的经历。 不久前，我在本地的微信公众号上看到了一篇关于苏超足球联赛的报道。
这是江苏省13个城市之间的足球联赛，业余球员和职业球员同场竞技。 比赛吸引了大量的人群和很多媒体报道。
看完之后，我非常感兴趣，于是决定报名参加志愿者。 比赛当天，我起得非常早——可能是很长时间以来起得最早的一次。
志愿者需要很早到场，加上我还需要通勤，所以我最终在早上大概五六点就起床了。 当时挺困的，但一到现场事情忙起来之后，困意就完全消失了。
在这样的大型活动中做志愿者，不是一个人能完成的——真的需要一个团队。 在我们的志愿者团队里，我的主要工作是引导人群。
但在某个时刻，来的人比预期多得多，入口处变得非常拥挤。 我们很快制定了一个计划，分成几个小组，各自负责不同的区域——每个人都主动承担，最后顺利解决了。
就是那一刻，我真正理解了团队合作的意义。 除了比赛本身，让我印象最深的是中场休息时大屏幕上播放的一个广告——姆巴佩代言电解质水，用非常搞笑的中文口音说"我是姆巴佩，补水啦"。
要知道，姆巴佩在场上一向专注而认真，所以看到他用这么可爱、这么搞怪的方式说中文，真的太出乎意料了。 周围的人都哄堂大笑。
我太好奇了，之后真的去买了一瓶。 喝起来还挺清爽的——也许这就是一个好广告的力量。
比赛结束后，主办方安排所有志愿者一起做苏式月饼——因为那时候快到中秋节了，那是一个家人团聚、共享月饼、象征团圆的节日。 苏式月饼和普通月饼很不一样——外皮是非常酥脆、层层叠叠的酥皮，馅料有玫瑰和豆沙等口味。
光是作为志愿者参与其中就已经是一次很特别的经历了，而最后大家一起做月饼，让这次经历变得更加难忘。

entries.text: Is it good to arrive early in any situation ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think arriving early is generally a good thing because it shows you respect other people's time and gives you a chance to settle in and prepare before things start.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为提前到达通常是好事，因为它表明你尊重他人的时间，并给你一个在事情开始之前安定下来和做准备的机会。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When you arrive early you feel much more calm and in control — you're not rushing, you're not stressed, and you have time to get your head in the right space. But if you're always cutting it close or running late, you show up flustered and unprepared, which can really affect how you perform or come across to others.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当你提前到达时，你会感到更加平静和掌控，你不需要赶忙，不会有压力，你有时间调整好状态。但如果你总是卡点或迟到，你会慌乱和没有准备地出现，这真的会影响你的表现或给别人的印象。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I always try to arrive at job interviews or important meetings at least ten minutes early — it gives me time to calm down, look over my notes, and feel ready, which makes such a difference to how confident I feel going in.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我总是尽量在工作面试或重要会议前至少十分钟到达，这给了我时间冷静下来、查看笔记、感到准备好了，这对我进去时的自信心有很大影响。• 转折【可选】 But then again, there are some situations where arriving too early can actually be a bit awkward — like showing up at someone's house way before a party starts when the host is still getting ready. 但反过来说，有些情况下到得太早实际上会有点尴尬，比如在聚会开始前很早就到达别人家，而主人还在准备中。

entries.text: Do you know anyone who likes to get up early?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, actually — my dad is someone who gets up really early every single day without fail, even on weekends.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，实际上，我爸爸是每天都非常早起床的人，从不例外，即使在周末也是如此。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: He always says that the early morning is the quietest and most peaceful part of the day, and it's the only time he has completely to himself before everything gets busy. He uses that time to exercise, read, or just sit quietly with a cup of tea, and he swears it sets him up for a much better day.
ideaNotes.textZh: 他总是说早晨是一天中最安静、最平静的部分，也是在一切变得忙碌之前他完全属于自己的唯一时间。他用那段时间锻炼、阅读或只是安静地喝杯茶，他发誓这让他度过更加美好的一天。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, he wakes up at around five thirty every morning — even on holidays — and by the time the rest of us are just getting out of bed, he's already exercised, had breakfast, and been out for a walk. It's honestly quite impressive even if I could never do it myself.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，他每天早上大约五点半起床，即使在假日也是如此，当我们其他人刚刚起床时，他已经锻炼完、吃完早饭、出去散步了。说实话这相当令人印象深刻，即使我自己永远做不到。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 I think people like my dad who have kept up an early morning routine for years genuinely feel the benefits — they tend to be more organised, calm, and productive than people who are always rushing around in the morning. 我认为像我爸爸这样多年坚持早起习惯的人真的感受到了好处，他们往往比早上总是匆忙的人更加有条理、平静和高效。

entries.text: Why do people get up early?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people get up early mainly because it gives them extra time and a head start on the day before everything gets busy and noisy.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为人们早起主要是因为它在一切变得忙碌和嘈杂之前给他们额外的时间和先机。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: For a lot of people, the early morning is the only time of day that feels truly theirs — the kids aren't up yet, work hasn't started, and the world is still quiet. That peace and quiet makes it much easier to focus, think clearly, or do something for yourself before the demands of the day take over.
ideaNotes.textZh: 对很多人来说，清晨是一天中唯一感觉真正属于自己的时间，孩子还没起床，工作还没开始，世界还是安静的。那种宁静使专注、清晰思考或为自己做点事情变得更容易，在一天的各种要求接管之前。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, a lot of people I know wake up early specifically to exercise or meditate because they know that if they leave it until after work, something will always come up and get in the way. Getting it done first thing just means it actually happens.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识的很多人专门早起来锻炼或冥想，因为他们知道如果等到下班后，总会有什么事情出现并阻碍。第一件事就完成意味着它真的会发生。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, some people just have no choice — early work shifts, long commutes, or kids who wake up early mean that getting up early isn't really a lifestyle choice for them, it's just something they have to do. 另外，有些人别无选择，早班工作、长途通勤或早起的孩子意味着早起对他们来说不是生活方式的选择，而只是他们必须做的事情。

entries.text: What kinds of occasions need people to arrive early?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think occasions like job interviews, exams, flights, and formal events are the ones where arriving early really matters the most.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为像工作面试、考试、航班和正式活动这样的场合是提前到达最重要的。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: In high-pressure situations, arriving early gives you time to calm your nerves, find your seat, and get organised before things begin. Being late to these kinds of events can have real consequences — you might miss your flight, be refused entry to an exam, or make a terrible first impression at an interview.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在高压情况下，提前到达给你时间在事情开始之前平静情绪、找到座位和做好准备。在这类活动中迟到可能会有真实的后果，你可能错过航班、被拒绝进入考场，或者在面试中留下糟糕的第一印象。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember arriving at an exam hall with just a few minutes to spare once and I was so out of breath and flustered that I could barely concentrate for the first ten minutes — it really affected my performance. After that I always make sure to arrive at least twenty minutes early for anything important.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得有一次只提前几分钟到达考场，我当时上气不接下气、慌乱不堪，以至于前十分钟几乎无法集中注意力，这真的影响了我的表现。之后我总是确保在任何重要事情上至少提前二十分钟到达。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, things like weddings and ceremonies where there's a fixed start time and a room full of people — walking in late is not just inconvenient, it's genuinely rude and disruptive to everyone else. 另外，像婚礼和典礼这样有固定开始时间且满屋子人的场合，迟到不仅不方便，对其他所有人来说真的是无礼和干扰。

entries.text: Why do some people like to stay up late?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think a lot of people stay up late because the night time feels like their own personal space — it's quiet, there are no demands on them, and they can finally do what they want.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为很多人熬夜是因为夜晚感觉像是他们的个人空间，安静、没有人对他们有要求，他们终于可以做自己想做的事。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: For many people, especially those with busy schedules, the late evening is the only time of day when nobody is asking anything of them — no work, no family responsibilities, no social obligations. That freedom feels really addictive, which is why so many people end up staying up way later than they planned.
ideaNotes.textZh: 对很多人来说，尤其是那些日程繁忙的人，深夜是一天中没有人要求他们任何事情的唯一时间，没有工作、没有家庭责任、没有社交义务。那种自由感觉真的很让人上瘾，这就是为什么很多人最终熬夜比计划晚得多。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I know a lot of people who say they only really start to feel alive and creative after ten or eleven at night — they do their best reading, studying, or creative work when everyone else is asleep and the world is completely quiet.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识很多人说他们只有在晚上十点或十一点之后才真正感到充满活力和创造力，当其他人都睡着、世界完全安静时，他们做最好的阅读、学习或创意工作。• 转折【可选】 Even so, the problem is that staying up late usually means not getting enough sleep, which builds up over time and ends up making people feel exhausted and run down during the day — it's a hard cycle to break. 即便如此，问题是熬夜通常意味着睡眠不足，这会随着时间积累，最终让人在白天感到精疲力竭，这是一个很难打破的循环。

entries.text: What kind of people like getting up early ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think people who are naturally disciplined and goal-oriented tend to be the ones who enjoy getting up early — they see the morning as valuable time that most people are wasting by sleeping.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为天生自律和有目标的人往往是喜欢早起的人，他们将早晨视为大多数人在睡眠中浪费的宝贵时间。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Early risers usually have something they want to get done before the day officially starts — whether it's exercising, reading, planning, or just having a quiet moment to themselves. These tend to be people who like to feel in control of their day rather than just reacting to whatever comes at them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 早起者通常在一天正式开始之前有想要完成的事情，无论是锻炼、阅读、计划还是只是有一个安静的时刻。这些往往是喜欢感到掌控自己一天而不是只是对发生的事情做出反应的人。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a lot of athletes, business owners, and high achievers are known for waking up very early — not because they have to, but because they genuinely believe that getting a head start while others are still sleeping gives them an edge.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，很多运动员、企业主和高成就者以非常早起床而闻名，不是因为他们必须如此，而是因为他们真心相信在别人还在睡觉时抢先一步会给他们优势。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, people who have young children or demanding jobs often end up becoming early risers out of necessity — and many of them actually come to enjoy the habit even once their situation changes. 另外，有年幼孩子或要求高工作的人往往出于必要成为早起者，他们中的许多人实际上即使在情况改变后也会享受这个习惯。

entries.text: Describe a time when you worked in a group

paragraphs: I'd like to talk about my experience volunteering at a Su Super football match. Not long ago, I came across a report on a local WeChat public account about the Su Super football league.
It's a football competition between 13 cities in Jiangsu Province, where amateur and professional players compete together. It attracted huge crowds and a lot of media coverage.
After reading about it, I was really intrigued and decided to sign up as a volunteer. On the day of the match, I got up really early — probably the earliest I had in a long time.

Volunteers had to show up really early, and I had to commute there on top of that, so I ended up waking up at around five or six in the morning. I was pretty sleepy, but once I got there and things got busy, the tiredness just disappeared.
Volunteering at a big event like this isn't something one person can do alone — you really need a team to make it work. In our volunteer team, my main job was to guide the crowd.

But at one point way more people showed up than expected and things got really crowded at the entrance. We quickly figured out a plan, split into smaller groups, and each took charge of a different area — everyone just stepped up, and it worked out pretty well.

That's when I truly understood what teamwork really means. Apart from the match itself, what really stayed with me was an ad that played on the big screen during half-time — Mbappé promoting an electrolyte drink, saying "我是姆巴佩，补水啦" in this really funny Chinese accent.

You know, Mbappé is known for being so intense and focused on the field, so seeing him say something that playful and goofy in Chinese was just so unexpected. Everyone around me just burst out laughing.
I was so curious that I actually went and bought a bottle afterwards. Pretty refreshing — maybe that's the power of a good advertisement.

After the match, the organisers arranged for all the volunteers to make Suzhou-style mooncakes together — it was coming up to Mid-Autumn Festival, a time when families come together and share mooncakes as a symbol of reunion. Suzhou mooncakes are quite different from the regular kind — the outside is made of this really crispy, layered pastry skin, with fillings like rose paste and red bean.
It was already a pretty special experience just being there as a volunteer, but making mooncakes together at the end made it feel even more memorable.
paragraphsZh: 我想说的是我在苏超足球比赛中做志愿者的经历。 不久前，我在本地的微信公众号上看到了一篇关于苏超足球联赛的报道。
这是江苏省13个城市之间的足球联赛，业余球员和职业球员同场竞技。 比赛吸引了大量的人群和很多媒体报道。
看完之后，我非常感兴趣，于是决定报名参加志愿者。 比赛当天，我起得非常早——可能是很长时间以来起得最早的一次。
志愿者需要很早到场，加上我还需要通勤，所以我最终在早上大概五六点就起床了。 当时挺困的，但一到现场事情忙起来之后，困意就完全消失了。
在这样的大型活动中做志愿者，不是一个人能完成的——真的需要一个团队。 在我们的志愿者团队里，我的主要工作是引导人群。
但在某个时刻，来的人比预期多得多，入口处变得非常拥挤。 我们很快制定了一个计划，分成几个小组，各自负责不同的区域——每个人都主动承担，最后顺利解决了。
就是那一刻，我真正理解了团队合作的意义。 除了比赛本身，让我印象最深的是中场休息时大屏幕上播放的一个广告——姆巴佩代言电解质水，用非常搞笑的中文口音说"我是姆巴佩，补水啦"。
要知道，姆巴佩在场上一向专注而认真，所以看到他用这么可爱、这么搞怪的方式说中文，真的太出乎意料了。 周围的人都哄堂大笑。
我太好奇了，之后真的去买了一瓶。 喝起来还挺清爽的——也许这就是一个好广告的力量。
比赛结束后，主办方安排所有志愿者一起做苏式月饼——因为那时候快到中秋节了，那是一个家人团聚、共享月饼、象征团圆的节日。 苏式月饼和普通月饼很不一样——外皮是非常酥脆、层层叠叠的酥皮，馅料有玫瑰和豆沙等口味。
光是作为志愿者参与其中就已经是一次很特别的经历了，而最后大家一起做月饼，让这次经历变得更加难忘。

entries.text: Why do some people prefer to work by themselves?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think some people prefer working alone because they feel they can focus better and get more done without having to deal with other people's opinions or pace.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为有些人更喜欢独自工作，因为他们觉得不需要应对他人的意见或节奏，可以更专注、效率更高。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Working in a group means you have to compromise, wait for others, and deal with disagreements, which can actually slow everything down. When you work alone you're completely in control — you decide how to do things, when to do them, and you don't have to explain yourself to anyone.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在团队中工作意味着你必须妥协、等待他人并处理分歧，这实际上可能让一切都变慢。独自工作时你完全掌控一切，你决定如何做事、何时做事，不需要向任何人

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: 解释

entries.text: Should students learn to do group work?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Yes, I think students should definitely do group work because it teaches them skills that are really hard to learn on your own or from a textbook.
ideaNotes.textZh: 是的，我认为学生绝对应该做小组作业，因为它教给他们很难独自或从课本上学到的技能。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: In real life, almost every job requires you to work with other people — you have to share ideas, deal with different personalities, and find ways to get things done together even when you disagree. If students only ever work alone at school, they'll be completely unprepared for that when they enter the working world.
ideaNotes.textZh: 在现实生活中，几乎每份工作都要求你与他人合作，你必须分享想法、应对不同性格，并找到即使在不同意时也能共同完成事情的方法。如果学生在学校只是独自工作，当他们进入职场时将完全没有准备。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember doing a big group presentation in school and it was really tough at first because everyone had different ideas about how to do it. But working through those disagreements and coming up with something together felt really satisfying in the end.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得在学校做一个大型小组展示，一开始真的很难，因为每个人对如何做有不同的想法。但克服这些分歧，共同想出一些东西，最终感觉非常令人满足。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸

entries.text: What group tasks are there in schools?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think there are quite a few different types of group tasks in schools, but the most common ones are group presentations, projects, and lab experiments.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为学校里有很多不同类型的小组任务，但最常见的是小组展示、项目和实验。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Group presentations usually involve researching a topic together and presenting it to the class, which pushes students to divide the work, practise speaking, and support each other. Lab experiments are a bit different because they require everyone to actually work with their hands at the same time and communicate in real time to get a result.
ideaNotes.textZh: 小组展示通常涉及共同研究一个话题并向全班展示，这促使学生分工、练习演讲并互相支持。实验室实验有点不同，因为它们要求每个人同时动手操作并实时沟通以获得结果。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, I remember in science class we had to do experiments in groups of four and everyone had a specific job — one person recorded the data, one handled the equipment, and so on. It felt very real and hands-on compared to just sitting and listening.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得在科学课上我们必须四人一组做实验，每个人都有特定的工作，一个人记录数据，一个人操作设备等等。与只是坐着听相比，感觉非常真实和实践。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, some schools have things like group reading activities or creative projects where students make something together — like a short film, a poster, or a model — which tends to be the kind of task students actually enjoy and remember. 另外，一些学校有小组阅读活动或创意项目，学生们一起制作一些东西，比如短片、海报或模型，这往往是学生真正喜欢和记住的那种任务。

entries.text: What advantages are there for students experiencing teamwork at school?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest advantage is that teamwork teaches students skills that no textbook or individual assignment can really give them — things that are actually essential for real life.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为最大的好处是团队合作教给学生没有任何课本或个人作业真正能给予的技能，这些技能在现实生活中实际上是必不可少的。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: When students work in a group, they have to communicate clearly, listen to others, divide tasks, and deal with disagreements — all of which are things they'll face constantly in any job or relationship later on. It also teaches them that not everyone thinks the same way, and learning to work with different personalities is one of the most valuable things you can experience while you're still in a safe environment like school.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当学生在小组中工作时，他们必须清晰沟通、倾听他人、分配任务和处理分歧，所有这些都是他们以后在任何工作或关系中会不断面对的事情。它还教会他们不是每个人都以同样的方式思考，学会与不同性格的人合作是你在学校这样安全环境中能体验到的最有价值的事情之一。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I remember doing a group project in school where everyone had very different ideas about how to do it, and we had a lot of disagreements at first. But working through it and coming up with something together felt really satisfying — and I learned more from that experience than from most individual assignments.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我记得在学校做一个小组项目，每个人对如何做有非常不同的想法，我们起初有很多分歧。但解决这些问题并共同想出一些东西感觉真的很令人满足，我从那次经历中学到的比大多数个人作业都多。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, teamwork gives students a chance to discover their own strengths — some people find they're naturally good at organising, others at presenting or coming up with ideas, and that kind of self-awareness is really useful to develop early. 另外，团队合作给学生一个发现自己优势的机会，有些人发现他们天生擅长组织，其他人擅长展示或提出想法，这种自我认知对于早期培养真的很有用。

entries.text: How can you tell if a person is a good leader?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the clearest sign of a good leader is that people genuinely want to follow them — not because they have to, but because they trust and respect that person.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为好领导者最明显的标志是人们真心想要跟随他们，不是因为必须如此，而是因为他们信任和尊重那个人。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: A good leader doesn't just give orders and take credit — they listen to the people around them, explain their reasoning, support others when things get tough, and own up to mistakes rather than blaming everyone else. You can usually tell pretty quickly whether someone leads by making people feel valued or by making people feel like they're just there to do what they're told.
ideaNotes.textZh: 好的领导者不只是发号施令和揽功，他们倾听周围的人，

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: 解释
ideaNotes.textZh: 自己的推理，在事情变困难时支持他人，并承认错误而不是责怪其他人。你通常可以很快判断一个人是通过让人感到被重视来领导，还是通过让人感觉他们只是在那里执行命令来领导。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I've had group project leaders at school who just sat back and told everyone what to do without contributing much themselves, and nobody really wanted to work hard for them. But I've also had leaders who got stuck in alongside everyone else, asked for opinions, and made the whole team feel like the success was shared — and those teams always worked so much better.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我在学校有过一些小组项目领导者，他们只是坐在那里告诉每个人该做什么，自己贡献不多，没有人真的想为他们努力工作。但我也有过和大家一起投入、征求意见、让整个团队感觉成功是共同的领导者，那些团队总是运转得好得多。

entries.text: Describe an interesting video

paragraphs: I'd like to talk about a video/advertisement I came across while volunteering at a Su Super match. Not long ago, I came across a report on a local WeChat public account about the Su Super football league.
It's a football competition between 13 cities in Jiangsu Province, where amateur and professional players compete together. It attracted huge crowds and a lot of media coverage.
After reading about it, I was really intrigued and decided to sign up as a volunteer. On the day of the match, I got up really early — probably the earliest I had in a long time.

Volunteers had to show up really early, and I had to commute there on top of that, so I ended up waking up at around five or six in the morning. I was pretty sleepy, but once I got there and things got busy, the tiredness just disappeared.
Volunteering at a big event like this isn't something one person can do alone — you really need a team to make it work. In our volunteer team, my main job was to guide the crowd.

But at one point way more people showed up than expected and things got really crowded at the entrance. We quickly figured out a plan, split into smaller groups, and each took charge of a different area — everyone just stepped up, and it worked out pretty well.

That's when I truly understood what teamwork really means. Apart from the match itself, what really stayed with me was an ad that played on the big screen during half-time — Mbappé promoting an electrolyte drink, saying "我是姆巴佩，补水啦" in this really funny Chinese accent.

You know, Mbappé is known for being so intense and focused on the field, so seeing him say something that playful and goofy in Chinese was just so unexpected. Everyone around me just burst out laughing.
I was so curious that I actually went and bought a bottle afterwards. Pretty refreshing — maybe that's the power of a good advertisement.

After the match, the organisers arranged for all the volunteers to make Suzhou-style mooncakes together — it was coming up to Mid-Autumn Festival, a time when families come together and share mooncakes as a symbol of reunion. Suzhou mooncakes are quite different from the regular kind — the outside is made of this really crispy, layered pastry skin, with fillings like rose paste and red bean.
It was already a pretty special experience just being there as a volunteer, but making mooncakes together at the end made it feel even more memorable.
paragraphsZh: 我想说的是一个视频/广告，是我在参加苏超比赛志愿者活动时看到的。 不久前，我在本地的微信公众号上看到了一篇关于苏超足球联赛的报道。
这是江苏省13个城市之间的足球联赛，业余球员和职业球员同场竞技。 比赛吸引了大量的人群和很多媒体报道。
看完之后，我非常感兴趣，于是决定报名参加志愿者。 比赛当天，我起得非常早——可能是很长时间以来起得最早的一次。
志愿者需要很早到场，加上我还需要通勤，所以我最终在早上大概五六点就起床了。 当时挺困的，但一到现场事情忙起来之后，困意就完全消失了。
在这样的大型活动中做志愿者，不是一个人能完成的——真的需要一个团队。 在我们的志愿者团队里，我的主要工作是引导人群。
但在某个时刻，来的人比预期多得多，入口处变得非常拥挤。 我们很快制定了一个计划，分成几个小组，各自负责不同的区域——每个人都主动承担，最后顺利解决了。
就是那一刻，我真正理解了团队合作的意义。 除了比赛本身，让我印象最深的是中场休息时大屏幕上播放的一个广告——姆巴佩代言电解质水，用非常搞笑的中文口音说"我是姆巴佩，补水啦"。
要知道，姆巴佩在场上一向专注而认真，所以看到他用这么可爱、这么搞怪的方式说中文，真的太出乎意料了。 周围的人都哄堂大笑。
我太好奇了，之后真的去买了一瓶。 喝起来还挺清爽的——也许这就是一个好广告的力量。
比赛结束后，主办方安排所有志愿者一起做苏式月饼——因为那时候快到中秋节了，那是一个家人团聚、共享月饼、象征团圆的节日。 苏式月饼和普通月饼很不一样——外皮是非常酥脆、层层叠叠的酥皮，馅料有玫瑰和豆沙等口味。
光是作为志愿者参与其中就已经是一次很特别的经历了，而最后大家一起做月饼，让这次经历变得更加难忘。

entries.text: What kind of videos do people in your country like to watch?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the most popular types of videos in China right now are short videos on platforms like Douyin and drama series on streaming apps — those are what pretty much everyone is watching.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为目前中国最受欢迎的视频类型是抖音等平台上的短视频和流媒体应用上的电视剧，几乎每个人都在看这些。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Short videos have become huge because they're so easy to consume — you can watch something funny or interesting in under a minute and just keep scrolling. People watch them on the bus, during lunch, before bed — basically any spare moment. Drama series are popular for the opposite reason — people want something to fully get into and follow over time, especially after a long day when they just want to switch off and escape.
ideaNotes.textZh: 短视频变得非常流行，因为它们非常容易消费，你可以在不到一分钟内看到有趣的东西，然后继续刷。人们在公交车上、午饭时间、睡前看，基本上任何空闲时刻都看。电视剧受欢迎的原因正好相反，人们想要完全投入并追踪的东西，尤其是在漫长的一天后只想放松和逃脱现实。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, almost everyone I know has Douyin on their phone and spends at least an hour on it every day without even realising — you just pick it up for five minutes and suddenly it's been an hour. And whenever a new drama drops on iQiyi, my friend group is always talking about it the next day.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我认识的几乎每个人手机上都有抖音，每天至少在上面花一个小时而没有意识到，你只是拿起来看五分钟，突然就过了一个小时。每当爱奇艺上有新剧上线，我的朋友圈第二天总是在谈论它。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, food and travel content has become really popular too — lots of people enjoy watching others try different foods or explore new places, even if they're not going anywhere themselves — it's a kind of easy and relaxing way to experience the world from your sofa. 另外，美食和旅行内容也变得非常受欢迎，很多人喜欢看别人尝试不同食物或探索新地方，即使他们自己哪里都不去，这是一种从沙发上轻松放松地体验世界的方式。

entries.text: Which is more helpful, watching videos or reading books?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: Honestly, I think it really depends on what you're trying to do — videos are better for some things and books are better for others, and comparing them directly isn't really fair.
ideaNotes.textZh: 说实话，我认为这真的取决于你想做什么，视频在某些方面更好，书在其他方面更好，直接比较并不公平。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Videos are great when you need to see something in action — like learning how to cook, fix something, or understand a concept visually. They're fast and easy to follow. But books are better when you want to go deep into a topic, build real knowledge, or think and reflect — reading forces your brain to stay active and engaged in a way that watching doesn't always do.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当你需要看实际操作时，视频很好，比如学做饭、修东西或直观理解概念。它们快速且容易跟上。但当你想深入了解一个话题、建立真正的知识或思考和反思时，书更好，阅读迫使你的大脑以观看不总是能做到的方式保持活跃和投入。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, when I want to learn how to make a new dish I always watch a video because seeing it done step by step is so much clearer than reading instructions. But when I actually want to understand something properly — like history or a complex idea — I find that reading about it sticks in my head so much better than just watching a short video about it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，当我想学做新菜时，我总是看视频，因为看着它一步一步完成比阅读说明清楚得多。但当我真正想正确理解某事时，比如历史或复杂想法，我发现阅读比只看一个短视频更能留在我脑海中。• 转折【可选】 Even so, for a lot of people who don't enjoy reading, a good video is still so much better than nothing — at least you're still taking in information and learning something, which is what matters in the end. 即便如此，对于很多不喜欢阅读的人来说，一个好的视频仍然比什么都没有好得多，至少你仍然在获取信息和学习东西，这才是最终重要的。

entries.text: What skills can people learn from watching videos?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think videos are especially useful for learning practical and hands-on skills — anything where you need to actually see how something is done rather than just read about it.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为视频对学习实用和动手技能特别有用，任何你需要看实际如何操作而不只是阅读的东西。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Things like cooking, drawing, playing an instrument, fixing things around the house, or even learning a language are all much easier to pick up through video because you can watch, pause, rewind, and copy at your own pace. A written explanation can only go so far — sometimes you just need to see it with your own eyes to really understand.
ideaNotes.textZh: 像做饭、画画、演奏乐器、修理家里的东西，甚至学语言这些事情都通过视频更容易学习，因为你可以按自己的节奏观看、暂停、倒回和模仿。文字

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: 解释
ideaNotes.textZh: 只能做到那么多，有时你只需要亲眼看到才能真正理解。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, I taught myself how to edit videos purely by watching tutorials on Bilibili — I just followed along, paused when I needed to, and tried it myself at the same time. There's no way I could have learned that just from reading a textbook.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我完全靠在哔哩哔哩上看教程自学了视频剪辑，我只是跟着做，需要时暂停，同时自己尝试。仅靠读教科书我不可能学会那个。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, soft skills like public speaking, confidence, or even social skills can actually be picked up from watching videos too — seeing how other people carry themselves, handle situations, or communicate clearly gives you a kind of model to follow in your own life. 另外，像公众演讲、自信，甚至社交技能这样的软技能实际上也可以从看视频中学到，看别人如何表现自己、处理情况或清晰沟通，给你一种在自己生活中可以效仿的榜样。

entries.text: Are there any differences between the videos that young people and old people like to watch?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the biggest difference is that young people tend to watch things for entertainment and trends, while older people generally prefer content that is more practical or informative.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为最大的区别是年轻人倾向于为娱乐和潮流看视频，而老年人通常更喜欢更实用或有信息量的内容。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Young people are mostly watching short funny videos, dramas, gaming content, or whatever is trending on Douyin that week — it's less about learning and more about just having fun and staying connected with what everyone else is talking about. Older people tend to prefer things like health tips, cooking tutorials, news summaries, or videos about gardening and travel — content that feels genuinely useful to their daily life.
ideaNotes.textZh: 年轻人大多在看短搞笑视频、电视剧、游戏内容或那周抖音上流行的任何东西，不太是关于学习，更多是关于享乐和了解大家在谈论什么。老年人倾向于喜欢健康贴士、烹饪教程、新闻摘要或关于园艺和旅行的视频，感觉真正对他们日常生活有用的内容。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For example, my grandparents mostly watch health and cooking videos on WeChat that their friends share in group chats, while my friends and I are constantly on Douyin watching comedy clips and following whatever drama everyone is talking about that week.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，我祖父母大多看朋友在群聊中分享的微信上的健康和烹饪视频，而我和朋友们则不断在抖音上看喜剧片段，追随那周大家在谈论的任何电视剧。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, the way they watch is different too — older people tend to sit and watch something properly from start to finish, while younger people are much more likely to just scroll and jump between things without finishing anything. 另外，他们观看的方式也不同，老年人倾向于从头到尾坐下来好好看某个东西，而年轻人更有可能只是刷屏和在不同内容之间跳转而不完成任何东西。

entries.text: Are there any differences between the videos that young men and young women like to watch ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think there are some general differences, but it's not black and white — a lot depends on the individual person rather than just their gender.
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为有一些普遍的差异，但不是非黑即白的，很大程度上取决于个人而不只是性别。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Generally speaking, young men tend to watch more gaming, sports, and tech content, while young women tend to gravitate more towards lifestyle, beauty, fashion, and emotional storytelling like dramas and vlogs. But honestly these lines are getting more and more blurry — plenty of women are into gaming and plenty of men watch lifestyle content, so it's really more about personal taste than gender.
ideaNotes.textZh: 一般来说，年轻男性倾向于看更多游戏、体育和科技内容，而年轻女性倾向于更多地偏向生活方式、美妆、时尚和情感故事叙述，比如电视剧和vlog。但说实话，这些界限越来越模糊，很多女性喜欢游戏，很多男性看生活方式内容，所以真的更多是关于个人品味而非性别。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, among my own friends, the guys are usually talking about the latest game streams or sports highlights, while the girls tend to share skincare routines, travel vlogs, or drama recommendations — but there's definitely crossover, and nobody really sticks strictly to one category.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，在我自己的朋友中，男生通常在谈论最新的游戏直播或体育集锦，而女生倾向于分享护肤程序、旅行vlog或电视剧推荐，但肯定有交叉，没有人真的严格坚持一个类别。

entries.text: What makes a video go viral online ?

ideaNotes.label: 观点
ideaNotes.text: I think the main thing that makes a video go viral is that it makes people feel something strongly enough to want to share it — whether that's laughing, crying, feeling amazed, or just thinking "everyone needs to see this".
ideaNotes.textZh: 我认为让视频走红的主要原因是它让人们感到某种足够强烈的情感想要分享它，无论是笑、哭、感到惊叹，还是只是想"每个人都需要看到这个"。

ideaNotes.label: 解释
ideaNotes.text: Videos spread when people pass them on, and people only pass things on when it makes them feel something or when they think it says something about who they are — like sharing a funny video shows you have a good sense of humour, or sharing something inspiring shows your values. The content also needs to be short and easy to watch — if it's too long or slow to get to the point, most people will just scroll past before it has a chance to grab them.
ideaNotes.textZh: 当人们转发时视频会传播，人们只有在它让他们感到某种情感或他们认为它说明了他们是谁时才会转发，比如分享有趣的视频显示你有良好的幽默感，或者分享励志的东西显示你的价值观。内容还需要短且容易观看，如果太长或太慢才切入正题，大多数人会在它有机会抓住他们之前直接划过。

ideaNotes.label: 例子
ideaNotes.text: For instance, a lot of videos that go viral on Douyin are either really funny, surprisingly heartwarming, or just completely unexpected — something that makes you stop scrolling because you didn't see it coming. And once a few people share it, the algorithm picks it up and pushes it to more people, and it just snowballs from there.
ideaNotes.textZh: 例如，很多在抖音上走红的视频要么非常有趣、出乎意料地暖心，或者完全出人意料，让你停止滑动是因为你没预料到。一旦几个人分享它，算法接收它并推送给更多人，然后就像滚雪球一样。

ideaNotes.label: 延伸
ideaNotes.textZh: 可选】 And also, timing matters a lot — a video that connects to something people are already talking about or feeling at that moment has a much better chance of spreading quickly than something that comes out of nowhere with no context. 另外，时机非常重要，一个与人们已经在谈论或感受的事情相联系的视频比凭空而来没有背景的东西有更好的快速传播机会。

entries.text: Describe an advertisement with a famous person in it

paragraphs: I'd like to talk about a video/advertisement I came across while volunteering at a Su Super match. Not long ago, I came across a report on a local WeChat public account about the Su Super football league.
It's a football competition between 13 cities in Jiangsu Province, where amateur and professional players compete together. It attracted huge crowds and a lot of media coverage.
After reading about it, I was really intrigued and decided to sign up as a volunteer. On the day of the match, I got up really early — probably the earliest I had in a long time.

Volunteers had to show up really early, and I had to commute there on top of that, so I ended up waking up at around five or six in the morning. I was pretty sleepy, but once I got there and things got busy, the tiredness just disappeared.
Volunteering at a big event like this isn't something one person can do alone — you really need a team to make it work. In our volunteer team, my main job was to guide the crowd.

But at one point way more people showed up than expected and things got really crowded at the entrance. We quickly figured out a plan, split into smaller groups, and each took charge of a different area — everyone just stepped up, and it worked out pretty well.

That's when I truly understood what teamwork really means. Apart from the match itself, what really stayed with me was an ad that played on the big screen during half-time — Mbappé promoting an electrolyte drink, saying "我是姆巴佩，补水啦" in this really funny Chinese accent.

You know, Mbappé is known for being so intense and focused on the field, so seeing him say something that playful and goofy in Chinese was just so unexpected. Everyone around me just burst out laughing.
I was so curious that I actually went and bought a bottle afterwards. Pretty refreshing — maybe that's the power of a good advertisement.

After the match, the organisers arranged for all the volunteers to make Suzhou-style mooncakes together — it was coming up to Mid-Autumn Festival, a time when families come together and share mooncakes as a symbol of reunion. Suzhou mooncakes are quite different from the regular kind — the outside is made of this really crispy, layered pastry skin, with fillings like rose paste and red bean.
It was already a pretty special experience just being there as a volunteer, but making mooncakes together at the end made it feel even more memorable.
paragraphsZh: 我想说的是一个视频/广告，是我在参加苏超比赛志愿者活动时看到的。 不久前，我在本地的微信公众号上看到了一篇关于苏超足球联赛的报道。
这是江苏省13个城市之间的足球联赛，业余球员和职业球员同场竞技。 比赛吸引了大量的人群和很多媒体报道。
看完之后，我非常感兴趣，于是决定报名参加志愿者。 比赛当天，我起得非常早——可能是很长时间以来起得最早的一次。
志愿者需要很早到场，加上我还需要通勤，所以我最终在早上大概五六点就起床了。 当时挺困的，但一到现场事情忙起来之后，困意就完全消失了。
在这样的大型活动中做志愿者，不是一个人能完成的——真的需要一个团队。 在我们的志愿者团队里，我的主要工作是引导人群。
但在某个时刻，来的人比预期多得多，入口处变得非常拥挤。 我们很快制定了一个计划，分成几个小组，各自负责不同的区域——每个人都主动承担，最后顺利解决了。
就是那一刻，我真正理解了团队合作的意义。 除了比赛本身，让我印象最深的是中场休息时大屏幕上播放的一个广告——姆巴佩代言电解质水，用非常搞笑的中文口音说"我是姆巴佩，补水啦"。
要知道，姆巴佩在场上一向专注而认真，所以看到他用这么可爱、这么搞怪的方式说中文，真的太出乎意料了。 周围的人都哄堂大笑。
我太好奇了，之后真的去买了一瓶。 喝起来还挺清爽的——也许这就是一个好广告的力量。
比赛结束后，主办方安排所有志愿者一起做苏式月饼——因为那时候快到中秋节了，那是一个家人团聚、共享月饼、象征团圆的节日。 苏式月饼和普通月饼很不一样——外皮是非常酥脆、层层叠叠的酥皮，馅料有玫瑰和豆沙等口味。
光是作为志愿者参与其中就已经是一次很特别的经历了，而最后大家一起做月饼，让这次经历变得更加难忘。
